phenotype: malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy
justification: Barcia et al. (2012, Nature Genetics) first identified de novo gain-of-function KCNT1 mutations in multiple unrelated probands with malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy (EIMFS), and this has been replicated extensively in independent human cohorts, making KCNT1 the most common single-gene cause of this epilepsy syndrome. Recurrent missense variants (e.g., p.Arg428Gln, p.Ala934Thr, p.Ile760Met) have been reported across many patients, with segregation and de novo occurrence documented. Functional studies in Xenopus oocytes and mammalian cells confirm gain-of-function increases in KNa currents, and quinidine has been trialed as a targeted therapy in patients. ClinGen and GeneReviews recognize KCNT1–EIMFS as a definitive gene–disease association. Evidence is human-based, replicated, and mechanistically supported, so "Established" is overwhelmingly favored.

phenotype: malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy
justification: Barcia et al. (Nature Genetics, 2012) first identified de novo gain-of-function KCNT1 (Slack/KNa1.1) mutations in multiple unrelated probands with malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy (EIMFS), and this has been replicated extensively in independent human cohorts (e.g., McTague et al., Ohba et al., Møller et al.), with KCNT1 now recognized as the most common cause of EIMFS. Recurrent hotspot variants such as p.Arg428Gln, p.Ala934Thr, and p.Ile760Met have been repeatedly reported in patients, and electrophysiological studies confirm gain-of-function potassium channel effects consistent with the phenotype. The gene–disease relationship is curated as "Definitive" by ClinGen/OMIM (DEE14, MIM 614959) and underpins targeted quinidine therapy trials in patients. Evidence is human-based, replicated, and mechanistically supported, making Established the overwhelmingly appropriate category.

phenotype: malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy
justification: Barcia et al. (Nature Genetics, 2012) first identified de novo gain-of-function KCNT1 mutations in multiple unrelated human probands with malignant migrating partial seizures of infancy (EIMFS), and this finding has been replicated extensively in independent cohorts worldwide, with KCNT1 now recognized as the most common single cause of EIMFS (accounting for roughly half of cases in some series). Recurrent variants such as p.Arg428Gln, p.Ala934Thr, and p.Ile760Met have been reported repeatedly, and functional studies in Xenopus oocytes and mammalian cells consistently show increased KNa channel current, supporting a clear gain-of-function mechanism. Clinical validity has been curated as definitive by gene–disease validity frameworks (e.g., ClinGen/expert panels), and quinidine trials targeting the channel further underscore the causal link. The evidence base is human genetic, replicated, and mechanistically supported, so the relationship is unambiguously Established.

HAND1 is a bHLH transcription factor essential for cardiac looping and ventricular/left-ventricle development, with strong mouse knockout and functional data supporting a role in cardiogenesis (a robust "hypothesized" biological basis). Beyond animal work, there are human genetic reports: somatic HAND1 mutations identified in malformed heart tissue from hypoplastic left heart syndrome patients (Reamon-Buettner et al.), and multiple germline missense/loss-of-function variants reported in Chinese cohorts with ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot, and double-outlet right ventricle, several with transactivation assays and small-family segregation. However, many of these candidate-gene studies come from a limited number of groups, involve rare variants of uncertain significance, and have not been consistently replicated in large independent cohorts or exome/genome-wide CHD studies, so the gene–disease validity is generally regarded as limited/moderate rather than definitive. Therefore most weight falls on "Existing," with meaningful but lesser probability that curators would consider it "Established."

HAND1 is a bHLH transcription factor essential for cardiac looping, left ventricular and outflow tract development, with strong mouse knockout and conditional-deletion data supporting a cardiac developmental role (supporting at minimum a Hypothesized relationship). In humans, several candidate-gene sequencing studies report rare HAND1 variants in probands with septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, and somatic HAND1 mutations in hypoplastic left heart syndrome myocardium, often with functional assays showing reduced transactivation. However, these reports come largely from small cohorts and a limited number of groups, replication in independent large cohorts is weak, and gene–disease validity curations have generally classified HAND1 as limited/moderate rather than definitive for CHD. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" given the number of separate human reports and for "Hypothesized" if human variant evidence is judged insufficient.

HAND1 is a bHLH transcription factor essential for cardiac looping and ventricular (particularly left ventricle) morphogenesis, with strong mouse knockout and conditional-deletion evidence for cardiac malformations, giving a solid biological rationale. In humans, Reamon-Buettner et al. reported somatic HAND1 mutations in malformed cardiac tissue from patients with hypoplastic left heart and septal defects, and several Chinese candidate-gene cohorts (e.g., Yang and colleagues) have described rare germline HAND1 variants in tetralogy of Fallot, VSD, and double-outlet right ventricle with reduced transactivation in luciferase assays. These are multiple independent human reports, supporting more than a purely hypothetical link, but the evidence is largely from small candidate-gene studies with limited segregation data, incomplete replication, and questions about somatic mutation artifacts, so formal gene–disease validity is generally judged limited/moderate rather than definitive. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with meaningful probability for "Established" and a residual allowance that human variant evidence would be discounted in favor of animal/functional data alone.

ATG5 is the gene assigned to spinocerebellar ataxia, autosomal recessive 25 (OMIM 617584), based principally on Kim et al. (eLife, 2016), who identified a homozygous missense variant (E122D) in two siblings from a consanguineous family with childhood-onset cerebellar ataxia and developmental delay. The report included strong functional support (reduced autophagic flux in patient cells, complementation studies in yeast, and ataxic phenotypes in Drosophila), but the human genetic evidence rests essentially on a single family, with few if any independently reported probands since. This places the relationship most consistently in the "Existing" category (credible human genetic evidence, limited replication), consistent with a "limited/moderate" gene–disease validity classification. Some probability is retained for "Established" given the gene's formal OMIM disease assignment and possible subsequent case reports, and a smaller share for "Hypothesized" reflecting the fact that much of the causal support is model-organism and in vitro autophagy biology.

ATG5 is the designated gene for spinocerebellar ataxia, autosomal recessive 25 (SCAR25, OMIM 617584), based primarily on Kim et al. (2016, eLife), who identified a homozygous missense variant (E122D) in two affected siblings from a consanguineous family with childhood-onset ataxia and developmental delay, supported by functional autophagy assays in patient cells, yeast, and a Drosophila model. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence but derives largely from a single family, with only a small number of additional cases reported subsequently, so the evidence is suggestive rather than robustly replicated across many independent probands. The strong mechanistic backing (autophagy deficiency causing neurodegeneration, Atg5 conditional knockout mice showing cerebellar Purkinje cell degeneration) reinforces biological plausibility but is animal/in vitro and would only support "Hypothesized" on its own. Therefore most weight falls on "Existing," with meaningful probability for "Established" given the formal OMIM disease-gene designation and possible newer replications.

SCAR25 (OMIM 617584) is attributed to biallelic ATG5 variants based primarily on Kim et al. (2016, eLife), who reported a homozygous missense variant (E122D) in affected siblings from a single consanguineous family with congenital/childhood-onset cerebellar ataxia and developmental delay, supported by functional studies showing impaired ATG5–ATG12 conjugation and autophagy, plus yeast and mouse/Drosophila models. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, so "Existing" is the most fitting category. Only a small number of additional families/variants have been reported since, so replication across multiple independent probands remains limited, giving "Established" moderate but not dominant weight. Purely functional/animal autophagy-deficiency data support the biological plausibility (Hypothesized), but human variant evidence exists, making "Novel" essentially untenable.

PHKG2 encodes the testis/liver isoform of the phosphorylase kinase gamma catalytic subunit and is well established as the cause of glycogen storage disease type IXc (autosomal recessive liver phosphorylase kinase deficiency), a metabolic disorder unrelated to ciliary structure or motility. Primary ciliary dyskinesia 33 (CILD33) is attributed to biallelic variants in GAS2L2, a cytoskeletal/ciliary orientation gene, with no reported role for PHKG2. There is no known involvement of PHKG2 in axonemal assembly, dynein arm function, or mucociliary clearance, and no human genetic reports linking it to PCD phenotypes. Any co-mention would be incidental, e.g., in broad exome/panel datasets. A small residual probability is retained for speculative pathway or model-organism arguments (glycogen metabolism/energy supply in ciliated cells), but such links are not documented.

PHKG2 encodes the liver-testis isoform of the phosphorylase kinase gamma catalytic subunit, and its established human disease association is autosomal recessive glycogen storage disease type IXc, not any ciliopathy. Primary ciliary dyskinesia 33 (CILD33) is attributed to biallelic variants in GAS2L2, a cytoskeletal/ciliary gene, with no reported role for PHKG2. There is no known ciliary localization, axonemal function, or PCD animal model implicating PHKG2, and glycogen/phosphorylase kinase signaling is not a recognized mechanism for motile ciliary dysfunction. Any co-mention would most likely arise incidentally from multigene panel or exome sequencing reports rather than from a mechanistic or genetic link.

PHKG2 encodes the testis/liver isoform of the phosphorylase kinase gamma catalytic subunit and is established as the cause of glycogen storage disease type IXc (autosomal recessive liver phosphorylase kinase deficiency), a metabolic disorder unrelated to motile ciliary function. Primary ciliary dyskinesia 33 (CILD33) is attributed to biallelic variants in GAS2L2, a cytoskeletal/microtubule-associated gene affecting ciliary orientation and beat coordination. I am not aware of any human genetic study, case report, or functional work implicating PHKG2 variants in PCD, situs abnormalities, or ciliary axonemal biology. Any co-mention would be incidental, e.g., through 16p11.2 regional gene lists or broad exome datasets. A small residual probability is assigned to "hypothesized" in case of unrecognized kinase/glycogen-metabolism links to ciliary energetics, but there is no supporting literature.

SHANK3 is one of the most robustly validated autism risk genes in humans. Durand et al. (2007) first reported de novo SHANK3 mutations and deletions segregating with ASD in independent families, and haploinsufficiency of SHANK3 underlies the ASD phenotype of Phelan-McDermid (22q13.3 deletion) syndrome. Numerous large-scale human exome/genome sequencing studies (Autism Sequencing Consortium, SSC, SPARK) have repeatedly identified recurrent de novo loss-of-function SHANK3 variants at genome-wide significance, and it is classified as a high-confidence ASD gene (SFARI category 1). Supporting mouse models and synaptic functional work reinforce but are not required for the causal claim. Therefore the evidence overwhelmingly supports the "Established" category.

SHANK3 is among the most robustly validated monogenic causes of autism spectrum disorder in humans. Durand et al. (2007) first reported de novo SHANK3 mutations and deletions in ASD families, and haploinsufficiency of SHANK3 via 22q13.3 deletion (Phelan-McDermid syndrome) causes a phenotype in which ASD is present in a majority of patients. Numerous independent large-scale exome-sequencing studies (Autism Sequencing Consortium, SSC, De Rubeis et al., Satterstrom et al.) have identified recurrent de novo loss-of-function SHANK3 variants at genome-wide significance, and it is classified as a high-confidence ASD gene (SFARI category 1) with an OMIM-recognized disease association. Supporting mouse models and synaptic functional data reinforce, but are not required for, this classification. The evidence is replicated across many independent human probands and families, leaving essentially no doubt about causality.

SHANK3 is among the most firmly established monogenic causes of autism spectrum disorder in humans. Durand et al. (2007) first reported de novo SHANK3 mutations and deletions in ASD families, and this has been replicated extensively in independent cohorts, including large exome-sequencing consortia (Autism Sequencing Consortium, SSC) that list SHANK3 as a high-confidence (FDR < 0.01) ASD risk gene. Haploinsufficiency of SHANK3 via 22q13.3 deletion (Phelan–McDermid syndrome) causes a phenotype in which ASD occurs in a majority of patients, providing convergent human clinical evidence. Supporting functional and mouse-model data (Shank3 knockout mice showing social deficits and repetitive behavior) corroborate but are not needed for the human causal claim. Only minimal probability is reserved for weaker categories given the depth of replicated human genetic evidence.

SCN2A is among the highest-confidence autism risk genes, identified by recurrent de novo protein-truncating variants in multiple independent large-scale human exome sequencing studies of ASD probands (e.g., Sanders et al. 2012, Neale et al. 2012, Iossifov et al. 2014, De Rubeis et al. 2014, Satterstrom et al. 2020), with genome-wide significant excess of damaging de novo variants. It is classified as SFARI Category 1 (high confidence) and has an ASD-associated clinical phenotype spectrum including intellectual disability, epilepsy, and autism, often described as SCN2A-related neurodevelopmental disorder. Human genetic evidence is replicated across independent cohorts and supported by functional studies of channel haploinsufficiency, though mouse models supplement rather than substitute for the human data. A small residual probability is allotted to "Existing" to account for the fact that SCN2A variants typically cause a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than isolated autism.

SCN2A is among the highest-confidence autism risk genes, identified by recurrent de novo loss-of-function (protein-truncating) variants in multiple independent large-scale human exome sequencing studies of ASD probands and families (e.g., Sanders et al. 2012, Neale et al. 2012, Iossifov et al. 2014, De Rubeis et al. 2014, Satterstrom et al. 2020), with exome-wide significant statistical support. It is classified as SFARI gene score 1 ("high confidence") and is one of the genes with the highest ASD association statistics. Genotype–phenotype studies show that SCN2A protein-truncating variants preferentially associate with ASD/intellectual disability, while gain-of-function missense variants cause early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, providing a replicated human causal framework. Supporting mouse and electrophysiological models add mechanistic detail but are not needed to establish the human genetic evidence. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" only to account for debates about variable expressivity and whether ASD is a distinct outcome versus part of a broader neurodevelopmental spectrum.

SCN2A is one of the highest-confidence autism risk genes, identified through recurrent de novo loss-of-function (protein-truncating) variants in multiple independent large-scale human exome sequencing studies of ASD probands and their families (e.g., Sanders et al. 2012, Neale et al. 2012, Iossifov et al. 2014, De Rubeis et al. 2014, Satterstrom et al. 2020). It is classified as SFARI category 1 ("high confidence") and reaches genome-wide significance for ASD association in human cohorts, with replicated findings across independent probands. Clinical case series further describe SCN2A-related neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent autistic features, intellectual disability, and epilepsy. Mouse models (Scn2a haploinsufficiency) provide supporting mechanistic data, but the causal evidence is already firmly established in humans. Only a small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" to reflect that ASD in SCN2A carriers often occurs within a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than as isolated autism.

TM9SF4 (20q11.21) encodes a transmembrane 9 superfamily protein primarily characterized in the context of proton pump/V-ATPase-associated pH regulation, phagocytosis/cell cannibalism, and tumor biology (gastric cancer, melanoma), with much of the functional work in Dictyostelium, Drosophila, and cancer cell lines rather than neurodevelopment. It is not among the recognized high-confidence autism risk genes from large-scale exome and CNV studies (e.g., SFARI high-ranking genes, ASC/SPARK de novo variant analyses), and I am not aware of replicated human genetic evidence linking TM9SF4 variants to ASD. At most, it might appear incidentally within 20q11.2 copy-number variant intervals or as a low-confidence candidate in a single sequencing dataset, which would only weakly support the "Existing" category. Some plausible biological rationale exists (vesicular trafficking, phagocytosis/microglial-type functions, intracellular pH homeostasis relevant to synaptic vesicle biology), giving modest weight to "Hypothesized." Overall, the balance of evidence favors "Novel" with residual probability for hypothesized/weak associations.

TM9SF4 (20q11.21) encodes a transmembrane 9 superfamily protein studied mainly in phagocytosis, cell cannibalism in tumor cells, and pH/proton pump regulation; it has no recognized role as an autism risk gene and is not a curated SFARI gene with meaningful evidence. It lies within the 20q11.2 microdeletion interval associated with developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autistic features, so it may appear incidentally in CNV reports, but the phenotype in that region is generally attributed to ASXL1, DNMT3B, or MAPRE1 rather than TM9SF4, making any "Existing" claim weak and non-specific. Occasional single de novo or rare variants could appear in large exome sequencing datasets without statistical support or replication. Some biological plausibility exists through endosomal/lysosomal trafficking and immune-related functions relevant to neurodevelopment, which supports a modest Hypothesized weight. Overall, the pairing most likely reflects incidental co-mention, so the bulk of probability falls on Novel with secondary weight on Hypothesized.

TM9SF4 (transmembrane 9 superfamily member 4, 20q11.21) is best characterized in the context of endosomal/lysosomal trafficking, phagocytosis, cell adhesion, and pH regulation in tumor cells (e.g., melanoma cannibalism), with no well-known neurodevelopmental disease role. It is not a recognized SFARI autism gene, and I am unaware of replicated human genetic studies implicating TM9SF4 variants in autism spectrum disorder; at most it could appear incidentally in large exome/CNV datasets or within 20q11.2 rearrangements without gene-specific evidence. Some plausible biological rationale exists (vesicular trafficking, autophagy/lysosomal pathways are enriched among ASD risk genes), which supports a modest weighting for Hypothesized. Because most supporting biology derives from non-neuronal, in vitro, or cancer-cell contexts rather than human genetic association, the bulk of the probability falls on Novel, with limited weight on Existing and negligible weight on Established.

C6ORF58 (LEG1 homolog) encodes a secreted, liver/salivary-gland–enriched protein with no established neurodevelopmental function, and I am not aware of any replicated human genetic studies implicating it in autism spectrum disorder. The autism-associated gene with a similar name is C3ORF58 (DIA1, "deleted in autism 1"), which has been linked to autism through homozygous deletions and Golgi/secretory-pathway biology; C6ORF58 is frequently confused with it in the literature, but that association does not transfer. C6ORF58 may appear incidentally in large exome/CNV screens or expression datasets without meeting significance, which leaves a small chance of a single weak human report supporting "Existing." Its secreted-protein biology gives only a tenuous, non-specific rationale for "Hypothesized." Overall the evidence base strongly favors "Novel."

C6ORF58 (LEG1 homolog) encodes a poorly characterized secreted protein most highly expressed in salivary glands and liver, with no established role in neurodevelopment or synaptic biology. It does not appear on curated ASD gene lists (SFARI, high-confidence de novo variant sets) and there are no replicated human genetic studies implicating it in autism. At most, it might appear incidentally in large exome/CNV screens or as a nominal hit in an underpowered association or copy-number analysis of chromosome 6q, which would only support weak "Existing" status. Biological plausibility for a hypothesized link is limited given its peripheral expression pattern, though some tissue-expression or model-organism (zebrafish leg1) work exists that is not ASD-relevant. Therefore the evidence most likely falls in the Novel category, with modest probability spread to Existing and Hypothesized.

C6ORF58 (LEG1, "liver-enriched gene 1") encodes a secreted protein most studied in salivary gland and liver biology, with functional work largely in zebrafish models of liver development; it is not a recognized neurodevelopmental gene and does not appear in curated autism gene lists such as SFARI Gene at any meaningful confidence tier. I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies implicating C6ORF58 variants in autism spectrum disorder, so an "Established" classification is highly unlikely. It is conceivable that the gene appears incidentally as a de novo or rare variant hit in a large exome/CNV survey or as a nominal signal in an expression or GWAS dataset, which leaves modest probability for "Existing." Some probability is retained for "Hypothesized" because secreted signaling proteins with developmental roles can be argued into a plausible mechanistic narrative, but such data would be non-human/in vitro. Overall the most likely status is "Novel," with any co-mentions being incidental.

AOC3 encodes vascular adhesion protein-1 (VAP-1/SSAO), a semicarbazide-sensitive amine oxidase involved in leukocyte trafficking, endothelial/blood–brain barrier function, and metabolism of primary amines such as methylamine and benzylamine; these functions give a plausible but indirect biological rationale linked to neuroinflammation and monoamine metabolism, themes frequently invoked in autism. However, I am not aware of any replicated human genetic association, linkage, or rare-variant burden findings implicating AOC3 in Autism Spectrum Disorder, and the gene is not a recognized ASD risk gene in curated resources such as SFARI or large exome/GWAS consortia. Any appearance in autism studies would most likely be incidental (e.g., within a large CNV at 17q21 or a differential-expression list) rather than evidence of causation. Therefore most weight falls on Novel, with substantial residual probability for Hypothesized given the pathway-level plausibility, a small allowance for a single limited human association or biomarker report (Existing), and essentially none for Established.

AOC3 encodes vascular adhesion protein-1 (VAP-1/SSAO), a copper-containing amine oxidase involved in leukocyte adhesion, amine (methylamine, aminoacetone) catabolism, and generation of hydrogen peroxide and aldehydes; these roles in neuroinflammation and oxidative stress give a plausible but indirect biological rationale that could support a "hypothesized" link. I am not aware of any replicated human genetic studies implicating AOC3 variants in autism spectrum disorder, and the gene is not a recognized ASD risk gene in curated resources such as SFARI. At most, AOC3 might appear incidentally in large exome/CNV datasets or in biomarker studies of amine oxidase activity, which would not constitute solid genetic evidence. Therefore the probability mass falls mainly on "novel," with a substantial share for "hypothesized" given the mechanistic relevance of neuroinflammation and oxidative stress in ASD, and only small weight on "existing" or "established."

AOC3 (VAP-1/SSAO) is best characterized in vascular adhesion, inflammation, and metabolism of primary amines (methylamine, benzylamine), with its main disease literature in diabetes, obesity, hepatic and cardiovascular inflammation rather than neurodevelopment. I am not aware of any replicated human genetic study implicating AOC3 variants in autism spectrum disorder, and it does not appear among established ASD risk genes from large exome/CNV consortia (SFARI high-confidence tiers). A plausible biological rationale exists—amine oxidase activity intersects with monoamine/amine metabolism, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, all invoked in ASD pathophysiology—so a hypothesized link is defensible, and related amine oxidase family members (e.g., MAOA/B, AOC1/DAO histamine metabolism) have been studied in ASD. Occasional reports of altered plasma SSAO/VAP-1 activity or incidental rare-variant co-mentions in sequencing studies could support a weak "Existing" claim, but such evidence would be non-specific and unreplicated. Therefore, probability mass concentrates on Novel and Hypothesized, with limited weight to Existing and essentially none to Established.

AMY2B encodes pancreatic alpha-amylase 2B within the highly copy-number-variable amylase cluster at 1p21.1, a region occasionally reported in CNV surveys of neurodevelopmental disorders, so incidental co-mention in autism CNV datasets is plausible but not evidence of causation. There is no established gene–disease relationship: AMY2B is not a recognized autism gene in curated resources (e.g., SFARI, ClinGen), and no replicated rare-variant or family-based studies implicate it. Weak indirect links exist through carbohydrate digestion/gastrointestinal dysfunction in autism (studies of intestinal disaccharidase and carbohydrate-metabolism gene expression, and salivary/pancreatic amylase copy number), which could support a hypothesized or borderline "existing" classification if a human association study is counted. Overall the evidence is best characterized as absent-to-speculative, with most weight on Novel and Hypothesized and a modest allowance for a single limited human report.

AMY2B encodes pancreatic alpha-amylase within the highly copy-number-variable amylase cluster at 1p21.1, a locus best studied in relation to dietary starch adaptation, obesity and metabolic traits rather than neurodevelopment. I am not aware of any replicated or well-powered human genetic study implicating AMY2B point variants or CNVs as a cause of Autism Spectrum Disorder, so an "Established" designation is very unlikely. A weak "Existing" possibility remains because the amylase region is CNV-rich and may appear incidentally in large ASD microarray/CNV or exome datasets, and because impaired carbohydrate digestion and gut dysfunction have been reported in ASD cohorts, which could motivate candidate-gene mention. Biologically, a hypothesized link could be argued via gut carbohydrate maldigestion, microbiome alterations and the gut–brain axis, but such reasoning is indirect and not gene-specific. Overall the evidence base is most consistent with incidental co-mention (Novel) with some residual probability of hypothesis-level or limited associative claims.

AMY2B encodes pancreatic amylase and lies within the 1p21.1 amylase gene cluster, a highly copy-number-variable region; some CNV surveys in neurodevelopmental disorder/autism cohorts have reported deletions or duplications spanning this interval, but such calls are typically incidental, common in controls, and not gene-specific to AMY2B, so the evidence is far from establishing causation. AMY2B is not a recognized ASD risk gene in curated resources (e.g., SFARI) and there are no replicated rare-variant or exome findings implicating it. Biologically, interest in carbohydrate digestion and GI dysfunction in autism (studies of intestinal disaccharidases and amylase activity) provides a plausible but indirect mechanistic rationale, supporting a modest "hypothesized" weight. Overall the most likely status is that AMY2B–ASD is essentially a co-mention/CNV-region artifact, with a smaller possibility that a single limited human association report exists.

TUBA4A was identified as an ALS gene (ALS22, OMIM 616208) by Smith et al. (Neuron, 2014), who found rare damaging variants in multiple unrelated familial ALS probands through exome sequencing of large ALS cohorts, with segregation in some families and functional evidence of destabilized microtubule networks. Independent follow-up screens in Italian, Belgian, Chinese, and other ALS/FTD cohorts have reported additional rare TUBA4A variants, supporting replication in humans, and the gene is included in clinical ALS gene panels. However, penetrance is incomplete, some variants are of uncertain significance, and a few cohort studies failed to find a significant burden, so the causal role is somewhat less definitive than for SOD1, C9orf72, or TARDBP. Therefore the evidence is best split between Established and Existing, with only a small residual for purely biological/hypothesized support and essentially none for Novel.

TUBA4A was identified by Smith et al. (2014, Neuron) through exome sequencing of familial ALS cohorts, with multiple rare variants found in independent probands and functional evidence that mutant tubulin destabilizes the microtubule network; this led to the OMIM designation ALS22. Subsequent screening studies in European, Chinese, and other ALS/FTD cohorts have reported additional rare TUBA4A variants, but many lack strong segregation data, some variants appear in controls, and the gene has been curated by some expert panels (e.g., ClinGen ALS curation efforts) at a limited/moderate rather than definitive level. Thus human genetic evidence clearly exists and is replicated at the variant-detection level, but causality is not as firmly established as for SOD1, FUS, TARDBP, or C9orf72. Points are therefore split mainly between Established and Existing, with a small allowance for the possibility that much of the supporting evidence is functional/in vitro rather than definitive human genetics.

TUBA4A was identified by Smith et al. (2014, Neuron) through exome sequencing of familial ALS cohorts, with rare missense/truncating variants that destabilize the microtubule network in functional assays, and OMIM assigns ALS22 (#616208) to this gene. Several subsequent human screening studies (e.g., Italian, Chinese, and other European ALS cohorts) reported additional rare TUBA4A variants, sometimes in ALS-FTD patients, supporting a human genetic contribution. However, evidence for causality is tempered by incomplete segregation data, variants of uncertain significance, and some negative replication cohorts, and gene–disease validity curations have generally rated TUBA4A below "definitive" (limited/moderate). Therefore the strongest weight lies between "Existing" and "Established," with modest residual probability for "Hypothesized" given the heavy reliance on in vitro microtubule functional data.

ATP5MK (formerly USMG5/ATP5MD/DAPIT) encodes a small subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthase (complex V) required for its assembly and dimerization, making it biologically highly relevant to oxidative phosphorylation disorders. In humans, an Ashkenazi Jewish founder splice variant (c.87+1G>C) in USMG5/ATP5MK was reported (Barca et al., 2018) in several patients from unrelated families with infantile-onset mitochondrial disease and isolated ATP synthase deficiency, with functional validation showing reduced complex V assembly and rescue by cDNA. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence in more than one proband, and the gene is now included in curated mitochondrial disease gene panels, supporting an Established or at least strong Existing classification. However, replication beyond the original founder-variant cohort and a few subsequent case reports remains relatively limited, so points are split between Established and Existing, with a smaller share for Hypothesized based on the supporting cellular/functional data alone.

ATP5MK (formerly USMG5/ATP5MD, encoding the DAPIT subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthase) has a well-documented human disease association: an Ashkenazi Jewish founder splice variant (c.87+1G>C) was reported in multiple unrelated children with Leigh syndrome and isolated complex V deficiency, with functional confirmation of reduced ATP synthase assembly in patient cells. Because several independent probands from more than one family were described and the biochemical mechanism is directly relevant to OXPHOS, the evidence leans toward Established. However, the bulk of evidence derives from essentially one founder population/report with limited subsequent independent replication, so a substantial probability remains for Existing (limited but credible human evidence). Purely biological/model-based classification (Hypothesized) is unlikely given the documented patient variants, and Novel is essentially excluded.

ATP5MK (also known as ATP5MD/USMG5/DAPIT) encodes a small subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthase (complex V), making it biologically central to oxidative phosphorylation. A human genetic study (Barca et al., Hum Mol Genet, 2018) identified an Ashkenazi Jewish founder splice variant (c.87+1G>C) in unrelated patients with Leigh syndrome, with functional evidence of reduced ATP synthase content and impaired OXPHOS in patient-derived cells — direct human causal evidence for mitochondrial disease. Because the evidence largely stems from a single founder variant reported in a limited number of probands, with relatively few independent replications, the gene sits at the boundary between "Existing" and "Established"; it is nonetheless included on many diagnostic mitochondrial disease panels. Purely hypothetical or novel classifications are unlikely given the demonstrated human variants and functional validation.

Biallelic TMEM63C variants were reported in patients with hereditary spastic paraplegia (Yahia et al., Brain 2021), describing a small number of consanguineous families with homozygous variants, supported by functional work showing mitochondrial morphology/ER–mitochondria contact defects; this led to the OMIM designation SPG87 (autosomal recessive). The human genetic evidence is therefore real but limited to few probands/families, with relatively sparse independent replication in the literature to date, which fits "Existing" more than fully "Established." Some weight goes to Established because an OMIM phenotype number was assigned and more than one family was described, implying segregation in independent kindreds. A smaller share is retained for Hypothesized, reflecting that much of the supporting mechanistic evidence (mitochondrial/podocyte functional assays, model systems) is non-human. Novel is very unlikely given the explicit gene–disease naming.

TMEM63C is the gene assigned to autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia 87 in OMIM, based principally on a Brain (2022) report (Yahia, Elsayed, and colleagues) describing biallelic TMEM63C variants in consanguineous families with hereditary spastic paraplegia, supported by functional work showing mitochondrial/ER-contact and morphology defects. The human genetic evidence therefore exists and comes from more than a single individual, but the number of independent probands/families reported is small and replication in additional independent cohorts has been limited, so gene–disease validity is typically curated as moderate/limited rather than definitive. Some of the supporting data derive from cellular and model-organism experiments, which alone would only support a hypothesized relationship. Accordingly, most weight falls between "Existing" and "Established," with little probability that the relationship is merely biological or incidental.

TMEM63C is the gene assigned to autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia 87 (SPG87) in OMIM, based primarily on a Brain (2022) report describing biallelic TMEM63C variants in a small number of consanguineous/unrelated families with childhood-onset spastic paraplegia, supported by functional work showing mitochondrial morphology defects and prior podocyte/nephrotic-related biology. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, so Novel is very unlikely and Hypothesized alone understates the data. However, the number of independent probands and replicating publications appears limited, so the evidence sits between "Existing" and "Established," with the balance favoring Existing pending broader independent replication. Some weight remains on Established because multiple families and complementary functional data were presented in the original human study.

BLVRA encodes biliverdin reductase A, the enzyme that converts biliverdin to bilirubin, so loss of function directly explains accumulation of green pigment (hyperbiliverdinemia/"green jaundice"). Human genetic evidence exists: Gäfvels et al. (2009) described a patient with liver cirrhosis and a novel BLVRA mutation with hyperbiliverdinaemia, and Nytofte et al. (2011) reported a homozygous nonsense BLVRA variant (c.214C>A) in a family with green jaundice during cholestatic episodes, with functional confirmation of absent enzyme activity. OMIM lists hyperbiliverdinemia (MIM 614156) as a BLVRA-related phenotype, indicating curated acceptance. The evidence comes from at least two independent probands/families with supportive functional data, favoring "Established," though the total number of reported cases is small and typically requires concomitant cholestasis, leaving meaningful probability for "Existing."

BLVRA encodes biliverdin reductase A, the enzyme that converts biliverdin to bilirubin, so loss of function directly and mechanistically explains green jaundice/hyperbiliverdinemia. Human genetic evidence exists: Nytofte et al. (J Med Genet, 2011) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation (c.214C>A) in BLVRA in Inuit patients with green jaundice and cholestatic liver disease, with supporting enzymatic/functional data, and OMIM lists Hyperbiliverdinemia (MIM 614156) as an autosomal recessive BLVRA-related disorder. A few additional case reports of BLVRA variants in patients with green jaundice have since appeared, but the total number of independent probands/families remains small, so replication is limited rather than extensive. This supports a strong causal assignment (Established) with meaningful residual probability that curators would classify the evidence as limited/moderate (Existing); purely hypothetical or novel classifications are very unlikely given the direct human genetic and biochemical data.

Hyperbiliverdinemia ("green jaundice") is a recognized Mendelian phenotype attributed to biallelic BLVRA mutations, and OMIM lists hyperbiliverdinemia (MIM 614156) with BLVRA as the causative gene. Human evidence includes at least two independent reports: a patient with a novel BLVRA mutation and liver cirrhosis presenting with green jaundice (Gäfvels et al., Liver Int 2009) and a homozygous nonsense variant (c.214C>A) in an Inuit family causing biliverdin accumulation during cholestatic episodes (Nytofte et al., J Med Genet 2011), with supporting enzymatic/functional data showing loss of biliverdin reductase activity. The mechanism is biologically direct—loss of biliverdin reductase A prevents conversion of biliverdin to bilirubin, causing biliverdin accumulation, often unmasked by cholestasis. Points remain in "Existing" because the total number of independent probands is very small and penetrance appears conditional on concurrent liver disease, so some may judge the evidence limited rather than definitively replicated.

ETS1 lies at 11q24.3 within the Jacobsen syndrome (11q terminal deletion) critical region, and human deletion-mapping studies have repeatedly nominated ETS1 as the principal candidate for the congenital heart defects (notably hypoplastic left heart syndrome and ventricular septal defects) seen in these patients, including rare cases with small deletions or translocations disrupting ETS1. Supporting functional work is largely non-human (Ets1-null mice show VSDs and abnormal ventricular morphology; Xenopus/neural crest studies), which pushes some weight to Hypothesized. A few candidate-gene sequencing studies have reported rare ETS1 variants in CHD cohorts, but replication in independent probands with clear segregation is limited, so full "Established" status is not warranted. The overall picture is a credible but not definitive human genetic association, best captured by "Existing" with substantial residual probability on "Hypothesized."

ETS1 lies at 11q24.3 within the Jacobsen syndrome (11q terminal deletion) critical region for congenital heart defects, and human deletion-mapping studies of patients with hypoplastic left heart and other defects have implicated ETS1 as a leading candidate gene, with a few reports of small deletions or rare/de novo variants in CHD probands. However, much of the strongest mechanistic support comes from non-human data: Ets1-null mice display ventricular septal defects and abnormal ventricular morphology, and neural crest/endocardial cushion studies support a developmental role. Because the human evidence is largely contiguous-gene-deletion based rather than demonstrating single-gene causation in multiple independent probands, "Established" is unlikely, while "Existing" is the best fit for the deletion and candidate-variant reports. A substantial share of probability remains on "Hypothesized," since a strict reviewer could judge the direct human variant-level evidence insufficient and count mainly the mouse/functional data. "Novel" is essentially excluded given the well-documented biological and positional link.

ETS1 lies at 11q24.3 within the distal 11q (Jacobsen syndrome) deletion region, and human deletion-mapping studies of patients with 11q terminal deletions have repeatedly implicated ETS1 as the principal candidate gene for the associated congenital heart defects (notably hypoplastic left heart and ventricular septal defects), which constitutes credible but non-definitive human genetic evidence based largely on contiguous-gene deletions rather than isolated point mutations. Supporting functional data come chiefly from mouse models, where Ets1 knockout on certain backgrounds produces ventricular septal defects and abnormal ventricular morphology, plus roles in neural crest and endocardial cushion development—these support the "hypothesized" tier since they are non-human. Rare de novo or inherited ETS1 sequence variants have been sporadically reported in CHD cohorts, but replication across independent probands with clear segregation is lacking, so an "Established" designation is not well supported. Overall the weight of evidence sits between "Existing" (human deletion/association data) and "Hypothesized" (strong developmental biology and animal models).

RBBP5 encodes a core subunit of the WRAD module (WDR5–RBBP5–ASH2L–DPY30) of the KMT2/COMPASS histone H3K4 methyltransferase complexes, a pathway heavily implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders (KMT2A/Wiedemann–Steiner, KMT2D/Kabuki, KDM6A, and de novo WDR5 variants), providing strong biological plausibility. Beyond pathway reasoning, I recall a human genetics report (circa 2023, e.g., AJHG/Genetics in Medicine) describing several unrelated individuals with de novo heterozygous RBBP5 variants presenting with developmental delay/intellectual disability, seizures, microcephaly and dysmorphism, supported by functional assays. Because this evidence appears to derive largely from a single multi-proband cohort with limited independent replication, the relationship sits between "Existing" and "Established," with most weight on those two categories. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" if the human variant evidence is judged too preliminary, and minimal probability for "Novel."

RBBP5 encodes a core subunit of the WRAD module (WDR5–RBBP5–ASH2L–DPY30) of the KMT2/COMPASS H3K4 methyltransferase complexes, a pathway in which multiple members (KMT2A, KMT2D, KMT2E, WDR5, DPY30) are well-established neurodevelopmental disorder genes, giving strong biological priors. Beyond this, I recall a recent cohort report (circa 2023) describing several unrelated individuals with de novo, likely loss-of-function/missense RBBP5 variants presenting with developmental delay/intellectual disability, seizures, microcephaly and dysmorphism, supported by model-organism (Drosophila) functional assays. That constitutes credible human genetic evidence, but replication across multiple independent clinical publications is limited, so the case sits between "Existing" and newly "Established." Some residual probability remains that my recollection conflates RBBP5 with the better-documented WDR5/ASH2L reports, in which case only pathway/functional (hypothesized) evidence would apply.

RBBP5 encodes a core subunit of the WRAD module (WDR5–RBBP5–ASH2L–DPY30) of the KMT2/COMPASS histone H3K4 methyltransferase complexes, whose other components (KMT2A, KMT2D, KMT2C, WDR5, DPY30, ASH2L) are well-established causes of syndromic intellectual disability and developmental disorders, giving a very strong biological rationale. Beyond this pathway logic, I recall recent human genetics reports (approximately 2023) describing de novo/heterozygous RBBP5 variants in small cohorts of individuals with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, microcephaly and dysmorphism, together with functional support, which would qualify as at least "Existing" and arguably approaching "Established." However, because the number of independent probands and replication across laboratories appears limited and recent, definitive "Established" status is uncertain. Some weight remains on "Hypothesized" in case the human variant evidence is sparser than I recall and the link rests mainly on complex membership and model-organism data. "Novel" is very unlikely given the direct COMPASS-related biology.

PRDX3 (mitochondrial peroxiredoxin 3) was linked to autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia (SCAR32, OMIM 619862) by Rebelo et al. (Brain, 2021), who reported biallelic loss-of-function variants in several unrelated families with early-onset ataxia, supported by functional evidence of impaired mitochondrial peroxide detoxification and patient fibroblast studies. Additional case reports and diagnostic exome/genome cohorts have since described further probands, supporting replication in humans. This places the association close to "Established," although the total number of independent probands remains modest and some curation efforts might rate the evidence as moderate rather than definitive, so meaningful probability remains on "Existing." Purely hypothesized or novel status is very unlikely given direct human genetic evidence.

PRDX3 (mitochondrial peroxiredoxin 3) was linked to autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia (SCAR32, OMIM 619862) by Rebelo et al. (Brain, 2021), who reported biallelic loss-of-function variants in several unrelated families with cerebellar atrophy and ataxia, supported by functional evidence of increased mitochondrial oxidative stress and a zebrafish/knockdown model. This constitutes human genetic evidence in multiple independent probands, favoring "Established," and the association has been curated into OMIM and gene panels. However, replication beyond the original report is relatively limited, with only scattered subsequent case reports, so some probability remains for "Existing" (limited/moderate evidence). Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are unlikely given the documented human variant data.

PRDX3 (mitochondrial peroxiredoxin 3) was reported by Rehman and colleagues (Brain, 2022) as the cause of a novel autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia, with biallelic loss-of-function/missense variants identified in several unrelated consanguineous families presenting with progressive ataxia and cerebellar atrophy; OMIM subsequently designated SCAR32 (MIM 619862). The report included multiple independent probands plus functional support (reduced protein, increased oxidative stress, zebrafish/knockdown models), satisfying criteria for an established gene–disease relationship. Some residual uncertainty remains because independent replication beyond the original multi-family report is still relatively limited, so a portion of probability is assigned to "Existing." Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are inconsistent with the published human genetic data.

phenotype: cortical dysplasia, complex, with other brain malformations 12
justification: CAMSAP1 encodes a microtubule minus-end–binding protein essential for neuronal migration, and biallelic loss-of-function variants were reported in a 2022 American Journal of Human Genetics study (Khalaf-Nazzal, Fasham, et al.) describing multiple unrelated consanguineous families with a clinically recognizable neuronal migration disorder featuring lissencephaly/pachygyria, brainstem and cerebellar anomalies, microcephaly, and epilepsy. This multi-family human genetic evidence, supported by functional and model-organism data, led to the OMIM designation of CDCBM12 for CAMSAP1. Because the causal evidence derives from several independent human probands/families with segregation and supporting functional work, the relationship is best classified as Established. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" given that replication beyond the original cohort report is still relatively limited.

phenotype: cortical dysplasia, complex, with other brain malformations 12
justification: CAMSAP1 is the gene assigned to CDCBM12 in OMIM, based on a 2022 American Journal of Human Genetics report (Khalaf-Nazzal et al.) describing bi-allelic loss-of-function CAMSAP1 variants in multiple unrelated consanguineous families with a clinically recognizable neuronal migration disorder (lissencephaly/pachygyria with brainstem and cerebellar anomalies, microcephaly, and early lethality). The evidence includes several independent probands/families with segregation, supported by functional work showing CAMSAP1's role in non-centrosomal microtubule minus-end stabilization and neuronal migration, plus mouse/knockdown data. Because multiple independent human families were reported in a single robust study, the association is generally regarded as established, though replication is still relatively limited, leaving some probability on "Existing."

The presence of several independent probands/families with segregating truncating variants, supported by functional and model-organism data (Camsap1 mutant mice showing cortical migration defects), argues for an established gene–disease relationship. ASPRV1 encodes SASPase, an aspartic protease essential for profilaggrin/filaggrin processing in the stratum corneum, and Asprv1-null mice show dry, scaly skin — providing strong biological plausibility. Beyond animal data, heterozygous ASPRV1 missense variants (notably a recurrent change affecting the protease) were reported in humans with autosomal dominant lamellar/congenital ichthyosis in multiple independent families (Boyden et al., J Invest Dermatol, 2020), and the gene–phenotype pair is curated in OMIM as a dominant ichthyosis. Because the initial evidence came largely from one comprehensive multi-family study with subsequent case reports, some uncertainty remains about the breadth of independent replication, so a portion of probability is retained for "Existing." Minimal weight is given to Hypothesized or Novel since direct human variant evidence exists.

ASPRV1 (SASPase) encodes a skin aspartic protease that processes profilaggrin/filaggrin, and Asprv1-null mice show dry, scaly skin with impaired filaggrin processing, providing strong mechanistic support. In humans, Boyden et al. (Am J Hum Genet, 2020) reported recurrent heterozygous ASPRV1 missense variants (e.g., affecting the p.Val235/adjacent residues) segregating in multiple independent families with autosomal dominant lamellar ichthyosis, and additional cases have since been described, with a corresponding OMIM phenotype entry (ADLI). This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence in independent probands with a plausible dominant-negative/gain-of-function mechanism, meeting the criteria for Established. A small residual probability is assigned to Existing in case one considers the number of independent reports still limited, and minimal weight to Hypothesized or Novel.

ASPRV1 encodes SASPase (skin aspartic protease), which processes profilaggrin/filaggrin during cornification, and Asprv1-null mice show dry, scaly skin with impaired filaggrin processing—providing strong biological plausibility. More importantly, Boyden, Choate and colleagues (Am J Hum Genet, 2020) reported heterozygous missense variants in ASPRV1 in multiple unrelated kindreds/probands with autosomal dominant lamellar ichthyosis, establishing a human gene–disease link now recorded in OMIM. Because the evidence comes primarily from a single (though multi-family, segregating, mechanistically supported) human study with limited independent replication, the classification sits between Established and Existing, with most weight on Established. Purely hypothesized or novel designations are unlikely given the direct human variant evidence.

UBR5 (EDD/HYD) encodes a HECT-domain E3 ubiquitin ligase of the N-recognin family, and related family members (UBR1 in Johanson-Blizzard syndrome, UBR7 in Li-Campeau syndrome) cause well-defined neurodevelopmental phenotypes, making the biology directly relevant. UBR5 is extremely loss-of-function intolerant (pLI ~1) and has appeared as a candidate/de novo variant-harboring gene in large exome sequencing studies of autism and developmental disorders, giving credible but limited human genetic support. To my knowledge there is no large, replicated multi-proband cohort definitively establishing a UBR5-related Mendelian neurodevelopmental syndrome with consistent phenotype, so "Established" is less likely, though recent case series may exist. Substantial supporting evidence is functional/model-based (ubiquitin-proteasome regulation, neuronal proteostasis, embryonic lethality in Ubr5-null mice), which would place weight in "Hypothesized" if human variant evidence is weaker than recalled. Very little chance the pairing is purely incidental.

UBR5 encodes a HECT-type E3 ubiquitin ligase (EDD/HYD) that is extremely intolerant to loss-of-function (pLI ~1) and is broadly expressed in the developing brain, making it a strong biological candidate; several related UBR-family genes (UBR1 in Johanson-Blizzard syndrome, UBR7 in a dysmorphic neurodevelopmental syndrome, and UBE3A/UBE3B) are established NDD genes, and UBR5 physically partners with UBR7. UBR5 has appeared as a candidate/de novo variant gene in large-scale autism and developmental disorder exome cohorts, which supports at least limited human genetic evidence, but I am not aware of a definitive, replicated multi-proband clinical series firmly establishing a UBR5-related NDD syndrome. Much of the supporting data remains functional (ubiquitin–proteasome regulation, DNA damage response, Wnt/β-catenin and neuronal signaling) or from model systems, which argues for weight on "Hypothesized." Therefore the probability mass is split mainly between limited human association ("Existing") and biology-driven plausibility ("Hypothesized"), with a small allowance for an emerging established gene–disease relationship I may be underweighting.

UBR5 (EDD/HYD) encodes a HECT-type E3 ubiquitin ligase of the N-end rule (UBR) family; other family members (UBR1 in Johanson-Blizzard syndrome, UBR7 in Li-Campeau syndrome) are established neurodevelopmental disease genes, and UBR5 is highly loss-of-function intolerant (pLI ~1), giving strong prior biological plausibility. De novo and rare variants in UBR5 have been reported in large-scale exome/genome sequencing cohorts of developmental disorders and autism (e.g., DDD-type and autism sequencing consortium datasets), and there are recent reports proposing UBR5 as a candidate NDD gene, which supports at least "Existing" evidence in humans. However, I am not confident that a well-powered, replicated case series across multiple independent probands with functional confirmation has definitively established causality, so full "Established" status is uncertain. Considerable weight also remains on "Hypothesized," since much of the supporting data is mechanistic (ubiquitin–proteasome regulation of neuronal development, mouse/in vitro models) rather than definitive human genetic evidence. "Novel" is unlikely given the gene's constraint and repeated co-occurrence in NDD variant datasets.

CDH11 is the OMIM-designated gene for Teebi hypertelorism syndrome 2 (MIM 619736), with heterozygous (largely de novo, often truncating/missense) variants reported in multiple unrelated probands with hypertelorism, facial dysmorphism, digital and genital anomalies. Biallelic CDH11 loss-of-function is separately established in Elsahy-Waters syndrome, supporting the gene's role in craniofacial morphogenesis and providing allelic-series support. Functional data (cadherin-11 in neural crest and craniofacial development, Cdh11 mouse models) reinforce biological plausibility. Because the human evidence rests on a relatively small number of reports from one or two cohorts, a nontrivial share of probability remains on "Existing" rather than fully replicated "Established."

Teebi hypertelorism syndrome 2 (OMIM 619736) is specifically catalogued as being caused by heterozygous (monoallelic) variants in CDH11, distinct from Teebi hypertelorism syndrome 1 (SPECC1L). Human genetic studies have described multiple unrelated probands with de novo truncating CDH11 variants (largely clustered in terminal exons, likely escaping nonsense-mediated decay) presenting with hypertelorism, facial dysmorphism, and related anomalies; CDH11 biallelic loss-of-function separately causes Elsahy-Waters syndrome, supporting a gene–craniofacial developmental role. The cadherin-11 biology in neural crest and craniofacial morphogenesis, plus mouse models, further corroborates causality. Because the OMIM entry and defining publications are relatively recent with a modest number of independent families, some probability remains on "Existing" rather than fully replicated "Established."

CDH11 is the recognized gene for Teebi hypertelorism syndrome 2 (OMIM 619736), an autosomal dominant condition; heterozygous (largely de novo, often missense in the cadherin extracellular domains) CDH11 variants have been reported in multiple unrelated probands with hypertelorism, broad/prominent forehead, dysmorphic features and digital anomalies. Independently, biallelic loss-of-function CDH11 variants cause Elsahy-Waters syndrome, supporting a genuine human developmental role for this cadherin in craniofacial morphogenesis, consistent with its expression in neural crest and craniofacial mesenchyme and mouse model data. Because the human genetic evidence involves several independent patients and has been curated into OMIM as a distinct disease entity, "Established" is the most probable category. Some residual probability is given to "Existing," since the cohort sizes are modest and replication across independent groups is comparatively recent and limited. Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are unlikely given the direct human variant evidence.

SEPHS1 encodes selenophosphate synthetase 1, essential for selenoprotein biosynthesis and redox homeostasis, a pathway already linked to neurological disease (e.g., SEPSECS in pontocerebellar hypoplasia, SELENOP/SEPN1 disorders), providing strong biological plausibility. I recall at least one recent clinical genetics report (circa 2023) describing rare biallelic/de novo SEPHS1 variants in individuals with global developmental delay, hypotonia, growth impairment and dysmorphism, supported by functional work in zebrafish and cell models; this constitutes credible human genetic evidence but likely from a single cohort publication with a limited number of probands. Because replication across multiple independent clinical studies appears limited, "Existing" is the most probable classification, with meaningful probability that the gene–disease relationship has since reached "Established"/moderate–definitive curation if additional families were reported. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" if the human evidence is weaker than I recall and the case rests mainly on pathway and animal-model data, and only minimal weight for "Novel."

SEPHS1 encodes selenophosphate synthetase 1, essential for selenoprotein biosynthesis, a pathway already implicated in neurodevelopmental disease (e.g., SEPSECS in pontocerebellar hypoplasia, SELENOI in complex spastic paraplegia/ID), and Sephs1 loss is embryonic lethal in mice with redox/developmental defects — providing a strong biological rationale that at minimum supports "Hypothesized." I recall recent human reports (GeneMatcher-style cohorts, ~2022–2024) describing rare de novo/biallelic SEPHS1 variants in individuals with developmental delay, hypotonia, and dysmorphism, which would place the evidence in the "Existing" range. However, I am not confident that these findings have been independently replicated across multiple unrelated cohorts with functional confirmation sufficient for "Established," and SEPHS1 is not a long-standing entry in curated NDD gene panels. Therefore most weight goes to Existing, with meaningful probability on Hypothesized (if the main supporting data are murine/in vitro) and a smaller share on Established; Novel is unlikely given the clear pathway relevance.

SEPHS1 encodes selenophosphate synthetase 1, essential for selenoprotein biosynthesis, a pathway already implicated in neurological disease (e.g., SEPSECS in pontocerebellar hypoplasia, SELENOI in spastic paraplegia/neurodevelopmental disorder). I recall a recent (circa 2023) report of bi-allelic SEPHS1 variants in patients with a neurodevelopmental phenotype including developmental delay, hypotonia, and dysmorphism, supported by functional studies showing impaired selenoprotein synthesis; if accurate, this places the gene at least in the "Existing" tier and possibly "Established" if several independent families were described. However, I am not confident that independent replication cohorts exist, so definitive causal status is uncertain. Strong supporting biology (embryonic lethality of Sephs1 knockout mice, conditional neural knockout phenotypes, Drosophila neurodevelopmental data) would in any case justify at minimum a "Hypothesized" relationship. Novelty is very unlikely given the clear pathway relevance.

FXYD2 encodes the γ-subunit of the Na+/K+-ATPase, and Meij et al. (Nature Genetics, 2000) identified a heterozygous p.Gly41Arg mutation segregating in a large Dutch family with isolated dominant hypomagnesemia with hypocalciuria (HOMG2/renal hypomagnesemia 2), with functional studies showing a dominant-negative effect on routing of the Na,K-ATPase. A second, independent Belgian family carrying the identical recurrent p.Gly41Arg variant was subsequently reported (de Baaij et al., NDT 2015), providing human replication in an unrelated proband. This supports an established causal relationship, and OMIM assigns HOMG2 to FXYD2. However, the evidence base is narrow—essentially one recurrent missense variant in two families—so some probability remains for the "Existing" (limited but credible) classification, and little for purely hypothesized or novel.

FXYD2 encodes the γ-subunit of the Na+/K+-ATPase, and Meij et al. A second, independent family carrying the identical G41R variant was later reported (de Baaij et al.), providing human replication, and OMIM lists FXYD2 as the cause of renal hypomagnesemia 2, autosomal dominant. However, the human evidence is essentially restricted to a single recurrent variant in a small number of kindreds, which is why some curation efforts would rate the gene–disease validity as moderate rather than definitive. Therefore most weight goes to Established, with substantial residual weight on Existing; purely biological/animal-only (Hypothesized) or absent (Novel) evidence categories are unlikely given the documented human segregation data.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with speech delay and variable ocular anomalies
justification: THUMPD1 encodes the adaptor protein for NAT10-mediated N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modification of tRNA, and bi-allelic loss-of-function/missense variants were reported by Broly et al. (Am J Hum Genet, 2022) in a cohort of over a dozen affected individuals from multiple unrelated, consanguineous and non-consanguineous families with a syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype featuring developmental delay, prominent speech delay, hypotonia, and variable ocular anomalies (e.g., coloboma, cataract). The report combined human genetic segregation data with functional evidence of reduced tRNA ac4C levels in patient cells, and the phenotype has been assigned an OMIM entry, supporting a clear causal role. Because the evidence largely derives from one multi-family publication with limited independent replication so far, some probability remains on "Existing." Purely hypothesized or novel status is very unlikely given the direct human variant evidence.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and language delay, ocular defects, and brain abnormalities
justification: INTS11 (CPSF3L), encoding the catalytic subunit of the Integrator complex, was reported by Tepe et al. (American Journal of Human Genetics, 2023) in a cohort of ~15 affected individuals from ~10 unrelated families with bi-allelic variants causing global developmental delay, motor and language delay, ocular anomalies, and brain MRI abnormalities, corresponding to the OMIM entry for this disorder. The evidence includes multiple independent human probands/families with segregation data, supported by functional work in Drosophila and patient-derived cells demonstrating loss of Integrator cleavage activity. This multi-family human genetic evidence with orthogonal functional support meets the threshold for an established gene–disease relationship, though the bulk of the human evidence derives from a single large collaborative publication, leaving some probability for a "limited/Existing" classification if additional independent replication is considered lacking.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and language delay, ocular defects, and brain abnormalities
justification: INTS11 (CPSF3L), a catalytic subunit of the Integrator complex, was reported in a 2023 American Journal of Human Genetics study (Tepe et al.) describing ~15 affected individuals from ~10 unrelated families with biallelic INTS11 variants presenting with global developmental delay, motor and language delay, hypotonia, ocular abnormalities, and brain MRI abnormalities including cerebellar/cerebral atrophy and hypomyelination. The phenotype has been assigned an OMIM entry (neurodevelopmental disorder with motor and language delay, ocular defects, and brain abnormalities, MIM 620428), indicating curated acceptance of causality. Supporting Drosophila and cellular functional studies demonstrated loss-of-function effects consistent with the human phenotype, complementing the multi-family human genetic evidence. Because the core evidence is human, involves multiple independent probands, and is OMIM-recognized, "Established" is strongly favored, with minor residual probability for "Existing" given that the evidence largely derives from a single (though large, multi-center) publication.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus, and seizures
justification: CPSF3 encodes the endonuclease subunit of the mRNA 3'-end cleavage and polyadenylation machinery, and biallelic (mostly missense/hypomorphic) variants have been reported in humans with a recognizable syndrome of global developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus/abnormal eye movements, and seizures, which is reflected in the existence of a specific named OMIM phenotype. The primary report(s) around 2022–2023 described multiple affected individuals from several independent, often consanguineous families, with segregation and supporting functional/RNA 3'-end processing assays, which supports an Established classification. However, the literature is still relatively recent and largely dominated by one or two multi-family cohort publications with limited independent replication, so meaningful probability remains for "Existing." Purely biological/animal-model support (CPSF3 knockdown effects on neurodevelopment) exists but is secondary to the human genetic data, so "Hypothesized" gets little weight and "Novel" is essentially excluded.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus, and seizures
justification: CPSF3 encodes CPSF73, the endonuclease of the mRNA 3'-end cleavage/polyadenylation and histone pre-mRNA processing machinery, a biologically plausible candidate for a severe neurodevelopmental phenotype. To my knowledge, biallelic CPSF3 variants have been reported in humans in multiple affected individuals from more than one unrelated family with global developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus/abnormal eye movements, and seizures, and this has been assigned a specific OMIM-style phenotype name matching the queried disorder, with supporting functional/RNA-processing studies. That level of evidence—independent probands plus mechanistic support—supports an Established relationship, though the total number of reported families is still relatively small and curation groups might rate it as limited/moderate, so substantial weight remains on Existing. Purely biological/animal-model-only evidence is unlikely to be the sole basis here, so Hypothesized and Novel receive little weight.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus, and seizures
justification: CPSF3 encodes CPSF73, the endonuclease of the mRNA 3'-end cleavage/polyadenylation and histone pre-mRNA processing machinery, biology highly relevant to neurodevelopment. I recall a recent (circa 2023) report of biallelic CPSF3 missense variants in multiple individuals from several unrelated families presenting with global developmental delay, microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus/ocular findings, and seizures, with supporting functional studies (patient cells and model organisms), and a corresponding OMIM entry for a neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, hypotonia, nystagmus, and seizures. If the original description included several independent probands/families with segregation and functional support, this meets the Established threshold; however, since the gene–disease link is recent and independent replication may be limited to that single multi-family cohort, substantial probability remains for "Existing." Purely hypothesized or novel status is unlikely given the specific, named clinical entity attributed to this gene in humans.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures
justification: CHKA (choline kinase alpha) has been linked to a recessive neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by microcephaly, global developmental delay, movement abnormalities/dystonia, and epilepsy, reported around 2022–2023 in a multi-family cohort study with supporting functional data (impaired choline kinase activity and phosphatidylcholine synthesis), and it has an assigned OMIM phenotype entry. This suggests more than a single anecdotal report, favoring Established; however, the evidence largely derives from one collaborative publication with a modest number of probands and limited independent replication, so a "moderate/limited" classification (Existing) remains plausible. The biology is highly relevant (Kennedy pathway phospholipid synthesis, analogous to other phospholipid-related neurodevelopmental disorders), which would at minimum support Hypothesized. Because the key genetic evidence is in human patients rather than solely animal/in vitro models, most weight belongs to Established/Existing, with little probability of Novel.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures
justification: CHKA (choline kinase alpha) is recognized in OMIM/GenCC with an autosomal recessive phenotype named essentially identically to the queried condition (neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures), which indicates published human genetic evidence. To my knowledge this derives from a recent report describing bi-allelic CHKA variants in several affected individuals from multiple unrelated, often consanguineous families, supported by functional/model-organism (e.g., Drosophila or in vitro enzyme activity) data and by the paralog CHKB's established role in megaconial congenital muscular dystrophy, strengthening biological plausibility. Because the human evidence may rest largely on a single multi-family publication with limited independent replication, the classification sits between Established and Existing, with a lean toward Established given the number of probands and functional corroboration. Purely hypothesized or novel status is unlikely since direct human variant-phenotype data exist.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities, and seizures
justification: CHKA (choline kinase alpha) has been linked to an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, movement abnormalities/dystonia, and epilepsy, reported in a multi-family cohort study (biallelic missense/loss-of-function variants) around 2022, with supporting functional work including reduced choline kinase activity and Drosophila models. The existence of a specific OMIM phenotype entry with this exact designation indicates the gene–disease pair has been curated as a recognized Mendelian entity based on human genetic evidence. Because the evidence largely derives from a single (though multi-proband, multi-family) publication with limited independent replication, some probability remains on "Existing" rather than fully "Established." Purely hypothesized or novel status is very unlikely given the direct human variant data plus functional validation.

Junctophilin-1 is a core component of the skeletal muscle triad junction, tethering the sarcoplasmic reticulum to T-tubules and enabling RyR1–DHPR excitation–contraction coupling; Jph1-null mice die perinatally with disorganized triads and impaired contraction, giving a very strong biological rationale (supporting at least "Hypothesized"). The existence of a specifically numbered OMIM-style phenotype ("congenital myopathy 25") implies that at least one human genetic report of (likely biallelic) JPH1 variants in patients with a congenital/early-onset myopathy has been published, which would qualify as "Existing." However, I am not aware of multiple independent, replicated cohorts or families confirming causality, so "Established" is less likely, and such recently designated gene–disease pairs typically rest on a small number of probands with supporting functional studies. A small residual probability is left for "Novel" in case the association is purely nominal or the numbering corresponds to another gene.

JPH1 encodes junctophilin-1, a skeletal-muscle triad junction protein essential for excitation–contraction coupling, and Jph1-null mice show disrupted triads and perinatal lethality, giving very strong biological plausibility. The existence of a formally numbered OMIM phenotype (congenital myopathy 25) implies at least one published human report of biallelic (or dominant) JPH1 variants segregating with a congenital myopathy, supported by functional/EC-coupling studies. However, this is a recently delineated, rare entity likely based on only one or a few probands/families, so replication across multiple independent studies is probably limited. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with meaningful probability for "Established" if additional cohorts have since been reported, and residual probability for "Hypothesized" if the human genetic evidence is weaker than assumed.

JPH1 encodes junctophilin-1, the principal skeletal-muscle junctophilin that tethers the sarcoplasmic reticulum to T-tubules and is essential for triad formation and excitation–contraction coupling; Jph1-null mice die perinatally with severe muscle weakness and disrupted triads, giving very strong biological plausibility (baseline "Hypothesized" support). The existence of a designated OMIM-style phenotype label "congenital myopathy 25" implies that at least one human genetic study has reported biallelic/dominant JPH1 variants in patients with a congenital myopathy, most likely a recent report in one or a few families with supporting functional data. Such initial reports typically satisfy "Existing" rather than "Established," since replication in multiple independent cohorts is usually lacking for newly named entities. Some probability remains for "Established" if the defining publication included several unrelated probands with segregation and functional validation. "Novel" is very unlikely given the direct triad/EC-coupling biology shared with RYR1, CACNA1S, STAC3 and other congenital myopathy genes.

Immunodeficiency 92 (OMIM 619652) is attributed to biallelic loss-of-function variants in REL (c-Rel), with the seminal human report by Beaussant-Cohen et al. describing a patient with combined immunodeficiency (mycobacterial/opportunistic infections, impaired T- and B-cell responses) carrying a homozygous REL mutation, supported by functional studies of NF-κB signaling in patient cells. A small number of additional cases/families have subsequently been reported, but the total human evidence remains limited to few probands, so the association sits between "Existing" and "Established."
