Strong corroborating biology exists from Rel-knockout mice with lymphocyte activation defects and from c-Rel's central role in NF-κB–dependent immune gene transcription, which alone would support "Hypothesized." Because credible human genetic and functional data exist, "Novel" is essentially excluded.

Immunodeficiency 92 (OMIM 619652) is attributed to biallelic loss-of-function variants in REL (c-Rel), based principally on the report of inherited human c-Rel deficiency (Beaussant-Cohen et al., JCI 2019), which described a patient with combined immunodeficiency and impaired myeloid/lymphoid responses, supported by functional studies in patient cells and consistent Rel-knockout mouse phenotypes. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence with mechanistic support, so the relationship is clearly at least "Existing." Whether it reaches "Established" depends on replication in independent probands/families, which appears limited (only one or very few reported cases), making the total human evidence relatively sparse. The strong NF-κB pathway biology and murine data reinforce plausibility but would only support "Hypothesized" on their own, so few points are placed there and essentially none on "Novel."

Immunodeficiency 92 (OMIM #619652) is explicitly defined as an autosomal recessive combined immunodeficiency caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in REL (c-Rel), an NF-κB family transcription factor essential for T-cell, dendritic-cell and IL-12/IFN-γ–axis function. The key human evidence comes from Beaussant-Cohen et al. (J Exp Med, 2019), describing a patient with homozygous REL deficiency and impaired immunity to BCG and Salmonella, with subsequent additional patient reports supporting the entity. This makes the association clearly more than hypothetical, but the total number of independently reported human probands/families remains small, so points are split between Established and Existing. Supporting Rel-knockout mouse and in vitro functional data reinforce biological plausibility but alone would only justify "Hypothesized," which retains a small share. A "Novel" classification is essentially excluded given the named OMIM disorder.

FLI1 is the recognized gene for bleeding disorder, platelet-type, 21 (OMIM 617443), an inherited thrombocytopenia/platelet function defect with Paris-Trousseau-like giant alpha-granules. Human evidence includes homozygous/biallelic FLI1 variants reported by Stevenson et al. (2015) in a consanguineous family, dominant-negative heterozygous ETS-domain variants identified in the UK GAPP cohort (Stockley et al., 2013), and additional independent probands/families described by Saultier et al. (2017) and others. Supporting context comes from FLI1 haploinsufficiency in Jacobsen/Paris-Trousseau syndrome, where 11q deletion including FLI1 causes the same megakaryocyte/platelet phenotype, plus concordant functional and murine data. Because multiple independent human probands and families with segregating, functionally validated variants exist, the association is best classified as Established, with a small residual allocation to Existing given the relative rarity of reported cases.

FLI1 is the recognized gene for OMIM 617443 (bleeding disorder, platelet-type, 21), with multiple independent human reports: Stevenson et al. (2015) described a homozygous FLI1 variant causing dense-granule deficiency and macrothrombocytopenia in a consanguineous family, Stockley et al. (2013, GAPP cohort) identified heterozygous ETS-domain FLI1 variants in patients with platelet dysfunction, and Saultier et al. (2017) reported additional dominant-negative FLI1 variants in several unrelated families with macrothrombocytopenia and giant alpha-granules. Supporting biology is strong, since FLI1 hemizygosity underlies the Paris–Trousseau thrombocytopenia of Jacobsen syndrome and Fli1-null mice show megakaryocyte defects. Because the causal role rests on several independent human probands/families with functional validation, "Established" is most appropriate, though some weight remains for "Existing" given the modest number of reported families and variable penetrance of heterozygous alleles.

FLI1 is the established gene for bleeding disorder, platelet-type, 21 (OMIM 617443), an inherited macrothrombocytopenia with alpha/dense granule abnormalities and giant alpha-granules resembling Paris-Trousseau/Jacobsen syndrome. Human genetic evidence includes homozygous/compound heterozygous FLI1 variants in consanguineous families (e.g., Stevenson et al.) and heterozygous dominant-negative ETS-domain variants identified through platelet-disorder exome/panel sequencing cohorts (e.g., Stockley et al., UK-GAPP, ThromboGenomics), with functional validation showing impaired transactivation of megakaryocytic target genes (ITGA2B, GP9, MPL). The hemizygous FLI1 loss in 11q terminal deletion (Jacobsen) provides strong corroborating human evidence for the gene–phenotype mechanism. Independent probands and families, plus curated gene-disease validity classifications, support an Established relationship; a small residual probability reflects debate over penetrance/pathogenicity of some heterozygous variants.

TRAC encodes the T-cell receptor alpha constant region, and biallelic loss-of-function variants cause "Immunodeficiency 7, TCR-alpha/beta deficient" (OMIM 615387), first described by Morgan et al. (J Clin Invest, 2011) in a consanguineous human family with multiple affected siblings showing absent TCR-alpha/beta T cells with preserved gamma/delta T cells. This is a direct human genetic demonstration with functional confirmation (loss of surface TCR-alpha/beta expression, impaired thymocyte development), and a small number of additional probands/case reports with distinct TRAC variants have since been described. The main caveat is the rarity of the condition and the limited number of independent families, so some curation bodies might rate the evidence as moderate rather than definitive. Therefore most weight goes to Established, with substantial residual probability on Existing; purely biological/animal-model-based (Hypothesized) or no-evidence (Novel) categories are very unlikely.

TRAC encodes the T-cell receptor alpha constant region, and biallelic loss-of-function variants are the recognized cause of immunodeficiency 7 (TCR-alpha/beta-deficient, OMIM 615387). The landmark human report (Morgan et al., J Clin Invest 2011) described a consanguineous family with affected siblings carrying a homozygous TRAC mutation, with absent surface TCRαβ+ T cells, expanded γδ T cells, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity, supported by functional/expression data. A small number of additional patients and confirmatory functional work have since been reported, but the total number of independent probands remains limited, which is why some curation efforts might rate the evidence as moderate rather than definitive. Because the causal human genetic evidence is direct and mechanistically unambiguous but based on few families, points are concentrated on Established with substantial weight on Existing, and little on Hypothesized or Novel.

TRAC is the recognized cause of OMIM #615387, "Immunodeficiency 7, TCR-alpha/beta deficient," and is listed in the IUIS inborn errors of immunity classification as a T-cell defect. The foundational human evidence is Morgan et al. (J Clin Invest, 2011), who identified a homozygous TRAC mutation in affected siblings from a consanguineous family presenting with absent TCRαβ+ T cells, preserved TCRγδ+ cells, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity, with supporting functional/expression data. Because the initial report involved a single family, some curation frameworks would rate the gene–disease validity as limited/moderate rather than definitive, though subsequent case reports (including transplanted patients) have added probands. The mechanism—loss of the TCR alpha constant region preventing surface αβTCR assembly—is directly and specifically explanatory for the phenotype, making a purely hypothesized or novel classification very unlikely.

Imai et al. (Nature Immunology, 2003) identified biallelic UNG (uracil-DNA glycosylase) mutations in patients from independent families with an autosomal recessive hyper-IgM syndrome characterized by impaired class-switch recombination and a skewed somatic hypermutation pattern, establishing OMIM entry 608106 (HIGM5). Follow-up human studies (e.g., Kavli et al., 2005) confirmed loss of UNG2 activity and the B-cell phenotype in these patients, and the mechanism fits directly downstream of AID in the DNA-deamination pathway shared with AICDA-deficient HIGM2. However, the disease is exceedingly rare with only a small number of reported probands and limited independent replication, so some curation efforts might rate the evidence as moderate rather than definitive. Supporting Ung-knockout mouse and biochemical data reinforce but do not substitute for the human genetic evidence, hence a small residual weight on "Hypothesized."

Imai et al. (Nature Immunology, 2003) identified biallelic loss-of-function UNG mutations in patients from unrelated families with hyper-IgM syndrome characterized by defective class-switch recombination and a biased somatic hypermutation pattern, establishing UNG deficiency as HIGM type 5 (OMIM 608106). The mechanism fits perfectly with the AID–uracil-DNA-glycosylase pathway in CSR, and Ung-deficient mice recapitulate the CSR defect, providing strong supportive functional evidence. However, only a handful of human probands have been reported worldwide, so some curation efforts might rate the evidence as moderate/limited rather than definitive, leaving meaningful weight on "Existing." Given the human genetic data with functional validation and inclusion in standard immunodeficiency gene panels/classifications, "Established" remains the most probable category.

Imai et al. (Nature Immunology, 2003) identified biallelic UNG mutations (e.g., F251S, splice-site variants) in unrelated patients with a class-switch recombination deficiency characterized by elevated IgM and low IgG/IgA, defining hyper-IgM syndrome type 5 (OMIM 608106). Functional work (Kavli, Krokan, Durandy groups) confirmed loss of uracil-DNA glycosylase activity and impaired AID-initiated CSR, giving a coherent mechanism downstream of AID. The association is widely accepted in immunodeficiency classifications (IUIS) and gene panels, supporting "Established." However, the total number of reported human probands remains very small (a handful of patients/families), so some probability is retained for "Existing" given limited replication, and minimal weight for purely hypothesis-level or no evidence.

phenotype: neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect
justification: SLC31A1 encodes CTR1, the principal high-affinity copper importer, and biallelic loss-of-function variants have been reported in humans with an early-onset copper-deficiency phenotype featuring seizures, hypotonia, developmental regression and neurodegeneration, leading to a recognized OMIM entity ("neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect"). The human genetic evidence, however, appears to rest on a small number of consanguineous families/siblings with supporting functional and cellular copper-transport assays and Ctr1-knockout mouse data, rather than broad independent replication. This places the pair beyond mere biological plausibility but likely short of firmly established/definitive gene–disease validity (comparable to a limited-to-moderate ClinGen classification). Therefore most weight falls on "Existing," with substantial residual probability for "Established" if additional independent probands have since been published, and a small allocation to "Hypothesized" reflecting the strong but supportive-only model/functional data.

phenotype: neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect
justification: SLC31A1 encodes CTR1, the high-affinity copper importer, and an OMIM phenotype ("neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect") has been assigned based on biallelic loss-of-function/missense variants identified in human patients with infantile-onset seizures, developmental regression, and low serum copper/ceruloplasmin, with functional support from copper-uptake assays and Ctr1 knockout mouse models. However, the human genetic evidence is drawn from a very small number of probands (initially one consanguineous family, with only a few subsequent case reports), so replication across many independent families is limited. This places the pair most plausibly in the "Existing" category, close to but not clearly meeting a fully "Established"/Definitive threshold, which is why substantial weight is retained for Established. Strong, directly relevant biology (copper homeostasis, cuproenzyme deficiency, animal models) would independently justify at least "Hypothesized," so a modest allocation remains there. "Novel" is essentially excluded given the recognized gene–disease entry.

phenotype: neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect
justification: SLC31A1 encodes CTR1, the principal high-affinity copper importer, and its loss of function is mechanistically expected to cause cellular copper deficiency with a Menkes-like neurodegenerative phenotype; mouse Ctr1 knockouts are embryonic lethal and hypomorphs show copper-deficiency neurologic disease, giving strong biological plausibility. Beyond animal data, human biallelic (homozygous) SLC31A1 variants have been reported in consanguineous families with infantile-onset seizures, developmental regression/neurodegeneration and low serum copper/ceruloplasmin, and OMIM recognizes a distinct autosomal recessive phenotype ("neurodegeneration and seizures due to copper transport defect"), indicating at least one credible human genetic study with functional support. The main uncertainty is whether the number of independent probands/families is sufficient and replicated enough to be considered definitively "Established" versus a limited but credible emerging association, since the entity is recent and reported in only a small number of kindreds. I therefore split points roughly evenly between Established and Existing, with a smaller allocation to Hypothesized to reflect the possibility that much of the supporting evidence is model/in vitro based, and essentially no weight to Novel.

GDF11 is the gene underlying the OMIM-recognized Mendelian condition "Vertebral hypersegmentation and orofacial anomalies" (VHO), defined after Ravenscroft et al. (2021, AJHG) reported heterozygous loss-of-function/missense GDF11 variants in multiple unrelated human probands with supernumerary/hypersegmented vertebrae, craniofacial and orofacial anomalies (cleft palate, micrognathia), and variable neurodevelopmental features. The human genetic evidence involves several independent families with segregation and de novo variants, plus strong supporting biology from Gdf11-null mice showing anterior homeotic vertebral transformations and increased vertebral number, which mechanistically mirrors the human phenotype. Because much of the definitive human evidence derives from a single large cohort paper with limited subsequent independent replication, some probability remains on "Existing." Animal-model and functional data alone would only support "Hypothesized," but the presence of confirmed human variant-based cases makes that unlikely, and "Novel" is essentially excluded.

GDF11 is the gene assigned to the OMIM entry "Vertebral hypersegmentation and orofacial anomalies" (VHO, autosomal dominant), based principally on Ravenscroft et al. (Genetics in Medicine, 2021), which reported multiple unrelated human probands/families with heterozygous loss-of-function or missense GDF11 variants presenting vertebral segmentation defects (extra/hypersegmented vertebrae), orofacial clefting/dysmorphism, and other skeletal features. This human evidence is strongly corroborated by Gdf11-null mouse models showing homeotic transformations and supernumerary vertebrae, providing a clear mechanistic basis in the TGF-β/myostatin-related pathway. Because the human data derive largely from a single, though multi-family, cohort with limited independent replication, some weight remains on "Existing" rather than fully "Established." Purely biological/animal-only interpretation is unlikely given the documented human variants, so little weight goes to Hypothesized or Novel.

GDF11 is the gene listed in OMIM for "vertebral hypersegmentation and orofacial anomalies" (VHO, MIM 619758), an autosomal dominant condition attributed to heterozygous loss-of-function/missense GDF11 variants. The key human evidence comes from Ravenscroft et al. (2021), who reported multiple unrelated probands/families with de novo or inherited GDF11 variants showing vertebral segmentation anomalies (extra vertebrae/ribs), craniofacial and orofacial features, consistent with a gene–disease relationship. This is strongly corroborated by Gdf11-null mouse models showing anterior homeotic transformations, supernumerary vertebrae, and palatal/craniofacial defects, providing a clear mechanistic basis. Because the human evidence largely derives from a single (albeit multi-family) report with limited independent replication, I weight Established most heavily but retain substantial probability for Existing.

GABRD encodes the GABA-A receptor δ subunit, long implicated in human epilepsy susceptibility (e.g., E177A and R220H variants in GEFS+ and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy families), which constitutes at least "Existing" level human genetic evidence linked to neurodevelopmental phenotypes. More decisively, Ahring et al. (Brain, 2022) reported multiple unrelated probands with de novo, mostly gain-of-function GABRD variants presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, intellectual disability, autistic features and other neurodevelopmental abnormalities, supported by electrophysiological functional validation; subsequent case reports and diagnostic cohorts have added further probands. This replication across independent human probands, combined with a coherent mechanism (altered tonic GABAergic inhibition), supports an established causal role, though some variants remain of uncertain significance and the gene is still relatively newly curated (ClinGen/gene2phenotype classifications have been moderate/limited at times). Residual probability is therefore assigned to "Existing," with only minor weight to purely biological/animal-model-based support.

GABRD encodes the δ subunit of the GABA-A receptor, mediating tonic inhibition, and early human genetic work (Dibbens et al., 2004) linked variants (e.g., E177A, R220H) to generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy — epilepsy phenotypes that are recognized precursors/comorbidities of neurodevelopmental impairment. More decisively, a multi-patient cohort study (Ahring et al., Brain 2022) reported recurrent de novo gain-of-function GABRD variants in independent probands with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, intellectual disability, and autistic features, supported by electrophysiological functional validation. This constitutes human genetic evidence in multiple unrelated probands, pushing toward Established, though the literature is still dominated by a small number of cohorts and gene–disease validity curations may still rate it moderate rather than definitive. Hence probability is split mainly between Established and Existing, with a small residual for Hypothesized given the strong supporting biology and mouse models, and negligible probability of Novel.

GABRD encodes the δ subunit of the GABA-A receptor, and early human genetic work linked variants to generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy susceptibility, i.e., epilepsy phenotypes rather than broad neurodevelopmental disease. More recently, a multi-patient cohort study (Ahring et al., Brain 2022) reported recurrent de novo gain-of-function GABRD variants (e.g., p.Arg191Trp, p.Thr127Ile) in individuals with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, intellectual disability, autistic features and movement abnormalities, supported by electrophysiological functional validation. This provides human, multi-proband, partly recurrent de novo evidence, and subsequent case reports and clinical databases (ClinGen/OMIM DEE-related entry) have reinforced it, pushing the relationship toward established. However, the number of independent replicating clinical studies remains modest and some earlier associations were weak susceptibility findings, so substantial probability remains for "Existing." Pure biological/animal-only evidence (Gabrd knockout mice with behavioral phenotypes) supports a smaller "Hypothesized" weight, and "Novel" is essentially excluded.

ALDH1A2 (RALDH2) encodes the main retinaldehyde dehydrogenase of the retinoic acid pathway, and Aldh1a2-null mice show severe cardiac, pulmonary, and diaphragmatic defects, providing strong biological plausibility. Beyond animal data, human genetic evidence exists: rare/deleterious ALDH1A2 variants were reported in congenital diaphragmatic hernia cohorts (retinoid pathway resequencing studies), and biallelic loss-of-function variants have been described in patients with a lethal syndrome comprising diaphragmatic hernia and cardiovascular/pulmonary malformations, prompting the designation of a distinct OMIM phenotype (diaphragmatic hernia 4, with cardiovascular defects). The existence of a numbered OMIM phenotype entry implies at least one, and likely several, independent probands/families with segregating variants and supportive functional work, favoring "Established." Some uncertainty remains because the human evidence may derive largely from a single recent report with a limited number of families, which would place it at the boundary with "Existing."

ALDH1A2 (RALDH2) is the key enzyme for embryonic retinoic acid synthesis, and retinoid signaling deficiency is a long-standing mechanistic hypothesis for congenital diaphragmatic hernia, supported by Raldh2-null mouse models with diaphragmatic, pulmonary, and cardiovascular malformations. Beyond animal data, human genetic evidence exists: biallelic loss-of-function/hypomorphic ALDH1A2 variants have been reported in consanguineous families with a lethal syndrome of diaphragmatic hernia, pulmonary hypoplasia, and cardiovascular defects, which is the basis of the OMIM entry "Diaphragmatic hernia 4, with cardiovascular defects" with a known molecular basis. Whether this rises to "Established" depends on the number of independent probands/families and replication, which appears limited to one or a few reports plus supportive rare-variant findings in CDH cohorts. I therefore split weight mainly between Established and Existing, with a smaller allocation to Hypothesized to account for the possibility that the strongest support remains murine/functional.

ALDH1A2 (RALDH2) is the key enzyme for embryonic retinoic acid synthesis, and the "retinoid hypothesis" of congenital diaphragmatic hernia is long-standing, with Aldh1a2-null mice showing diaphragmatic, pulmonary and severe cardiovascular malformations—strong biological grounding. Beyond animal data, human evidence exists: biallelic loss-of-function/hypomorphic ALDH1A2 variants have been reported in fetuses/neonates with a lethal syndrome comprising diaphragmatic defects, pulmonary hypoplasia and cardiovascular anomalies, which prompted creation of the OMIM entry "Diaphragmatic hernia 4, with cardiovascular defects." Because this designation typically requires at least one report of multiple affected individuals (often from more than one consanguineous family) with supportive functional validation, Established is the most likely category, though the total number of independent probands remains small and replication is limited, keeping Existing a strong alternative. Purely hypothesized status is unlikely given documented human variants, and Novel is essentially excluded.

phenotype: retinal dystrophy, optic nerve edema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and migraine headache syndrome
justification: ROSAH syndrome (Retinal dystrophy, Optic nerve edema, Splenomegaly, Anhidrosis, and Headache/migraine) was defined by Williams et al. (2019, AJHG) as an autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous missense variants in ALPK1, most commonly p.Thr237Met, identified in multiple independent families with segregation. Subsequent reports (e.g., Kodati/Sen and colleagues at NEI, Kozycki et al.) replicated the finding in additional unrelated probands and characterized the ocular and inflammatory phenotype, and functional work supports a gain-of-function mechanism in ALPK1's ADP-heptose/TIFA-NF-κB signaling pathway. OMIM lists ROSAH syndrome (614979) as caused by ALPK1 mutation, and the gene–disease relationship is widely regarded as definitive in human genetics. Therefore virtually all weight belongs to "Established," with only minimal residual probability for a lower tier.

phenotype: retinal dystrophy, optic nerve edema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and migraine headache syndrome
justification: ROSAH syndrome (Retinal dystrophy, Optic nerve edema, Splenomegaly, Anhidrosis, and Headache/migraine) was definitively linked to heterozygous missense variants in ALPK1 by Williams et al. (Genetics in Medicine, 2019), who identified the recurrent p.Thr237Met variant segregating in multiple independent autosomal dominant families. Subsequent reports from independent groups have confirmed this and expanded the allelic spectrum (e.g., p.Ser277Phe), with additional probands described in ophthalmology and immunology/autoinflammation literature. Functional work supports a gain-of-function mechanism with NF-κB/inflammatory pathway activation, complementing the human genetic data. The evidence is human, replicated, and disease-defining, so the relationship is Established; only minimal residual probability is assigned to lesser categories.

phenotype: retinal dystrophy, optic nerve edema, splenomegaly, anhidrosis, and migraine headache syndrome
justification: ROSAH syndrome (Retinal dystrophy, Optic nerve edema, Splenomegaly, Anhidrosis, Headache/migraine) is a recognized autosomal dominant Mendelian disorder caused by missense variants in ALPK1. Williams et al. (2019, Genetics in Medicine) identified the recurrent p.Thr237Met variant segregating in multiple independent families, and subsequent reports (e.g., Kozycki et al., additional ophthalmology and rheumatology cohorts) confirmed this and other variants such as p.Ser277Phe in further unrelated probands. Functional studies in human cells demonstrate gain-of-function ALPK1 signaling through TIFA/NF-κB with an interferon signature, providing mechanistic support. OMIM lists ROSAH syndrome (MIM 614979) with ALPK1 as the causative gene, making the association clearly established in humans.

SELENOI (also known as EPT1, ethanolaminephosphotransferase 1 of the Kennedy pathway) is the OMIM-designated gene for autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia 81 (SPG81, MIM 618768). Biallelic variants were first reported by Ahmed et al. in a consanguineous family with complex HSP, intellectual disability and seizures, with demonstrated loss of ethanolaminephosphotransferase activity and altered phosphatidylethanolamine species. Additional independent families/probands (e.g., Horibata et al. and subsequent case reports) have replicated the association with a consistent complicated spastic paraplegia phenotype, supporting a causal role in humans. The number of reported families remains relatively small and largely consanguineous, which leaves some probability for the "Existing" (limited but credible) category, but the human genetic plus functional evidence is generally considered sufficient for gene–disease validity.

SELENOI (also known as EPT1), encoding the selenoprotein ethanolaminephosphotransferase of the Kennedy phospholipid biosynthesis pathway, was first linked to a human neurodevelopmental disorder with spasticity in a consanguineous family (Ahmed et al., Brain 2017), with biochemical demonstration of impaired phosphatidylethanolamine synthesis in patient cells. Subsequent reports (e.g., Horibata et al. and later cohorts) described additional unrelated consanguineous families with biallelic SELENOI variants causing complicated autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability, leading to the OMIM designation SPG81 (#618768). Evidence therefore comes from multiple independent human families with segregating biallelic variants plus supportive functional lipidomic data, supporting an Established relationship. Some residual uncertainty remains because the total number of reported probands is still relatively small and largely from consanguineous pedigrees, so a portion of probability is assigned to Existing.

SELENOI (also known as EPT1), which encodes ethanolaminephosphotransferase 1 in the Kennedy pathway of phosphatidylethanolamine synthesis, is the recognized gene for autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia 81 (OMIM #618768). Biallelic loss-of-function/missense variants were first described by Ahmed et al. (Brain, 2017) in a consanguineous family with complex HSP, intellectual disability and microcephaly, with supporting lipidomic evidence of disrupted PE synthesis in patient cells. Additional independent families (e.g., Horibata et al. and subsequent reports) have replicated the association, and the gene–disease pair is curated in OMIM/ClinGen-type resources as a defined Mendelian entity. Because replication rests on a modest number of consanguineous families, some residual weight remains for "Existing" rather than fully definitive status.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity
justification: Biallelic TMX2 variants were reported by Vandervore et al. (2019, AJHG) in a cohort of multiple unrelated patients/families with microcephaly, polymicrogyria and other cortical malformations, spasticity, epilepsy and severe developmental delay, with functional support showing TMX2 dysfunction alters cellular redox and mitochondrial/ER homeostasis. This condition is recognized in OMIM as neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity (NEDMCMS, MIM 618730), and additional case reports/cohorts have since replicated the association in independent probands. The human genetic evidence is therefore replicated across multiple families with segregation and supportive functional data, meeting the criteria for an Established gene–disease relationship. Only a small residual probability is allocated to "Existing" to account for any view that the number of independent reports remains modest.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity
justification: Biallelic TMX2 variants were reported by Vandervore et al. (2019, AJHG) in a cohort of ~14 affected individuals from multiple unrelated families with microcephaly, polymicrogyria/cortical malformations, epilepsy, and spasticity, with functional support showing TMX2's role in cellular redox regulation and mitochondrial function. This entity is recognized in OMIM as neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity (NEDMCMS, MIM 618730). Additional case reports and cohort studies have since replicated the association in independent probands, including recurrent founder-type variants. The evidence is human-based, replicated across independent families, and supported by segregation and functional data, meeting criteria for Established.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity
justification: Biallelic TMX2 variants were reported by Vandervore et al. (2019, AJHG) in a cohort of ~14 affected individuals from multiple unrelated families with microcephaly, polymicrogyria/cortical malformations, spasticity, epilepsy, and severe developmental delay, with supporting functional work on redox/ER homeostasis and mitochondrial function. This established the OMIM entity "neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cortical malformations, and spasticity" (MIM 618730), and additional case reports/cohorts have since replicated the association in independent probands. The evidence is human genetic, multi-family, and mechanistically supported, meeting criteria for Established. Small residual probability is retained for the possibility that some reviewers would consider the replication base still modest.

PRKG2 (cGMP-dependent protein kinase II) is the recognized gene for acromesomelic dysplasia type 4 (OMIM 619636), based on reports of biallelic loss-of-function variants in consanguineous families with acromesomelic shortening and short stature (e.g., Díaz-González, Heath and colleagues, ~2022). The mechanism is highly plausible because PRKG2 acts downstream of the NPR2/CNP–cGMP axis, the same pathway whose disruption causes acromesomelic dysplasia Maroteaux type, and Prkg2-null mice and the KMI dwarf rat show growth-plate dwarfism. Whether the human evidence reaches "established" depends on the number of independent probands/families and replication, which is still relatively limited, so a substantial portion of probability remains on "Existing." The strong animal/functional data alone would only justify "Hypothesized," but human genetic reports clearly exist, making "Novel" very unlikely.

Acromesomelic dysplasia type 4 (OMIM 619636) was defined specifically on the basis of biallelic loss-of-function variants in PRKG2, reported in consanguineous families with disproportionate short stature and acromesomelic limb shortening. PRKG2 (cGKII) lies directly downstream of the CNP/NPR2 signaling axis in growth-plate chondrocytes, the same pathway whose disruption causes acromesomelic dysplasia Maroteaux type, and Prkg2-null rodents show dwarfism—providing strong supporting functional and animal evidence. Because the human genetic evidence rests on a small number of families/probands with limited independent replication, the relationship is best viewed as newly established but not yet extensively replicated, so points are split between Established and Existing. A minority of weight goes to Hypothesized to account for the possibility that much of the supporting evidence is model-organism/functional rather than replicated human genetic data.

Acromesomelic dysplasia type 4 (OMIM 619636) is attributed to biallelic loss-of-function variants in PRKG2, based on a human study (Díaz-González et al., J Med Genet, 2022) describing affected individuals from more than one unrelated consanguineous family with homozygous truncating variants plus supporting functional work. PRKG2 encodes cGMP-dependent protein kinase II, acting downstream of the CNP/NPR2 signaling axis in growth-plate chondrocytes, and Prkg2-deficient rodents (e.g., the KMI rat, Prkg2-null mice) show dwarfism with disproportionate short limbs—strong biological plausibility consistent with the acromesomelic dysplasia spectrum (NPR2, BMPR1B, GDF5, NPPC). The main uncertainty is the limited number of independent human probands reported to date, so the gene–disease validity may be classified as moderate rather than definitive, which is why substantial weight remains on "Existing." Very little probability is assigned to "Novel," as the relationship is clearly documented in humans.

Biallelic PYCR2 variants were identified as the cause of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 10 (HLD10, OMIM 616420) by Nakayama et al. (2015, AJHG) through exome sequencing in multiple consanguineous families with microcephaly, progressive hypomyelination, and postnatal growth failure. Subsequent independent reports (e.g., Zaki et al., Meng et al., Escande-Beillard et al. 2020) replicated the association in additional unrelated probands and expanded the phenotypic spectrum, with functional studies showing impaired mitochondrial proline synthesis and increased apoptosis. The gene–disease relationship is curated as definitive in OMIM and gene-disease validity resources. Evidence derives from human patients across multiple independent families, satisfying the criteria for "Established."

Biallelic PYCR2 variants were identified by Nakayama et al. (2015, AJHG) as the cause of a postnatal microcephaly with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, designated HLD10 (MIM 616420), in multiple unrelated consanguineous families. Subsequent independent reports (e.g., Zaki et al., Meng et al., and additional Middle Eastern and Asian cohorts) replicated the association with recurrent missense and loss-of-function variants, expanding the phenotype to include failure to thrive, spasticity, and seizures. Functional studies support impaired proline biosynthesis and mitochondrial dysfunction as the mechanism, complementing the human genetic data. The evidence is human-based, replicated across independent probands, and the gene–disease pair is curated as definitive in OMIM/ClinGen-type resources, so the association is clearly Established.

Biallelic PYCR2 variants were identified by Nakayama et al. (2015, AJHG) in multiple consanguineous families with microcephaly, progressive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy and failure to thrive, defining HLD10 (MIM 616420). Independent replication followed, notably Zaki et al. (2016, Brain) describing additional families with a recognizable phenotype, plus further case reports and cohort studies from various populations expanding the mutational spectrum. Functional work supports loss of proline biosynthesis function and increased apoptosis, complementing the human genetic data. The gene–disease association is curated as definitive in OMIM/ClinGen-type resources, so the evidence strongly supports the "Established" category.

SAMD11 was proposed as a novel cause of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa by Corton et al. (Scientific Reports, 2016), who identified homozygous loss-of-function (frameshift) variants segregating in Spanish arRP families, supported by functional data showing SAMD11 acts within the CRX-regulated photoreceptor transcriptional network and Samd11 knockout mouse retinal phenotypes. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, but replication in independent cohorts has been sparse, and SAMD11 is often flagged as a difficult, GC-rich, poorly covered gene, so most gene–disease validity assessments would classify it as limited/moderate rather than definitive. Therefore "Existing" carries the most weight, with a meaningful minority probability for "Established" should additional probands have been reported since. Biological/animal-model support alone would only justify "Hypothesized," and outright "Novel" is essentially excluded given the published human variants.

SAMD11 was reported by Corton et al. (Scientific Reports, 2016) as a novel cause of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa, with homozygous truncating variants identified in Spanish families and supporting evidence that SAMD11 is a CRX-regulated photoreceptor transcriptional co-repressor expressed in the retina. It is listed on RetNet as an RP gene, and a small number of subsequent case reports/cohort studies have described additional biallelic variants, though independent replication remains limited. Because the primary human genetic evidence comes largely from one study (with a few families) plus sparse later reports, the association is credible but not yet firmly established at the level of well-replicated RP genes such as USH2A or EYS. Strong supporting functional/expression data in photoreceptors reinforces biological plausibility but does not by itself elevate the classification. Therefore the weight is split mainly between "Existing" and "Established," with a small residual for "Hypothesized."

SAMD11 was reported by Corton et al. (2016, Scientific Reports) as a novel cause of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa, with a homozygous truncating variant identified in Spanish families, supported by evidence that SAMD11 is a photoreceptor-specific transcriptional co-repressor associated with PRC1 and by Samd11 mouse retinal data. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, and the gene appears in retinal disease gene lists (RetNet) for arRP. However, independent replication in additional unrelated probands has been limited, and the gene is only rarely implicated in large IRD cohort screens, so the causal role is not as firmly established as for classic RP genes. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with a moderate possibility that accumulated subsequent case reports elevate it to "Established," and a smaller residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the human evidence is considered insufficiently definitive.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with structural brain anomalies and dysmorphic facies
justification: De novo missense variants in RAC3 were first reported by Costain et al. (2019, AJHG) in multiple unrelated patients with a distinctive neurodevelopmental disorder featuring structural brain anomalies (corpus callosum abnormalities, cortical malformations) and dysmorphic facial features, leading to OMIM designation NEDBAF (#618577). Additional independent probands were subsequently described by Hiraide et al., Scala et al. (2022, expanded cohort of ~20 patients), and others, confirming recurrence of specific residues and genotype–phenotype correlations. Functional studies (constitutive activation of Rho GTPase signaling, altered neuronal migration) corroborate the mechanism, but human genetic evidence alone is replicated across multiple independent clinical reports. This meets criteria for an Established gene–disease relationship, as also curated by ClinGen/gene curation efforts.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with structural brain anomalies and dysmorphic facies
justification: De novo missense variants in RAC3 (a Rho GTPase closely related to RAC1) have been reported in multiple unrelated probands with a distinctive neurodevelopmental phenotype including corpus callosum abnormalities, cortical malformations (e.g., polymicrogyria, dysgenesis), microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, and dysmorphic facies; this is catalogued in OMIM as NEDBAF (#618577). Key human reports include Costain et al. (2019, AJHG), Hiraide et al. (2019), and subsequent case series/cohort expansions (e.g., Scala et al., 2022) confirming recurrent hotspot variants across independent patients. Functional studies in cells and model systems support a gain-of-function/dominant mechanism affecting neuronal migration and cytoskeletal signaling, complementing the human genetic evidence. Given replication in independent human probands and clear genotype–phenotype correlation, the association is best classified as Established.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with structural brain anomalies and dysmorphic facies
justification: De novo missense variants in RAC3 (a Rho GTPase closely related to RAC1) were reported by Costain et al. (2019, AJHG) and Hiraide et al. (2019) in unrelated probands with severe developmental delay, structural brain malformations (corpus callosum abnormalities, cortical dysgenesis, ventriculomegaly) and dysmorphic facial features, defining the OMIM entity NEDBAF (#618577). Subsequent cohort reports (e.g., Scala et al., 2022) expanded the phenotype in additional independent patients, with functional studies showing gain-of-function effects on PAK/Rho signaling supporting causality. Multiple independent human probands, recurrent hotspot variants, and consistent phenotypes meet criteria for an established gene–disease relationship. Only a small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" given the relatively small total number of reported cases.

phenotype: encephalopathy, neonatal severe, with lactic acidosis and brain abnormalities
justification: LIPT2 encodes lipoyl(octanoyl) transferase 2, essential for mitochondrial lipoic acid synthesis, and biallelic LIPT2 variants were reported by Habarou et al. (2017, AJHG) in a small number of patients from unrelated consanguineous families with severe neonatal encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and brain abnormalities, supported by functional evidence of reduced lipoylation of PDH/KGDH complexes and rescue experiments. This underpins the OMIM entry #617668 for this specific phenotype, so the gene–disease link is human-based and mechanistically coherent. However, the total number of reported probands remains very small with limited independent replication beyond the original report, so curation bodies would likely rate the evidence as limited-to-moderate rather than definitive. Accordingly, most weight falls on "Existing," with substantial residual probability for "Established" given OMIM recognition and strong functional corroboration.

phenotype: encephalopathy, neonatal severe, with lactic acidosis and brain abnormalities
justification: LIPT2 encodes lipoyl(octanoyl) transferase 2, part of the mitochondrial lipoic acid synthesis pathway, and biallelic LIPT2 variants were reported by Habarou et al. (2017, AJHG) in a small number of unrelated patients with severe neonatal encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and brain abnormalities (OMIM 617668). This is credible human genetic evidence supported by functional studies showing reduced lipoylation of PDH/KGDH complexes, but the number of independent probands is very small and replication has been sparse, so the evidence base resembles "limited/moderate" rather than definitively established. Additional single case reports may exist, which leaves some probability for the Established category. Pure biological plausibility alone (Hypothesized) understates the fact that human pathogenic variants have been described, and Novel is essentially excluded.

phenotype: encephalopathy, neonatal severe, with lactic acidosis and brain abnormalities
justification: LIPT2 encodes lipoyl(octanoyl) transferase 2, an enzyme in the mitochondrial lipoic acid biosynthesis pathway, and biallelic LIPT2 variants were reported by Habarou et al. (2017, AJHG) in patients from two unrelated families with severe neonatal encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and brain abnormalities, with functional confirmation of a lipoylation defect (OMIM 617668). This is credible human genetic evidence with supporting biochemistry, establishing a clear gene–disease link, but the number of reported probands and independent replicating publications remains small, so most curation efforts classify the evidence as limited/moderate rather than definitive. The biology is highly consistent with related lipoic acid pathway disorders (LIPT1, LIAS, BOLA3, NFU1), which strengthens plausibility. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with substantial probability for "Established" if subsequent case reports have accumulated, and only minor probability for purely hypothesized or novel status.

TMEM106B is the recognized gene for hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 16 (HLD16, OMIM 617964), established by Simons et al. (Brain, 2017), who identified the same recurrent de novo missense variant (p.Asp252Asn) in multiple unrelated patients with a distinctive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. Subsequent independent case reports (including Japanese and Chinese probands) replicated the same recurrent variant, and functional work in oligodendrocytes/lysosomal trafficking supports a mechanistic role. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence in independent probands, meeting the criteria for "Established." A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because the evidence rests largely on one recurrent variant with a limited number of reported cases, and minimal weight to purely biological/hypothesized support.

TMEM106B is the recognized gene for hypomyelinating leukodystrophy 16 (HLD16, OMIM 617964), defined by a recurrent de novo missense variant (p.Asp252Asn) first reported by Simons et al. (2017, AJHG) in multiple unrelated affected individuals with hypomyelination and developmental delay. Subsequent independent case reports and cohort studies in humans have confirmed the same recurrent variant and expanded the phenotype, satisfying replication in independent probands. Functional work (aberrant lysosomal trafficking, oligodendrocyte studies) supports the mechanism but is supplementary to the human genetic evidence. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" given the reliance on a single recurrent allele rather than a broad allelic spectrum.

TMEM106B is the recognized gene for hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 16 (OMIM 617964), established by Simons et al. (2017, AJHG), who reported a recurrent de novo missense variant (p.Asp252Asn) in multiple unrelated affected individuals with hypomyelination, developmental delay, and nystagmus. Subsequent independent case reports and cohort studies (including additional patients from Japanese and other series) have replicated this recurrent variant and described related de novo changes, supporting causality in humans. Functional work in cells and model systems shows the variant perturbs lysosomal function and oligodendrocyte maturation, providing a plausible mechanism consistent with the human genetic data. Given multiple independent human probands with a recurrent de novo variant, the relationship is best classified as Established, with a small residual probability that an evaluator would judge the number of reported families as still limited (Existing).

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cataracts, and renal abnormalities
justification: GEMIN4 encodes a component of the SMN (survival motor neuron) complex involved in snRNP biogenesis, and biallelic (mostly missense) variants have been reported in humans to cause a recognizable autosomal recessive syndrome of neurodevelopmental delay, microcephaly, cataracts, and renal abnormalities (OMIM 617913, NEDMCR), originally described in consanguineous families from the Arabian peninsula/South Asia with functional support for impaired snRNP assembly. Because more than one family/proband and, to my knowledge, subsequent independent case reports support this specific gene–phenotype pair, the evidence leans toward Established. Some residual uncertainty remains because the total number of independently reported probands is relatively small and much of the evidence stems from a limited number of publications, which would support only "Existing." Purely biological/animal-model-based support (SMN complex function, snRNP biogenesis) is secondary here since direct human genetic evidence exists, so little weight goes to Hypothesized or Novel.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cataracts, and renal abnormalities
justification: GEMIN4 is the recognized gene for the autosomal recessive OMIM entity "neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cataracts, and renal abnormalities" (NEDMCR, MIM 617913), first defined by biallelic missense variants identified through exome sequencing in consanguineous families with a shared phenotype of developmental delay, microcephaly, cataracts, and renal anomalies. Subsequent case reports and cohort studies have expanded the phenotype and added additional unrelated probands, supporting replication in humans. GEMIN4 biology (component of the SMN complex, snRNP biogenesis) provides a plausible mechanism, and functional/expression data support pathogenicity, but the total number of independent families remains modest and some variants are missense with incomplete functional validation, so the gene–disease validity may be judged moderate rather than definitive. Points are therefore concentrated on Established with substantial weight on Existing, and minimal weight on Hypothesized or Novel.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cataracts, and renal abnormalities
justification: GEMIN4 is the established gene for the autosomal recessive disorder "neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, cataracts, and renal abnormalities" (NEDMCR, OMIM #617913), a phenotype defined specifically by biallelic GEMIN4 variants. The initial report described homozygous missense variants segregating in multiple affected individuals from consanguineous families, with functional support relating to GEMIN4's role in the SMN complex and snRNP biogenesis. Subsequent case reports have expanded the phenotype in additional independent probands, supporting replication, though the total number of published families remains relatively small. Because the human genetic evidence is direct and the phenotype term was coined from this gene, "Established" is most likely, with residual probability on "Existing" if one judges the evidence to be limited to few families.

Biallelic ATG7 variants were identified as the cause of a childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder with cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy and ataxia (SCAR31, OMIM 619422), most notably in Collier et al. (2021, New England Journal of Medicine/Cell-related reports) describing multiple affected individuals from several unrelated consanguineous families. The evidence included segregation in independent human families, loss of ATG7 protein and impaired LC3 lipidation/autophagic flux in patient cells, plus supporting model organism data. Because multiple independent human probands/families with functional validation support causality, the relationship is best classified as Established. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" given the relatively small number of reported families and the recency of the gene–disease association.

Biallelic ATG7 loss-of-function variants were identified as the cause of a complex neurodevelopmental syndrome with cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy and ataxia (designated SCAR31, OMIM 619422) in a landmark human study (Collier et al., 2021, Cell) that reported multiple affected individuals from several unrelated consanguineous families, with segregation and functional validation showing absent ATG8 lipidation and impaired autophagy. Additional patient reports and clinical exome findings have since supported the association, and the gene–disease pair is curated in OMIM/ClinGen-type resources. The evidence base is human genetic, multi-family, and functionally corroborated, favoring "Established." Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because much of the evidence derives from a single large report with relatively few independent replications since.

Biallelic ATG7 variants were reported by Collier et al. (Nature, 2021) in multiple unrelated families (approximately a dozen affected individuals from five families) with a complex neurodevelopmental disorder featuring cerebellar hypoplasia/atrophy, ataxia, developmental delay, and facial dysmorphism, which was designated spinocerebellar ataxia, autosomal recessive 31 (SCAR31; OMIM 619422). The report included segregation data and functional demonstration of impaired ATG7-mediated autophagy in patient cells, plus supporting model organism work. Subsequent case reports have added further probands, supporting replication. This meets criteria for an Established gene–disease relationship, with a small residual probability that some curators would consider the evidence limited to a single primary publication and thus only "Existing."

GDAP2 is the gene assigned to OMIM entry for spinocerebellar ataxia, autosomal recessive 27 (SCAR27), based on human genetic findings. Eldomery et al. (2016) first identified a homozygous GDAP2 variant in a consanguineous family with late-onset cerebellar ataxia, and Eidhof et al. (Brain, 2018) reported additional independent families with biallelic loss-of-function GDAP2 variants causing ataxia with intellectual disability/behavioral features, supported by a Drosophila model showing cellular stress susceptibility. This constitutes replicated human evidence across independent probands, favoring "Established," though the total number of reported families remains small and some curation efforts might rate the validity as moderate rather than definitive, leaving meaningful probability on "Existing." Functional/animal data alone would only support "Hypothesized," but human segregation data clearly exceed that threshold, so little weight goes to the lower categories.

GDAP2 is the recognized gene for autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia 27 (SCAR27, OMIM 618369), based principally on Eidhof et al. (Brain, 2018), which reported biallelic loss-of-function GDAP2 variants in several unrelated consanguineous families/probands with adult-onset cerebellar ataxia, sometimes with pyramidal signs and cognitive involvement, supported by a Drosophila knockdown model showing motor and neurodegenerative phenotypes. Because multiple independent human families were described in that report and additional case reports have since appeared, the evidence leans toward "Established," though the total number of reported patients remains small and independent replication is sparse, which keeps meaningful probability on "Existing." Functional/animal data alone would only support "Hypothesized," but the core human genetic evidence is present, so that category receives little weight. "Novel" is essentially excluded given the gene–disease relationship is formally curated in OMIM.

GDAP2 biallelic loss-of-function variants were linked to an autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia syndrome (SCAR27, OMIM 618369) by Eidhof et al. (Brain, 2018), who identified homozygous variants in affected individuals from more than one consanguineous family, supported by Drosophila knockdown models showing cellular stress susceptibility and motor phenotypes. Subsequent case reports/small series (including additional families with ataxia, spasticity, and cognitive impairment) have provided some replication in independent probands, strengthening the association. However, the total number of reported families remains relatively small, and curation bodies may still regard the evidence as moderate rather than definitive. Thus the relationship is most likely "Established," with substantial residual probability for "Existing" if the human evidence is judged limited; purely hypothetical or novel classifications are very unlikely given direct human genetic data.

phenotype: progressive essential tremor-speech impairment-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability-abnormal behavior syndrome
justification: SLC6A17 (a synaptic vesicular neutral amino acid transporter, NTT4/XT1) is the gene underlying autosomal recessive intellectual disability type 48 (OMIM 615850), and the Orphanet term describing progressive tremor, speech impairment, facial dysmorphism, intellectual disability and behavioral abnormalities corresponds to this SLC6A17-related condition. Iqbal et al. (2015, Human Mutation) reported biallelic SLC6A17 variants segregating in several independent consanguineous families with this clinical constellation, and subsequent case reports/cohorts have added patients, supporting causality in humans. Functional work (transport assays, Slc6a17 knockout mice with learning/behavioral deficits) provides mechanistic corroboration but is supplementary to the human genetic data. The main residual uncertainty is the relatively small number of independent replication reports for this rare, recently delineated syndrome, so some probability is retained for "Existing" rather than fully "Established."

phenotype: progressive essential tremor-speech impairment-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability-abnormal behavior syndrome
justification: This phenotype description corresponds directly to the Orphanet/OMIM entity of autosomal recessive intellectual disability (MRT48) caused by biallelic SLC6A17 variants, delineated by Iqbal et al. (Am J Hum Genet, 2015), who reported homozygous SLC6A17 mutations in multiple independent consanguineous families with intellectual disability, progressive tremor, speech impairment, dysmorphism, and behavioral problems. The nosologic term itself was coined around that gene-defined cohort, indicating a well-accepted gene–disease relationship. Additional case reports and functional work on the neuronal vesicular amino acid transporter, including Slc6a17 knockout mouse models showing synaptic and behavioral deficits, further support causality. Because the defining human evidence includes several unrelated probands/families with segregating biallelic variants, "Established" is most appropriate, with a small residual probability that the evidence is judged limited (few families, mostly one report) and thus "Existing."

phenotype: progressive essential tremor-speech impairment-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability-abnormal behavior syndrome
justification: SLC6A17 (NTT4/XT1), a synaptic vesicular neutral amino acid transporter, was implicated by Iqbal et al. (2015, Human Mutation) who reported homozygous variants in multiple consanguineous families with autosomal recessive intellectual disability accompanied by progressive tremor, speech impairment, dysmorphic features and behavioral abnormalities (MRT48) — the exact phenotype named here, which is essentially defined by this gene. Supporting functional work (mislocalization of mutant transporter, Slc6a17 mouse models) reinforces plausibility, and additional case reports/exome cohorts have since described further probands. Because the core evidence comes from several independent human families with segregating biallelic variants, "Established" is most likely, though some curation bodies might still consider the total number of independent reports limited, justifying substantial weight on "Existing." Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are very unlikely given the direct human genetic data.

Hengel-Maroofian-Schols syndrome is the eponymous OMIM-recognized disorder (MIM #619641) defined by biallelic loss-of-function/missense variants in BCAS3, described by Hengel et al. (2021, AJHG/Genetics in Medicine) in multiple unrelated, largely consanguineous families with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, seizures, microcephaly, and dysmorphic features. Additional independent case reports and cohort studies have since expanded the phenotype, providing replication in humans. Functional and model-organism work (BCAS3's role in cytoskeletal/vesicular trafficking and neuronal development) supports the mechanism but is supplementary to the human genetic evidence. The gene–disease pair is therefore essentially definitional, leaving only small residual probability for "Existing" if one judged the number of independent probands limited.

Hengel-Maroofian-Schols (HEMARS) syndrome is an OMIM-recognized autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder (microcephaly, developmental delay, seizures, brain and eye anomalies) that is defined by biallelic variants in BCAS3; the eponym derives directly from the authors (Hengel, Maroofian, Schöls) who reported the gene-disease association. The original description (published around 2020–2021) included multiple unrelated consanguineous families with segregating homozygous BCAS3 variants, providing replication across independent probands, and additional cases have subsequently been reported. Because the phenotype entity itself was delineated from human genetic data with several families and consistent clinical features, the evidence meets criteria for an established gene–disease relationship. Small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" to account for the relative recency and modest total number of reported patients.

Hengel-Maroofian-Schols syndrome is the eponymous OMIM-recognized disorder (MIM 619641) defined by biallelic loss-of-function/missense variants in BCAS3, named after the authors (Hengel, Maroofian, Schöls) who reported it. The original human genetics report described multiple affected individuals from several unrelated, largely consanguineous families with a consistent phenotype of global developmental delay/intellectual disability, microcephaly, seizures, and dysmorphic features, with segregation and homozygosity mapping/exome data. Subsequent case reports and diagnostic cohorts have added further probands, supporting replication in independent families. Functional/model data (BCAS3 role in angiogenesis, cytoskeleton/vesicle trafficking) supplement but are not the primary evidence. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Established, with a small residual probability that some evaluators would consider the number of independent human reports still limited.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and speech and walking impairment
justification: DHPS encodes deoxyhypusine synthase, which catalyzes the first step of hypusine modification of eIF5A. Ganapathi et al. (AJHG, 2019) reported biallelic hypomorphic DHPS variants in multiple affected individuals from several independent families with a syndrome of developmental delay, seizures, and impaired speech and walking, with functional validation showing reduced hypusination; this entity is catalogued in OMIM as "neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and speech and walking impairment" (NEDSSWI, MIM 618480). Subsequent case reports and functional/model studies (including yeast and mouse neuronal models) have supported and extended these findings. The gene–disease pair is therefore human-proven with independent probands, supporting an Established classification, though the total number of reported patients remains modest, leaving some weight on Existing.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and speech and walking impairment
justification: Biallelic DHPS (deoxyhypusine synthase) variants were reported by Ganapathi et al. (2019, AJHG) in multiple affected individuals from several unrelated families with a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring seizures, speech impairment, and delayed/impaired walking, and this entity is catalogued in OMIM as NEDSSWI (#618480). The original report combined human genetic data with functional evidence showing reduced hypusination of eIF5A, and additional patients have subsequently been described, supporting replication in independent probands. Because the total number of reported families remains relatively small, some curation frameworks might score the evidence as moderate rather than definitive, so a portion of probability is placed on "Existing." Supporting animal/in vitro data (yeast, mouse Dhps models, eIF5A hypusination pathway) reinforce but are not the primary basis of the human causal claim.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and speech and walking impairment
justification: Biallelic DHPS (deoxyhypusine synthase) variants were reported by Ganapathi et al. (AJHG, 2019) in multiple affected individuals from several unrelated families with a syndrome of developmental delay, seizures, and impaired speech and walking, which is the basis for OMIM entry NEDSSWI (#618480). The evidence included segregation in independent families plus functional demonstration of reduced hypusination of eIF5A in patient cells, supporting a causal hypusination-pathway mechanism. Additional case reports and diagnostic cohort findings have since expanded the phenotype, though the total number of reported probands remains modest, so some curation bodies may still rate the evidence as moderate rather than definitive. Human genetic data, not merely animal or in vitro work, underpin the association, favoring Established with residual weight on Existing.

Pitt-Hopkins-like syndrome 2 (OMIM 614325) is defined by biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) loss-of-function variants/deletions in NRXN1, first reported by Zweier et al. (2009) in consanguineous families with severe intellectual disability, breathing anomalies, and autistic features resembling Pitt-Hopkins syndrome. Subsequent independent human reports (e.g., Harrison et al., Duong et al., and later cohort/review studies of biallelic NRXN1 alterations) replicated the association in additional unrelated probands. The evidence is human genetic, with segregation in consanguineous families and consistent phenotype, supporting an established causal relationship. Some residual uncertainty exists because the total number of reported biallelic cases is modest and the phenotype is variable, which is why a portion of probability is retained for "Existing."

Pitt-Hopkins-like syndrome 2 (OMIM 614325) is defined as an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants/deletions in NRXN1, first reported by Zweier et al. (2009) in consanguineous families with severe intellectual disability, breathing anomalies, and Pitt-Hopkins-like features. Additional independent probands with homozygous or compound heterozygous NRXN1 deletions/truncating variants have been reported subsequently, supporting replication in humans. Heterozygous NRXN1 deletions are separately linked to susceptibility for autism, schizophrenia, and developmental delay, which reinforces the gene's role in neurodevelopment. The main uncertainty is the relatively modest number of biallelic cases and phenotypic variability, which could lead some curators to a "moderate/limited" rather than "definitive" classification, so a portion of the weight is assigned to Existing.

Pitt-Hopkins-like syndrome 2 (OMIM 614325) is defined in the literature as an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic NRXN1 (alpha-neurexin) loss-of-function variants, first delineated by Zweier et al. (2009), who reported homozygous NRXN1 deletions/mutations in patients with severe intellectual disability, breathing anomalies and a Pitt-Hopkins-like phenotype. Subsequent independent human reports (e.g., Harrison et al. 2011, Duong et al. 2012, and additional consanguineous families) have described further probands with homozygous or compound heterozygous NRXN1 alterations and overlapping features, providing replication in humans. Supporting biology (Nrxn1α knockout mice, synaptic adhesion function) reinforces plausibility but is not the primary evidence base. The main residual uncertainty is the relatively small number of biallelic cases and phenotypic heterogeneity, which leaves some weight on "Existing" rather than fully definitive classification.

THAP1 was identified by Fuchs et al. (2009, Nature Genetics) as the gene for DYT6 (torsion dystonia 6) through linkage and sequencing in Amish–Mennonite families, with a founder insertion/deletion frameshift mutation. Since then, well over a hundred distinct pathogenic THAP1 variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, largely in the THAP DNA-binding domain and coiled-coil domain) have been reported in independent probands and families of diverse ethnic backgrounds with autosomal dominant, reduced-penetrance craniocervical and laryngeal dystonia. Functional studies confirm impaired DNA binding and dysregulation of TOR1A transcription, supporting causality. This is a canonical, replicated human gene–disease association recognized by OMIM (#602629) and gene curation efforts, so the evidence is unambiguously "Established."

THAP1 was identified as the gene for DYT6 (torsion dystonia 6) by Fuchs et al. (2009) through linkage and sequencing in Amish–Mennonite families, and the finding has been extensively replicated in independent probands and families worldwide. Dozens of pathogenic missense, nonsense, and frameshift variants have been reported, largely clustering in the THAP DNA-binding domain, with autosomal dominant inheritance and reduced penetrance. Functional studies demonstrate impaired DNA binding and dysregulated transcription (e.g., of TOR1A), supporting the mechanism, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive. THAP1–DYT6 is a canonical, curated gene–disease relationship in OMIM and ClinGen-level resources.

THAP1 was identified as the causative gene for DYT6 (torsion dystonia 6) by Fuchs et al. (2009) through linkage and sequencing in Amish-Mennonite families, with subsequent identification of numerous pathogenic missense, nonsense, and frameshift mutations in independent probands and families of diverse ethnic backgrounds worldwide. Mutations cluster in the THAP DNA-binding domain and impair transcriptional regulation of TOR1A, providing a coherent mechanism. Segregation with reduced penetrance has been repeatedly demonstrated in multigenerational human families, and THAP1 sequencing is standard clinical practice for early-onset craniocervical/laryngeal dystonia. This is an unambiguous, replicated human gene–disease relationship (OMIM 602629 / DYT6, #602629).

SACS was identified in 2000 (Engert et al., Nature Genetics) as the causative gene for autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS), with founder mutations (e.g., 6594delT and R2502X) in the Quebec Charlevoix-Saguenay population. Since then, hundreds of distinct loss-of-function and missense variants have been reported in independent probands and families worldwide (Japan, Turkey, Tunisia, Italy, Netherlands, Spain, etc.), consistently segregating with the classic triad of spastic ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, and retinal nerve fiber hypermyelination. Functional studies of sacsin (a chaperone-like protein affecting mitochondrial dynamics and neurofilament organization) and Sacs knockout mouse models further corroborate the mechanism, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive. This is a textbook gene–disease pair with ClinGen/OMIM-level "definitive" classification.

SACS (encoding sacsin) was identified in 2000 by Engert et al. as the gene mutated in autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS), with founder mutations (e.g., 6594delT, R2502X) in the Quebec Charlevoix-Saguenay population. Since then, hundreds of distinct loss-of-function and missense variants have been reported in independent probands and families worldwide (Tunisia, Japan, Turkey, Italy, Netherlands, Spain), establishing a clear recessive causal relationship with a characteristic phenotype of spasticity, cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, and retinal nerve fiber thickening. Functional and mouse-model data (Sacs knockout) corroborate the mechanism, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive. This is a textbook example of an Established gene–disease relationship, curated as "Definitive" by ClinGen/gene curation panels.

SACS was identified by Engert et al. (2000, Nature Genetics) as the gene mutated in autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) through linkage and mutation analysis in Quebec founder populations, with the recurrent 6594delT and R2502X founder mutations. Since then, hundreds of distinct biallelic SACS variants have been reported in independent probands and families worldwide (Japan, Turkey, Tunisia, Italy, Netherlands, Spain, etc.), with consistent genotype–phenotype correlation including retinal nerve fiber hypermyelination and pontine hypointensities. Functional studies of sacsin (an HSP70/J-domain chaperone affecting mitochondrial dynamics and neurofilament organization) and Sacs knockout mice further support causality, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive. This is a textbook Mendelian gene–disease pair with ClinGen/OMIM-level definitive classification.

phenotype: mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 22
justification: COX16 encodes a cytochrome c oxidase assembly factor implicated in copper delivery to COX2, and functional studies (e.g., knockout human cell lines) firmly establish its role in complex IV biogenesis, providing a strong biological rationale. Beyond this, human genetic evidence exists: biallelic COX16 variants have been reported in patient(s) with fatal infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/encephalopathy and isolated COX deficiency, which prompted the OMIM designation of mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 22. However, the number of independent probands/families is very small (roughly one to two reports), so the evidence is credible but not yet extensively replicated. This places most weight on "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Established" if additional families have been described, and a smaller share for "Hypothesized" given the largely in vitro nature of much supporting work.

phenotype: mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 22
justification: COX16 encodes an assembly factor required for COX2 maturation and copper delivery in cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) biogenesis, a biology directly relevant to complex IV deficiency, and this was first established in yeast and human cell knockout studies. Human genetic evidence exists: biallelic loss-of-function COX16 variants have been reported in patients with fatal infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis and isolated complex IV deficiency, which underlies the OMIM designation MC4DN22. However, to my knowledge the human evidence is limited to only one or very few probands/families, with supportive functional rescue experiments rather than broad replication. This favors "Existing" over "Established," with residual weight on "Established" in case additional independent probands have since been reported, and some weight on "Hypothesized" reflecting the heavy reliance on cell-based functional data.

phenotype: mitochondrial complex IV deficiency, nuclear type 22
justification: COX16 is a well-characterized COX2 copper-delivery/assembly factor for cytochrome c oxidase, and human cell studies (e.g., Aich et al.) demonstrated that its loss causes complex IV assembly failure, providing strong biological plausibility. Beyond functional work, at least one clinical report describes biallelic COX16 variants in a patient with fatal infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis and isolated complex IV deficiency, which formed the basis for the OMIM entry MC4DN22 (619062). However, the human genetic evidence appears limited to one or very few probands, without broad independent replication, so gene–disease validity is likely "limited/moderate" rather than definitive. Therefore most weight goes to Existing, with some probability that additional confirmatory cases have since accumulated (Established) and a small residual for purely functional-only evidence (Hypothesized).

Osteootohepatoenteric syndrome (OMIM 619377) is defined by biallelic loss-of-function variants in UNC45A, first reported by Esteve et al. (AJHG, 2018) in multiple unrelated consanguineous families presenting with cholestasis, congenital diarrhea, sensorineural hearing loss, and bone fragility. Subsequent human cohort reports (e.g., Duclaux-Loras et al. and additional case series in congenital diarrheal disorder/cholestasis cohorts) replicated the association in independent probands, with supporting functional work on UNC45A as a myosin co-chaperone affecting enterocyte and hepatocyte polarity/microvillus organization. The evidence base therefore includes multiple independent human families with segregating biallelic variants plus mechanistic support, satisfying criteria for an Established gene–disease relationship. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" given the relatively limited total number of reported patients for this ultra-rare disorder.

Osteootohepatoenteric syndrome (OMIM 619377) is defined by biallelic loss-of-function variants in UNC45A, first reported by Esteve et al. (Genetics in Medicine, 2018) in multiple unrelated consanguineous families presenting with congenital diarrhea, cholestasis/bile duct paucity, sensorineural deafness, and bone fragility. Subsequent independent reports and functional studies (e.g., Duclaux-Loras et al.) confirmed additional patients and demonstrated defects in myosin chaperone function affecting enterocyte brush border and epithelial trafficking, providing mechanistic support in patient-derived cells.
