Because the evidence includes multiple independent human probands/families with segregating biallelic variants plus supporting functional work, the relationship is best classified as Established. A small residual probability is assigned to Existing to account for the relatively limited total number of reported cases for this ultra-rare syndrome.

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in UNC45A were reported by Esteve et al. (2018, J Med Genet/Genetics in Medicine) in multiple unrelated consanguineous families with a syndrome combining cholestatic liver disease, congenital diarrhea, sensorineural hearing loss, and bone fragility — the phenotype now designated osteootohepatoenteric syndrome (OMIM 619377). Subsequent independent case reports and cohort studies of congenital diarrheal disorders/microvillus-inclusion-like enteropathy have replicated the association in additional human probands, with supportive functional work on UNC45A as a myosin (NM-II/MYO5B) co-chaperone explaining the epithelial trafficking defect. The mechanistic and animal/cell data are consistent with, and reinforce, the human genetic findings rather than substituting for them. Therefore the gene–disease relationship is best classified as Established, with only small residual probability for "Existing" given the relatively small number of reported families.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies
justification: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SMPD4 (a neutral sphingomyelinase, nSMase3) were reported by Magini et al. (AJHG, 2019) in over 20 affected individuals from multiple unrelated, consanguineous and non-consanguineous families presenting with congenital microcephaly, arthrogryposis, simplified gyration/structural brain anomalies, and early lethality. This gene–disease pair is recognized in OMIM as "neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies" (NEDMABA, MIM 618622), and additional case reports/cohorts have since replicated the association with expanded phenotypes. Segregation in multiple independent families, consistent recessive loss-of-function mechanism, and supportive functional data (altered sphingolipid metabolism, cell-cycle/nuclear envelope defects in patient cells) constitute strong human evidence. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Established, with only minimal residual probability for a weaker classification.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies
justification: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SMPD4 (a neutral sphingomyelinase, nSMase3) were reported by Magini et al. (2019, AJHG) in a large cohort of over 20 affected individuals from multiple unrelated, consanguineous and non-consanguineous families with congenital microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies; this defined the OMIM entity NEDMABA (MIM 618622). Additional independent case reports and cohort studies (including further families from Middle Eastern, Asian, and European populations) have replicated the association, and functional work supports a role for SMPD4 in nuclear envelope/ER membrane dynamics and neural progenitor proliferation. The gene–disease relationship is curated as definitive/strong by clinical resources such as OMIM and GenCC. Evidence is human genetic and replicated across independent probands, so the relationship is clearly Established, with only minimal residual probability for a lesser category.

phenotype: neurodevelopmental disorder with microcephaly, arthrogryposis, and structural brain anomalies
justification: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SMPD4 (neutral sphingomyelinase 3) were reported by Magini et al. (AJHG 2019) in over 20 affected individuals from multiple unrelated, consanguineous and non-consanguineous families with congenital microcephaly, arthrogryposis, simplified gyration/structural brain anomalies, and early lethality. This gene–disease pair is recognized in OMIM as a distinct entity (NEDMABA, MIM #618622) and has been replicated in subsequent independent case reports and cohorts from different populations, including prenatal/fetal presentations. Functional work in patient fibroblasts and cell models supports a nuclear envelope/sphingomyelin metabolism mechanism, complementing the human genetic evidence rather than substituting for it. The evidence is therefore multi-family, human, and replicated, meeting the "Established" threshold with little residual uncertainty.

Biallelic TRNT1 variants are well known to cause a phenotypic spectrum ranging from severe SIFD (sideroblastic anemia with B-cell immunodeficiency, periodic fevers and developmental delay) to a milder, later-onset phenotype of retinitis pigmentosa with erythrocytic microcytosis (RPEM), which has its own OMIM entry (#616959) following DeLuca et al. (2016), who identified hypomorphic TRNT1 mutations in human patients with sideroblastic anemia-free retinal degeneration. Additional independent patients and families with partial/hypomorphic TRNT1 alleles presenting with retinal dystrophy, microcytosis, and variable immunodeficiency have subsequently been reported, supporting replication in humans. Functional work (CCA-adding enzyme deficiency affecting mitochondrial and cytoplasmic tRNA maturation) provides a coherent mechanism, and patient fibroblast/zebrafish models corroborate the retinal phenotype. Some residual uncertainty remains only because the number of reported RPEM-specific probands is modest and the phenotype overlaps a continuum with SIFD, so a small weight is left for "Existing."

TRNT1 encodes the CCA-adding enzyme for tRNA maturation; biallelic loss-of-function variants cause SIFD (sideroblastic anemia with immunodeficiency, fevers, developmental delay), while hypomorphic variants produce a milder allelic phenotype of retinitis pigmentosa with erythrocytic microcytosis (RPEM; OMIM 616959), first delineated by DeLuca et al. (2016) in multiple probands from independent families with functional validation. Subsequent case reports and cohort studies of TRNT1 deficiency have described additional patients with retinal dystrophy and microcytosis, supporting replication in humans. This gene–disease pair is recognized in OMIM and clinical retinal dystrophy gene panels. The main residual uncertainty is that the number of independent RPEM-specific probands is modest relative to classic SIFD, leaving some weight on "Existing."

TRNT1 (CCA-adding tRNA nucleotidyltransferase) biallelic variants cause a spectrum ranging from severe SIFD (sideroblastic anemia with B-cell immunodeficiency, periodic fevers and developmental delay) to a milder, later-onset phenotype of retinitis pigmentosa with erythrocytic microcytosis, recognized as a distinct OMIM entry (RPEM, #616959). Multiple independent human reports (e.g., DeLuca et al. 2016; Hull et al. 2016; subsequent case series of retinal dystrophy cohorts) describe hypomorphic TRNT1 variants in unrelated probands/families with sideroblastic anemia-free microcytosis and progressive rod-cone degeneration, often with segregation and functional validation of reduced CCA-adding activity. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence supporting causation, so "Established" dominates. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because the milder RPEM phenotype is rarer and some might consider the case count modest relative to the classic SIFD presentation.

TMEM135 is best characterized as a regulator of mitochondrial fission/fusion balance and peroxisomal dynamics (acting with DRP1/FIS1), with most published work in mouse models (retinal degeneration, adipose/lipid metabolism) and cell lines rather than in patients. Because disturbances of mitochondrial dynamics (e.g., DNM1L, MFF, MFN2) are a well-recognized mechanism of neurodevelopmental and neurological disease, there is a strong biological rationale supporting a "Hypothesized" relationship. I am not aware of replicated human clinical genetic studies reporting pathogenic TMEM135 variants in probands with intellectual disability, autism, or global developmental delay, so "Established" is very unlikely. A small probability is retained for "Existing" given the possibility of isolated case reports, CNVs spanning 11q14.2, or incidental de novo variants appearing in large exome cohorts of developmental disorders, though such evidence would be limited and non-definitive. The remaining weight on "Novel" reflects the real chance that no human variant-based or phenotype-relevant neurodevelopmental evidence exists at all.

TMEM135 encodes a peroxisomal/mitochondrial transmembrane protein that regulates mitochondrial fission–fusion balance and lipid metabolism; the best-characterized phenotypes come from mouse models (Fun014/TMEM135 mutants with retinal degeneration and altered mitochondrial dynamics) and from links to peroxisomal biology, which is a mechanism broadly relevant to neurodevelopment. I am not aware of replicated human clinical genetic studies establishing pathogenic TMEM135 variants as a cause of intellectual disability, autism, or other neurodevelopmental disorders. At most, TMEM135 may appear incidentally within CNV intervals, candidate-gene lists from exome/GWAS screens, or single unreplicated reports, which would support only limited "Existing" evidence. Because the strongest supporting data are animal/in vitro and pathway-based rather than human variant-based, the bulk of probability belongs in "Hypothesized," with meaningful residual weight on "Novel" given the absence of any clear neurodevelopmental phenotype attribution.

TMEM135 is best characterized as a regulator of mitochondrial fission/fusion balance and peroxisomal dynamics (acting with DRP1/DNM1L), and its mouse models show retinal degeneration, altered mitochondrial morphology and metabolic phenotypes — biology that is directly relevant to neurodevelopmental disease because related fission machinery genes (DNM1L, MFF, PEX genes) cause encephalopathy and developmental delay. However, the strongest evidence remains from mouse and cellular work rather than human genetics, favoring the Hypothesized category. Human association data are sparse: TMEM135 appears mainly in GWAS/expression contexts (adiposity, retinal aging) and occasionally within large CNV/exome candidate lists, without replicated proband-level evidence for a neurodevelopmental phenotype. I therefore assign modest weight to Existing for the possibility of isolated case reports or candidate variants in NDD cohorts, minimal weight to Established, and a substantial residual to Novel given the lack of any well-known human gene–disease entity.

OMIM defines bleeding disorder, platelet-type, 22 as an autosomal recessive condition attributed to EPHB2, based principally on a single consanguineous family (Berrou et al., Blood 2018) in which two brothers with a lifelong bleeding tendency carried compound heterozygous/homozygous EPHB2 variants, supported by platelet functional assays showing defective aggregation, granule secretion and outside-in signaling. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence with strong mechanistic support (EPH/ephrin signaling is known to contribute to platelet contact-dependent activation and clot stability). However, replication in independent probands or families is sparse to absent, so the evidence falls short of the "established/definitive" threshold typically requiring multiple unrelated cases. A minority of probability is retained for "Established" in case additional families have since been reported, and a small share for "Hypothesized" since much of the supporting data is functional/in vitro or from mouse models rather than replicated human genetics.

Bleeding disorder, platelet-type, 22 (BDPLT22) is attributed in OMIM to biallelic EPHB2 variants, based principally on a single consanguineous/related family reported by Berrou et al. (Blood, 2018), in which two siblings with compound heterozygous/homozygous EPHB2 mutations had a severe platelet function defect, supported by functional studies showing impaired platelet aggregation, granule secretion, and signaling. This is credible human genetic evidence but derives from very few probands, so the gene–disease relationship is best described as limited rather than replicated across independent families. Supporting biology (EphB2/ephrin signaling in platelet contact-dependent activation, murine and in vitro data) reinforces plausibility but would itself only justify "Hypothesized." Therefore most weight goes to Existing, with some residual probability for Established should additional independent probands have since been reported.

Bleeding disorder, platelet-type, 22 (BDPLT22; OMIM 618462) was defined on the basis of biallelic EPHB2 variants reported by Berrou et al. (Blood, 2018) in a consanguineous/affected family with a severe platelet function defect, supported by functional studies showing impaired platelet aggregation, granule secretion, and outside-in signaling in patient platelets. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence with strong functional corroboration, but the number of independent probands/families is very small, and replication in additional unrelated patients is limited. EPHB2 biology in platelets (Eph/ephrin contact-dependent signaling stabilizing thrombi) provides a coherent mechanism, which would support at least a hypothesized link even absent genetics. Given the essentially single-family human evidence, "Existing" is most appropriate, with some probability that additional reported cases have elevated it toward "Established."

DHX34 encodes an RNA helicase that acts as a key activator of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), promoting UPF1 phosphorylation by SMG1 and remodeling of the surveillance complex. Multiple NMD pathway genes (UPF3B, UPF2, SMG9, SMG8, EIF4A3, RBM8A) are well-established intellectual disability/neurodevelopmental genes, giving DHX34 a strong biological rationale for an ID link, which places most weight on "Hypothesized." However, the human genetic evidence for DHX34 itself points to a different phenotype — germline DHX34 variants have been reported in familial myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukemia — and I am not aware of replicated clinical reports of DHX34 variants causing intellectual disability. Sporadic candidate variants could appear in large ID/autism exome cohorts, so a small allowance is made for "Existing," and "Established" is very unlikely. A meaningful residual is given to "Novel" in case the only connection is pathway-level inference without any phenotype-specific literature.

DHX34 is an RNA helicase that acts as a key activator of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) by promoting SMG1-mediated UPF1 phosphorylation, a pathway in which several components (UPF3B, UPF2, SMG9, SMG8, EIF4A3) are established or strong candidate intellectual disability genes; this provides a direct biological rationale placing most weight on "Hypothesized." The best-documented human genetic association for DHX34 is germline variation predisposing to familial myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukemia, not neurodevelopmental disease. I am not aware of replicated clinical reports of DHX34 variants causing intellectual disability, so "Established" is very unlikely. There remains a modest chance that DHX34 has appeared as a candidate gene in large exome/genome sequencing cohorts of developmental disorders or consanguineous ID families, which would support "Existing." A small residual probability is given to "Novel" if no ID-relevant literature exists beyond generic NMD pathway biology.

DHX34 is an RNA helicase that functions as an activator of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), promoting SMG1-mediated UPF1 phosphorylation. The NMD pathway is strongly and repeatedly implicated in intellectual disability through genes such as UPF3B, UPF2, SMG9, SMG8, EIF4A3 and RBM8A, giving DHX34 a biologically compelling but indirect link, which best fits the "Hypothesized" category. The best-characterized human disease association for DHX34 is germline variation in familial myelodysplasia/acute myeloid leukemia, not neurodevelopmental disease. I am not aware of replicated, or even clearly documented single, reports of DHX34 variants causing intellectual disability in patients, though incidental candidate-gene listings in large NDD exome cohorts cannot be excluded, hence a modest weight on "Existing." Established evidence appears absent.

SLC35B2 encodes the Golgi PAPS transporter (PAPST1) required for sulfation of proteoglycans and sulfatides, biology that directly explains a combined skeletal (chondrodysplasia) and hypomyelinating CNS phenotype. To my knowledge, biallelic SLC35B2 variants were reported in patients with a chondrodysplasia plus hypomyelinating leukodystrophy phenotype (a Brain-type report circa 2022), which led to the OMIM designation HLD26 with chondrodysplasia; this is human genetic evidence with supportive functional sulfation assays. Because the reported cohort appears small (a few probands/families) and independent replication is limited, the evidence sits between definitive and limited, so points are split largely between Established and Existing. A small residual probability is given to Hypothesized in case the human evidence is confined to a single family with mainly mechanistic/in vitro support, and minimal weight to Novel since the gene–disease link is explicitly recognized in disease nomenclature.

SLC35B2 encodes the Golgi PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate) transporter required for sulfation of glycosaminoglycans and sulfatides, biology that plausibly links to both cartilage/skeletal dysplasia and myelin abnormalities. A homozygous missense variant in SLC35B2 was reported in a consanguineous family with hypomyelinating leukodystrophy and chondrodysplasia (basis for OMIM HLD26, #619653), supported by functional studies of impaired sulfation. However, to my knowledge the human genetic evidence rests on a very small number of probands from essentially one family with limited independent replication, so the association is credible but not definitively established. Therefore most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful probability for "Established" if additional cohorts have since been described, and residual weight to "Hypothesized" if the primary support is judged largely functional/in vitro.

SLC35B2 encodes the Golgi PAPS (3'-phosphoadenosine 5'-phosphosulfate) transporter required for sulfation of glycosaminoglycans and sulfatides, biology directly relevant to both cartilage/skeletal development and myelination. OMIM designates "Leukodystrophy, hypomyelinating, 26, with chondrodysplasia" (HLD26) as caused by biallelic SLC35B2 variants, based on a report of affected individuals from more than one family with functional support (impaired sulfation), which indicates a curated gene–disease relationship. However, the total number of independently reported probands appears small and replication beyond the original describing study is limited, so the evidence may be judged moderate rather than definitive. I therefore weight Established most heavily but retain substantial probability for Existing (single credible human study with limited replication), with only minor weight on Hypothesized or Novel.

USP44 encodes a deubiquitinase acting on H2BK120ub (and on the mitotic checkpoint via APC/C-Cdc20), placing it directly in the histone-modification/chromatin pathway highlighted in congenital heart disease exome studies. My recollection is that USP44 appeared among candidate genes with de novo variants in the Zaidi et al. (Nature 2013) CHD trio study, presented within the H3K4me/H2BK120ub network, which would constitute human but limited, non-replicated evidence—fitting "Existing." However, no independent replication, family segregation, or gene-level statistical significance in larger cohorts (e.g., PCGC/Jin et al.) is established, so "Established" is very unlikely. Substantial probability remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the support is pathway/chromatin-biology-based (and USP44's ciliogenesis/centrosome roles are relevant to laterality defects) rather than from confirmed causal human variants. A small residual probability of "Novel" accounts for the chance that my recollection of a specific human variant report is inaccurate.

USP44 is a deubiquitinase that removes ubiquitin from H2BK120 (and regulates Cdc20/spindle checkpoint), and it was highlighted in large-scale human congenital heart disease exome studies (e.g., the Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium de novo mutation analyses) as part of the H3K4 methylation/H2BK120 ubiquitination pathway enriched for damaging de novo variants in CHD probands. That constitutes at least one credible human genetic report, but the evidence rests on very few probands without independent replication or segregation data, so it falls short of "Established." Much of the supporting rationale is pathway- and chromatin-biology based (shared mechanism with RNF20, UBE2B, KMT2D), which also supports a "Hypothesized" assignment if the human variant evidence is judged too sparse. There is no gene-level statistical association or recurrent variant burden specifically implicating USP44 as a CHD gene, making "Established" unlikely, and complete absence of any plausible link ("Novel") is also improbable given the pathway membership.

USP44 is an H2BK120 deubiquitinase and spindle-assembly-checkpoint regulator, placing it in the histone H2B ubiquitination/H3K4 methylation pathway that was highlighted by large de novo mutation exome studies of congenital heart disease (e.g., the Pediatric Cardiac Genomics Consortium/Zaidi et al. work), where USP44 was cited among candidate chromatin-pathway genes carrying rare damaging de novo variants in CHD probands. This provides at most single-proband, pathway-level human evidence rather than replicated causal proof, which fits "Existing" but falls well short of "Established" gene–disease validity (it is not a ClinGen-validated or clinically actionable CHD gene). A substantial share of probability also belongs to "Hypothesized," since much of the support is mechanistic/pathway-based (chromatin regulation, mitotic checkpoint, aneuploidy models) rather than direct human variant-phenotype association. A modest residual is left for "Novel" in case my recollection of USP44 in the CHD de novo variant lists is inaccurate and the gene is only incidentally co-mentioned.

OFC10 (OMIM 613705) is attributed to SUMO1 based largely on a single landmark human case (Alkuraya et al., Science 2006) in which a de novo balanced translocation disrupted SUMO1 in a patient with cleft lip and palate, supported by Sumo1 haploinsufficient mice showing cleft palate and by expression in the palatal shelf/lip fusion regions. Subsequent human association/sequencing studies of SUMO1 variants in nonsyndromic cleft lip/palate cohorts have given inconsistent or weak replication, so causality is not firmly established across multiple independent probands or families. This makes "Existing" the best fit: credible human genetic evidence exists but is limited and not definitively replicated. Some weight goes to "Established" because OMIM formally designates OFC10 for SUMO1, and some to "Hypothesized" because much of the supporting mechanistic evidence is murine/functional rather than human variant-based.

SUMO1 is the designated gene for orofacial cleft 10 (OMIM 613705) based largely on a single human proband reported by Alkuraya et al. (Science, 2006) with a de novo balanced translocation disrupting SUMO1 at 2q33 and cleft lip/palate, supported by haploinsufficient Sumo1 mice showing clefting and expression at the palatal seam. Some candidate-gene association studies of SUMO1 variants in nonsyndromic CL/P populations have been reported, but results are inconsistent and several replication efforts (e.g., large Irish and other cohorts) were negative. Thus there is at least one credible human genetic observation, but the evidence rests on a single disruptive case plus equivocal association data rather than multiple independent probands/families, favoring "Existing" over "Established." A meaningful share of points goes to "Hypothesized" because much of the causal support is animal/functional rather than human variant data, and some curation efforts consider the human evidence limited or disputed.

OFC10 (MIM 613705) was designated on the basis of a single human proband reported by Alkuraya et al. (Science, 2006), in whom a de novo balanced translocation t(2;8) disrupted SUMO1, causing cleft lip and palate; supporting functional data came from Sumo1 haploinsufficient mice showing clefting and from expression in palatal/lip fusion regions. Subsequent human association and resequencing studies (e.g., in Chinese and other populations) have given mixed or weak results, and no large series of independent probands with clearly pathogenic SUMO1 coding variants has been replicated. This places the pair firmly above "hypothesized" (there is at least one credible human genetic observation) but short of "established" causal evidence from multiple independent families. Some weight remains for "hypothesized" because much of the compelling mechanistic evidence derives from mouse and in vitro work, and gene–disease curation efforts might consider the human evidence limited or disputed.

phenotype: encephalopathy, progressive, early-onset, with episodic rhabdomyolysis
justification: TRAPPC2L is the accepted gene for OMIM #618331 (progressive early-onset encephalopathy with episodic rhabdomyolysis), first reported by Milev et al. (2017) in two siblings from a consanguineous family with a homozygous missense variant (p.Asp37Tyr), supported by patient fibroblast studies showing altered RAB11 activation and TRAPP complex dysfunction. A subsequent independent report (Al-Deri et al.) described another homozygous TRAPPC2L variant in a patient with a similar neurodevelopmental phenotype with disrupted TRAPP complex assembly, providing replication in humans. The total number of reported probands and families remains small, so gene–disease validity is typically curated as moderate rather than definitive, leaving the choice between "Established" and "Existing" genuinely balanced. Robust functional/mechanistic data exist but are supplementary to the human genetic evidence, so little weight goes to "Hypothesized" and essentially none to "Novel."

phenotype: encephalopathy, progressive, early-onset, with episodic rhabdomyolysis
justification: TRAPPC2L biallelic variants were reported by Milev et al. (2018, J Med Genet) in patients from two unrelated families with early-onset progressive encephalopathy and episodic rhabdomyolysis, including a homozygous p.Asp37Tyr in a consanguineous sibship and compound heterozygous variants in another proband, supported by yeast complementation and fibroblast studies showing impaired TRAPP complex function and RAB11 dysregulation. This underpins the OMIM entry EPEOR (#618331). Because the gene–disease relationship rests on a small number of probands from only a couple of families with limited independent replication, the evidence sits at the boundary between limited/moderate ("Existing") and definitively "Established." Human genetic evidence clearly exists, so Hypothesized and Novel receive minimal weight.

phenotype: encephalopathy, progressive, early-onset, with episodic rhabdomyolysis
justification: TRAPPC2L is the recognized gene for OMIM 618331 (encephalopathy, progressive, early-onset, with episodic rhabdomyolysis), first described by Milev et al. (2017, AJHG) in two affected siblings from a consanguineous family with a homozygous missense variant (p.Asp37Tyr), supported by patient-fibroblast and yeast functional studies showing disrupted TRAPP complex assembly and Golgi trafficking. A subsequent independent report (Al-Deri et al., 2021, J Med Genet) described an additional family with a distinct homozygous TRAPPC2L variant and a related neurodevelopmental phenotype, providing replication in humans. Thus there is credible human genetic evidence from more than one independent family plus mechanistic support, favoring an Established relationship, though the total number of reported probands remains small, which keeps meaningful probability on "Existing" (limited/moderate evidence). Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are unlikely given the direct, disease-specific human variant reports.

PITX1 is the best-known Mendelian gene for isolated/familial clubfoot: Gurnett et al. (2008) identified a heterozygous PITX1 E130K missense variant segregating with clubfoot and lower-limb anomalies in a large multigenerational human family, and OMIM lists "Clubfoot, congenital, with or without deficiency of long bones and/or mirror-image polydactyly" (119800) as caused by PITX1 variants. Additional human evidence includes 5q31 microdeletions/duplications encompassing PITX1 in probands with clubfoot and tibial hemimelia (Alvarado et al., 2010) and copy-number variation studies in clubfoot cohorts. Supporting functional data (Pitx1 haploinsufficient mice develop hindlimb/clubfoot-like phenotypes) reinforce causality but are not the primary basis. Because the human evidence rests on a limited number of families and rare CNVs rather than broad replication across many independent probands, some probability remains on "Existing."

PITX1 is the best-established Mendelian gene for isolated congenital clubfoot: Gurnett et al. (2008) identified a heterozygous PITX1 E130K missense variant segregating in a large multigenerational family with clubfoot, tibial hemimelia and preaxial polydactyly, and functional assays showed reduced transactivation. Subsequent human studies (Alvarado et al., 2010/2011; Klopocki et al.) reported 5q31 microdeletions and microduplications encompassing PITX1 in additional independent clubfoot probands and families, providing replication across independent human cohorts and variant types. OMIM lists "Clubfoot, congenital, with or without deficiency of long bones and/or mirror-image polydactyly" (CCF) as PITX1-related, and Pitx1 heterozygous mouse models recapitulate hindlimb clubfoot-like phenotypes, supporting biological plausibility. Some uncertainty remains because the number of pathogenic point mutations in unrelated probands is still small and penetrance is variable, which is why a substantial share of probability is retained for "Existing." Minimal weight is given to Hypothesized or Novel since direct human genetic evidence clearly exists.

PITX1 is the best-characterized gene for isolated congenital clubfoot: Gurnett et al. (2008, AJHG) identified a heterozygous PITX1 p.E130K missense variant segregating with clubfoot and asymmetric lower-limb malformations in a large multigenerational family, and Alvarado et al. subsequently reported 5q31 microdeletions and duplications encompassing PITX1 in additional independent clubfoot probands. OMIM recognizes "Clubfoot, congenital, with or without deficiency of long bones and/or mirror-image polydactyly" (%119800) as PITX1-related, supporting a curated gene–disease relationship. Supporting biology (Pitx1-null and heterozygous mice with hindlimb/clubfoot-like defects, hindlimb-specific transcription factor role) reinforces causality but is not the primary evidence. The main uncertainty is the relatively small number of independent human families and incomplete penetrance/variable expressivity, which is why some weight remains on "Existing."

ASB10 (ankyrin repeat and SOCS box containing 10) was proposed as the gene underlying the GLC1F locus on chromosome 7q35-q36 by Pasutto et al. (2012), who reported rare coding variants in POAG probands from an Oregon GLC1F-linked family and additional German and US cohorts, supported by functional data showing reduced aqueous outflow with ASB10 knockdown in perfused human anterior segments and trabecular meshwork expression. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence, so "Existing" is the most fitting category. However, replication has been inconsistent—Fingert et al. (2012) and other cohort studies found similar rates of ASB10 variants in cases and controls, arguing against a causal role—so "Established" is not warranted. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the supporting mechanistic evidence is functional/in vitro rather than definitive human genetic causality, and a small amount for "Novel" given the failed replications.

ASB10 lies within the GLC1F interval on chromosome 7q36, and Pasutto, Keller and colleagues (Hum Mol Genet, 2012) reported rare coding variants in ASB10 in adult-onset POAG cohorts from Germany and Oregon, with supportive functional work showing effects on aqueous outflow facility in perfused anterior segments and trabecular meshwork expression. However, an independent replication study (Fingert et al., 2012) found no association between ASB10 variants and POAG, and subsequent curation efforts have regarded the gene–disease relationship as limited or disputed rather than definitive. Thus there is credible human genetic evidence from at least one study, but replication has been inconsistent, making "Existing" the most appropriate category. A minority of weight goes to "Established" (given the original multi-cohort report) and to "Hypothesized" (given that much supporting evidence is expression/functional rather than definitive human genetics).

ASB10 lies within the GLC1F locus on chromosome 7q36, and Keller et al. (2011) reported rare nonsynonymous ASB10 variants segregating with primary open-angle glaucoma in the original GLC1F family and enriched in independent US and German POAG cohorts, with supporting functional work (knockdown reducing aqueous outflow facility in perfused human anterior segments). Additional human case–control studies (e.g., in Pakistani and other cohorts) have reported ASB10 variants in POAG patients, supporting a human genetic association. However, a notable replication study (Fingert et al., 2012) found no significant association, and ASB10 is not consistently accepted as a definitively causal glaucoma gene by curation efforts. This mixture of at least one credible human genetic study plus functional support, but contested replication, best fits "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" and for a purely biological/functional (Hypothesized) interpretation.

ASCL1 (MASH1) is a proneural bHLH transcription factor with a central, well-documented role in neurogenesis, neural progenitor proliferation, interneuron and autonomic neuron specification, and Mash1-null mice show severe neuronal developmental defects — strong biological grounds for a hypothesized link to neurodevelopmental disorders. In humans, rare ASCL1 variants have been reported in small numbers of patients with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome/Haddad syndrome and Hirschsprung disease (neurocristopathies affecting autonomic nervous system development), which provides limited human genetic evidence that could be construed as a neurodevelopmental phenotype. However, ASCL1 is not a recognized gene for intellectual disability, autism, or developmental delay in ClinGen/DDG2P curation, and no replicated cohorts of NDD probands with pathogenic ASCL1 variants exist. Therefore the weight falls mainly on hypothesized (biology/animal models), with meaningful but non-definitive support for existing based on the CCHS/HSCR human variant reports.

ASCL1 (MASH1) is a proneural bHLH transcription factor central to neurogenesis, neural progenitor proliferation, and autonomic/neural crest development, and Ascl1-null mice show severe defects in olfactory, autonomic, and CNS neuronal differentiation — very strong biological grounding for a hypothesized role in neurodevelopmental disease. Human genetic evidence exists but is limited: rare ASCL1 variants have been reported in congenital central hypoventilation syndrome and Hirschsprung disease/Haddad syndrome (e.g., de Pontual et al.), largely as candidate or modifier alleles alongside PHOX2B, and ASCL1 has been examined in neuroblastoma and some neuropsychiatric association studies. These neurocristopathy phenotypes are developmental nervous-system disorders, supporting some "Existing" weight, but ASCL1 is not an established intellectual disability/autism/developmental delay gene in curated databases (e.g., DDG2P, SFARI high-confidence, ClinGen), and there are no replicated multi-proband cohorts demonstrating causation of a classic NDD. Therefore most weight falls on Hypothesized, with meaningful but minority weight on Existing and very little on Established or Novel.

ASCL1 (MASH1) is a master proneural bHLH transcription factor essential for neurogenesis and autonomic/neural crest development, and Ascl1-null mice show severe defects in neuronal differentiation — strong biological grounds for a hypothesized role in neurodevelopmental phenotypes. In humans, rare heterozygous ASCL1 variants (e.g., polyalanine expansions and missense changes) have been reported in patients with congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, Haddad syndrome, and Hirschsprung disease, often as modifiers alongside PHOX2B, which supports limited human genetic evidence for a neurodevelopmental (neurocristopathy/autonomic) disorder. However, ASCL1 is not an established gene for intellectual disability, autism, or global developmental delay, and it does not appear as a definitive gene on diagnostic NDD panels or in ClinGen/DDG2P curation. Replication in independent probands for a core NDD phenotype is lacking, so the weight falls mainly between hypothesized biology and limited existing human evidence.

CRIPTO (TDGF1) is an EGF-CFC family Nodal co-receptor central to left–right patterning and cardiac morphogenesis, with strong mouse and in vitro data (Tdgf1-null embryos show cardiac and axial defects), which robustly supports at least a "Hypothesized" relationship. Beyond animal work, human mutation screening of NODAL-pathway genes (e.g., Roessler et al., AJHG 2008, and subsequent cohorts of conotruncal defects/heterotaxy/transposition of the great arteries) has reported rare TDGF1 variants with reduced signaling activity in patients with congenital heart disease and holoprosencephaly, supporting "Existing." However, these reports involve few probands, incomplete segregation data, and TDGF1 is often overshadowed by its paralog CFC1/CRYPTIC, for which the human CHD/heterotaxy evidence is much stronger; conflation between the two genes is common. Replication across independent families sufficient for gene–disease validity ("Established") is lacking, so most weight falls on Existing with substantial residual probability on Hypothesized.

CRIPTO (TDGF1) encodes an EGF-CFC co-receptor essential for Nodal signaling and left–right axis specification, and mouse/zebrafish models (oep, Cripto-null) show severe laterality and cardiac malformations, providing strong biological plausibility (Hypothesized floor). Beyond animal data, human studies—most notably Roessler et al. (AJHG 2008) screening NODAL-pathway genes (NODAL, FOXH1, TDGF1, CFC1) in patients with conotruncal heart defects and heterotaxy—reported rare TDGF1 missense variants with reduced signaling activity in patients, and TDGF1 variants have also been described in holoprosencephaly cohorts. This constitutes credible but limited, sparsely replicated human genetic evidence, favoring "Existing." Evidence falls short of "Established" because there are few independent probands/families, no clear segregation data, and gene–disease validity curations generally rate such Nodal co-factor genes as limited. "Novel" is essentially excluded given the direct pathway relevance and functional data.

CRIPTO (TDGF1) encodes an EGF-CFC co-receptor essential for Nodal signaling, left–right axis specification and cardiac morphogenesis, and murine Cripto-null embryos show severe cardiac and laterality defects, providing a very strong biological/animal rationale (Hypothesized floor). In humans, rare missense variants in TDGF1 have been reported in patients with conotruncal/laterality-related congenital heart disease in Nodal-pathway resequencing studies (e.g., Roessler et al., with NODAL, FOXH1, GDF1, CFC1), and TDGF1 variants were also identified in holoprosencephaly cohorts, supporting at least "Existing" human evidence. However, these reports involve few probands, often with incomplete segregation or functional-only support, and the related gene CFC1/CRYPTIC—not TDGF1 itself—carries the more robust human heterotaxy/CHD evidence, so replication for CRIPTO is limited. Therefore the weight sits mainly on Existing, with meaningful residual probability that reviewers would judge the human data insufficient (Hypothesized) and only a small chance of Established.

SCLT1 encodes a centriolar distal appendage protein that partners with CEP164 and FBF1 and is required for ciliogenesis, biology that is directly relevant to the photoreceptor connecting cilium and thus to retinal degeneration, giving strong support for at least a "Hypothesized" relationship. In humans, biallelic SCLT1 variants have been reported in orofaciodigital syndrome type IX and related ciliopathies, phenotypes that include ocular/retinal involvement (e.g., retinal coloboma, retinal dystrophy) and occasional nephronophthisis-with-retinal-degeneration presentations, which could qualify as limited "Existing" evidence for an RP-spectrum phenotype. However, SCLT1 is not a standard RetNet/diagnostic panel gene for non-syndromic retinitis pigmentosa, and I am not aware of replicated, independent human families in which SCLT1 variants clearly segregate with isolated RP. Therefore "Established" is very unlikely, "Existing" is plausible but uncertain, and a modest residual probability remains that any co-mention is incidental.

SCLT1 encodes a centriolar distal appendage protein that, with CEP83, CEP89, FBF1 and CEP164, is essential for ciliary vesicle docking and ciliogenesis—biology directly relevant to photoreceptor connecting cilium function and retinal degeneration, giving strong grounds for at least a "Hypothesized" relationship. Human mutations in SCLT1 have been reported in orofaciodigital syndrome type IX and other ciliopathy phenotypes that can include retinal/ocular abnormalities (e.g., coloboma, retinal dystrophy), which provides some limited human genetic support for retinal involvement, though not clearly for isolated retinitis pigmentosa. I am not aware of replicated, independent reports of SCLT1 variants causing classic non-syndromic RP, so "Established" is unlikely. Much of the supporting retinal evidence comes from ciliary biology and animal/cell models rather than direct RP genetics, so the bulk of weight sits between Hypothesized and Existing, with a residual chance the pairing is essentially unsupported (Novel).

SCLT1 encodes a centriolar distal appendage protein that partners with CEP164 and FBF1 in ciliogenesis, a pathway central to photoreceptor connecting-cilium function, so a biological rationale for retinal degeneration is strong (supporting "Hypothesized"). Human genetic evidence exists for SCLT1 in ciliopathies—biallelic variants were reported in orofaciodigital syndrome type IX (Adly et al., 2014), a condition featuring retinal anomalies such as coloboma, and isolated case reports describe SCLT1 variants in nephronophthisis-associated retinal dystrophy—which could qualify as limited "Existing" evidence for a retinitis pigmentosa–related phenotype. However, SCLT1 is not an accepted non-syndromic RP gene in curated resources such as RetNet/ClinGen, and replication in independent RP probands is lacking, so "Established" is very unlikely. Some probability remains for "Novel" if the reported retinal findings are colobomatous/syndromic rather than true rod-cone degeneration. Overall the evidence is best characterized as biologically compelling with sparse, non-definitive human data.

phenotype: gaze palsy, familial horizontal, with progressive scoliosis, 2
justification: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in DCC (netrin-1 receptor) were reported by Jamuar et al. (Nat Genet 2017) in multiple consanguineous families with "developmental split brain syndrome," featuring horizontal gaze palsy, progressive scoliosis, corpus callosum agenesis and intellectual disability, which is the basis of OMIM HGPPS2 (617542). Heterozygous DCC variants also cause congenital mirror movements and callosal agenesis in humans, supporting the gene's role in commissural axon midline guidance, mechanistically consistent with ROBO3-related HGPPS1. Supporting mouse Dcc/netrin-1 knockout data show failure of commissural crossing, reinforcing biological plausibility. Because human evidence comes largely from a small number of families in one landmark report with subsequent case additions, "Established" is most likely but some probability remains for "Existing" if replication is judged limited.

phenotype: gaze palsy, familial horizontal, with progressive scoliosis, 2
justification: HGPPS2 (OMIM 617542) is specifically defined by biallelic loss-of-function variants in DCC, reported by Jamuar et al. (Nature Genetics, 2017) in consanguineous families with "developmental split brain syndrome" featuring horizontal gaze palsy, progressive scoliosis, absent commissures, and intellectual disability. Multiple unrelated families/probands with distinct homozygous DCC variants were described, and additional case reports have since expanded the phenotype, supporting replication in humans. The mechanism is biologically coherent: DCC is the netrin-1 receptor essential for midline commissural axon guidance, paralleling ROBO3 in HGPPS1, and Dcc-null mice show commissural defects. The main uncertainty is the relatively small number of independent families, which leaves some weight on "Existing" rather than fully "Established."

phenotype: gaze palsy, familial horizontal, with progressive scoliosis, 2
justification: HGPPS2 (OMIM 617542) is specifically attributed to biallelic loss-of-function variants in DCC, most notably reported by Jamuar et al. (2017, Nature Genetics) describing "developmental split-brain syndrome" with horizontal gaze palsy, scoliosis, and intellectual disability in multiple consanguineous human families. DCC encodes the netrin-1 receptor essential for commissural axon midline crossing, providing a strong mechanistic rationale consistent with the ROBO3-related HGPPS1 phenotype, and Dcc-null mouse models recapitulate commissural defects. Heterozygous DCC variants are separately established in congenital mirror movements and corpus callosum agenesis, reinforcing human genetic relevance. Because the causal evidence rests largely on a small number of families from one landmark study plus subsequent case reports, points are split between Established and Existing, with the bulk favoring Established given curation by OMIM/ClinGen-type resources.

Ring dermoid of cornea (OMIM 180550) is an autosomal dominant anterior segment disorder, and a human genetic study (Xia et al., J Med Genet 2004) reported a PITX2 mutation segregating in a Chinese family with this phenotype, which is the basis for the OMIM molecular annotation. PITX2 is a well-established anterior segment dysgenesis gene (Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome, Peters anomaly), providing strong biological plausibility for corneal/limbal developmental defects. However, to my knowledge the ring dermoid association rests essentially on a single family with limited independent replication, which fits "Existing" rather than "Established." Some probability is retained for Established given the gene's robust role in overlapping anterior segment phenotypes, and a small amount for Hypothesized if the single report is considered insufficient direct variant evidence.

Ring dermoid of cornea (OMIM 180550) is listed in OMIM as an autosomal dominant phenotype attributed to PITX2, based largely on a report (Xia et al., Chinese family) identifying a PITX2 mutation segregating with annular limbal dermoids and associated anterior segment anomalies. PITX2 is a well-validated anterior segment developmental transcription factor causing Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome, iridogoniodysgenesis, and Peters anomaly, so the biological plausibility for corneal/limbal developmental defects is strong. However, replication in independent probands or families for the specific ring dermoid phenotype is scarce, so the evidence appears limited to essentially one human family rather than multiple independent studies. This places the weight on "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Established" given OMIM's gene–phenotype assignment and the broader spectrum of PITX2 anterior segment dysgenesis.

Ring dermoid of cornea (OMIM 180550) is an autosomal dominant limbal/corneal dermoid disorder that has been linked to PITX2 primarily through a single report (Xia et al., J Med Genet 2004) describing a PITX2 mutation segregating in a Chinese family with ring dermoid of the cornea. PITX2 is a well-established anterior segment dysgenesis gene (Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome), making its role in aberrant limbal/corneal development biologically highly plausible and supporting the causal interpretation. However, independent replication in additional unrelated probands with this specific phenotype is sparse, so the evidence falls short of firmly "Established" and is best characterized as credible but limited human genetic evidence. A minority probability is retained for "Hypothesized," reflecting the possibility that the association rests mainly on one family plus developmental/functional plausibility, and very little for "Novel."

VANGL1 is a core planar cell polarity gene, and its paralog Vangl2 underlies the loop-tail mouse craniorachischisis model, providing strong biological rationale. In humans, Kibar et al. (NEJM 2007) reported rare missense variants (V239I, R274Q, M328T) in familial and sporadic neural tube defect patients, and OMIM lists "Neural tube defects, susceptibility to" (NTD1) with VANGL1 variants; subsequent independent cohorts (Chinese, Italian, North American) identified additional rare heterozygous variants with functional effects on Dishevelled binding. However, evidence remains largely rare-variant case series with limited segregation data, incomplete penetrance, some variants seen in controls, and no robust replicated statistical association, so many curation efforts consider the relationship limited/disputed rather than definitively established. This favors "Existing" as most likely, with meaningful probability for "Established" given the human data across multiple independent probands.

Kibar et al. (NEJM 2007) first reported rare missense variants (V239I, R274Q, M328T) in VANGL1 in familial and sporadic human cases of caudal regression/spina bifida, and several subsequent human cohort studies (Italian, Chinese, Mexican, North American) identified additional rare, largely private missense variants in patients with neural tube defects, with functional data showing impaired Dishevelled binding. The planar cell polarity pathway role and Lp/Vangl2 mouse models with craniorachischisis provide strong supporting biology. However, evidence remains mostly rare variants in sporadic cases with limited segregation data, incomplete penetrance, and some non-replicating or negative studies, so the causal role is best described as reported but not definitively established. This places the bulk of probability on "Existing," with meaningful weight on "Established" given multiple independent human cohorts, and a small residual on "Hypothesized" reflecting the possibility that human variant evidence is judged insufficient/disputed.

VANGL1 is a core planar cell polarity gene, and the Vangl2 looptail mouse provides strong biological support, but human evidence is what matters here. Kibar et al. (NEJM 2007) reported the V239I variant segregating in a familial case of caudal regression/spina bifida plus additional missense variants (M328T, R274Q) in sporadic NTD patients, and follow-up studies in Italian, French-Canadian, and Chinese NTD cohorts identified further rare heterozygous missense variants, some with demonstrated loss of Dishevelled binding in vitro. OMIM lists "Neural tube defects, susceptibility to" for VANGL1, indicating recognized human genetic association. However, the variants are rare, mostly missense of incomplete penetrance, occasionally seen in controls, and no large replicated causal series exists, so most curation efforts classify the evidence as limited-to-moderate rather than definitive. Hence the bulk of probability falls on "Existing," with substantial residual weight on "Established."

CCT7 encodes a subunit of the CCT/TRiC chaperonin, which folds tubulin, actin, and other cytoskeletal/proteostasis clients essential for neuronal development; related subunits (CCT5 in hereditary sensory neuropathy, CCT2 in retinal dystrophy, CCT3 in neurodevelopmental phenotypes) give strong biological plausibility, supporting a "Hypothesized" relationship. I am not aware of any replicated human clinical cohort or family studies establishing CCT7 variants as a cause of complex neurodevelopmental disorder, so "Established" is very unlikely. There is a modest possibility that CCT7 appears as a candidate de novo or biallelic variant gene in large autism/developmental disorder exome datasets or single case reports, which would justify "Existing," but such evidence would be limited and unconfirmed. Because chaperonin biology is directly relevant rather than incidental, "Novel" is also less likely than "Hypothesized," though it remains plausible if no literature specifically links CCT7 to neurodevelopment.

CCT7 encodes a subunit of the CCT/TRiC cytosolic chaperonin, which folds tubulin, actin and other substrates essential for neuronal cytoskeletal function and proteostasis, giving strong biological plausibility for neurodevelopmental relevance; related subunits (e.g., CCT5 in hereditary sensory neuropathy with spastic paraplegia, CCT2 in retinal degeneration) have established human disease links, supporting a pathway-based hypothesis. However, I am not aware of a replicated, definitive human genetic study establishing CCT7 variants as a cause of a complex neurodevelopmental disorder, so "Established" is very unlikely. There may be occasional de novo or candidate variants reported in large autism/developmental disorder sequencing cohorts or interaction-network analyses, which would support limited "Existing" evidence, but such reports would be single, non-definitive observations. Much of the supporting data is functional/model-organism or proteomic (TRiC interaction with huntingtin and other neuronal proteins), which places most weight on "Hypothesized." Some probability remains for "Novel" if all co-mentions are incidental.

CCT7 encodes the eta subunit of the CCT/TRiC chaperonin, which folds tubulin and actin and modulates aggregation-prone proteins (e.g., huntingtin), making it biologically highly plausible for neurodevelopmental phenotypes; other subunits of the same complex have confirmed human neurological/ophthalmological disease associations (CCT5 in mutilating sensory neuropathy with spastic paraplegia, CCT2 in retinal dystrophy), reinforcing pathway-level relevance. However, I am not aware of replicated clinical genetic studies establishing that CCT7 variants cause a complex neurodevelopmental disorder, and CCT7 is not a recognized gene on major NDD/ID gene panels or in ClinGen/DDG2P curations. There may be incidental occurrences of CCT7 de novo or rare variants in large exome/genome NDD cohorts or in constrained-gene candidate lists, which would support a limited "Existing" claim, but such reports are not definitive. Consequently, most weight falls on "Hypothesized" (strong biology and model/pathway data without confirmed human variant evidence), with residual probability split between limited human evidence and true novelty.

TMOD1 encodes tropomodulin-1, the pointed-end capping protein of sarcomeric thin filaments, making it biologically highly relevant to cardiac contractile function. The strongest and best-known evidence is from animal work: cardiac-specific Tmod1 overexpression in transgenic mice (TOT mice) produces a severe dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype, and Tmod1 knockout mice show embryonic cardiac developmental failure; these are functional/model data supporting a "Hypothesized" classification rather than human genetic causation. Human evidence is sparse — TMOD1 has occasionally been included as a candidate on cardiomyopathy sequencing panels and rare variants have been reported anecdotally, but there is no robust, replicated segregation or case-control data, and it is not recognized as a definitive DCM gene by curation efforts such as ClinGen. Therefore most weight falls on Hypothesized, with some probability that a single limited human report qualifies it as Existing, and little support for Established.

TMOD1 (tropomodulin-1) is a pointed-end capping protein of sarcomeric thin filaments with clear biological relevance to cardiac contractility, and cardiac-specific Tmod1 overexpression in transgenic mice (the classic "TOT" model) produces a well-characterized dilated cardiomyopathy with myofibrillar disarray, providing strong but animal-based/mechanistic support. Altered TMOD1 expression has also been reported in failing human myocardium, again functional rather than genetic evidence. Human genetic data are sparse: TMOD1 has occasionally appeared as a candidate in sarcomere-gene resequencing or exome panels of cardiomyopathy cohorts with rare variants of uncertain significance, but there is no robust, replicated segregation or case–control evidence, and it is not an established/curated DCM gene in ClinGen or standard clinical panels. Therefore the weight falls heavily on "Hypothesized," with some allowance for isolated human variant reports supporting "Existing," and very little for "Established."

TMOD1 (tropomodulin 1) caps the pointed end of sarcomeric thin filaments and is directly relevant to cardiac myofibril length regulation, making biological plausibility high. The strongest evidence is non-human: cardiac-specific Tmod1 overexpression in transgenic mice produces a dilated cardiomyopathy phenotype, and Tmod1 knockout mice have lethal cardiac developmental defects; human data are largely limited to altered TMOD1 protein/expression levels in explanted failing/DCM hearts, which supports "Hypothesized" rather than variant-level causation. Some cardiomyopathy sequencing panels include TMOD1 and occasional rare variants have been reported in probands, giving modest weight to "Existing," but these are sparse, unreplicated, and TMOD1 is not recognized as a definitive DCM gene by curation efforts such as ClinGen. Therefore most probability falls on Hypothesized, with a secondary allocation to Existing and minimal support for Established.

POLD3 encodes an accessory subunit of DNA polymerase delta, and defects in the polymerase delta complex (POLD1, POLD2) are already recognized causes of syndromic combined immunodeficiency with replicative stress, T/B cell developmental defects and susceptibility to herpesviruses, providing strong biological plausibility. The existence of a numbered OMIM phenotype (immunodeficiency 122) implies at least one credible human report of biallelic POLD3 variants with functional validation (impaired replication, reduced polymerase delta activity, lymphopenia/hypogammaglobulinemia). However, POLD3 deficiency appears to be extremely rare, likely described in only one or a very small number of probands/families, so replication across independent cohorts is limited. Accordingly, most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful but lesser probability that the evidence is now considered definitive/established, and residual probability that the link rests mainly on pathway/functional inference.

POLD3 encodes an accessory subunit of DNA polymerase delta, and defects in the other polymerase delta subunits (POLD1, POLD2) are already established causes of syndromic combined immunodeficiency with replicative stress, providing a strong biological framework. For POLD3 specifically, I recall human reports of biallelic hypomorphic variants in patients with combined immunodeficiency/T-cell lymphopenia and syndromic features (developmental delay, metabolic abnormalities), which is consistent with a designated OMIM phenotype number (immunodeficiency 122). That evidence appears limited to one or a few small kindreds with supporting functional studies rather than broad independent replication, so "Existing" is the most probable category, with a substantial chance the entity is now considered "Established" if two or more unrelated families were described. A smaller share remains for "Hypothesized," in case the human genetic evidence is thinner than recalled and rests mainly on paralog biology and cellular/animal models. "Novel" is very unlikely given the clear mechanistic and nosological link to polymerase delta deficiency syndromes.

Human DNA polymerase delta subunit defects are an established cause of syndromic combined immunodeficiency, with POLD1 and POLD2 biallelic variants reported (Conde et al., JACI 2019) causing T-cell deficiency with replicative stress; POLD3 is the third accessory subunit of the same complex, and biallelic POLD3 variants have subsequently been reported in patients with immunodeficiency, giving rise to the OMIM designation "immunodeficiency 122." The evidence therefore appears to be human genetic and mechanistically supported (impaired replication, reduced polymerase delta function, T-cell lymphopenia), but is likely based on a small number of probands/families rather than broad replication. This favors "Existing" over "Established," with residual probability for "Established" if multiple independent kindreds have now been described. "Hypothesized" retains some weight because part of the supporting data is functional/in vitro rather than purely clinical genetic, and "Novel" is unlikely given the clear pathway and phenotype match.

SS18L1 encodes CREST, a calcium-responsive transactivator of the nBAF chromatin-remodeling complex, and was implicated in ALS by Chesi et al. (2013, Nature Neuroscience), who performed exome sequencing of sporadic ALS trios and identified de novo mutations in SS18L1 in human probands. Supporting biology exists: CREST interacts with FUS, localizes to stress granules, and mutant CREST impairs neurite outgrowth, providing a plausible mechanism shared with other ALS genes. However, subsequent screening of independent ALS cohorts has yielded few additional pathogenic variants, and SS18L1 is generally regarded as a candidate/limited-evidence ALS gene rather than a definitively established one (it is not among the confidently curated ALS genes in most gene-curation efforts). Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with a modest chance that curators would call it "Established" and some probability that the human genetic evidence is judged too weak, leaving mainly functional/mechanistic support ("Hypothesized").

SS18L1 encodes CREST, a calcium-responsive transactivator, which was implicated in ALS by Chesi et al. (2013), who identified de novo mutations (including a truncating variant) in sporadic ALS patient–parent trios by exome sequencing — a human genetic study. Functional work supports biological plausibility, as CREST interacts with FUS and mutant CREST alters stress-granule dynamics and neurite outgrowth in neurons. However, subsequent screening of additional ALS cohorts has yielded few confirmatory pathogenic variants, and gene-curation efforts generally regard the evidence as limited or disputed rather than definitive. This places the gene–disease relationship most consistently in the "Existing" category, with residual probability for "Established" (if replication is considered adequate) or "Hypothesized" (if the human variant evidence is judged insufficient and only mechanistic/functional data count).

SS18L1 encodes CREST, a calcium-responsive transactivator implicated in ALS by Chesi et al. (2013, Nature Neuroscience), who performed exome sequencing of sporadic ALS trios and identified de novo variants in SS18L1 in patients, with functional evidence of impaired dendritic outgrowth. Additional human support includes CREST's physical interaction with FUS, its recruitment to DNA damage sites, and its presence in stress granules, plus subsequent mutation screening in ALS cohorts that reported rare variants but with limited and inconsistent replication. This places the evidence clearly above the "hypothesized" threshold because human genetic variants in probands have been reported, but the small number of independent, well-replicated families/probands and lack of definitive segregation prevent an "established" classification (ALS gene curation efforts typically list SS18L1 as limited/disputed evidence). Some probability remains for "hypothesized" because much of the supporting mechanistic work is cell-based or animal-model derived, and for "established" if one weighs the multiple cohort screens reporting variants.

ELP2 (Elongator complex subunit 2) is listed in OMIM as the gene for autosomal recessive intellectual disability 58 (MRT58), based initially on Cohen et al. (2015), who reported compound heterozygous ELP2 variants in siblings with ID, spasticity and neurodevelopmental impairment. Subsequent work (Kojic et al., Nat Commun 2021) described additional patients with biallelic ELP2 variants together with a mouse model showing tRNA wobble modification defects and neurodevelopmental abnormalities, supporting causality and mechanism. The human genetic evidence therefore exists in more than one publication/family, but the total number of independent probands remains small, so the relationship is best regarded as credible yet not overwhelmingly replicated (ClinGen-style "limited/moderate"). Points are thus split between Established and Existing, with a smaller share for Hypothesized reflecting the strong supporting animal/functional data, and minimal weight for Novel.

ELP2 (Elongator complex subunit 2) is linked to MRT58 (OMIM 617270) primarily through Cohen et al. (2015), who reported two siblings with compound heterozygous missense ELP2 variants presenting with intellectual disability and a cerebral palsy–like neurodevelopmental phenotype. This is credible human genetic evidence but is essentially a single family, with few independent replications reported since, so the association is best characterized as limited rather than definitively established. Supporting functional work, including Elp2 knock-in/knockout mouse models (e.g., Kojic et al.) showing tRNA modification defects and neurodevelopmental abnormalities, strengthens biological plausibility but is non-human and therefore reinforces the hypothesized tier rather than proving causation. A small probability remains for "established" if additional probands have been published, and minimal weight for "novel" given the OMIM-recognized entry.

ELP2 (Elongator complex subunit 2) is listed in OMIM as the cause of autosomal recessive intellectual disability 58, based largely on a single consanguineous/compound-heterozygous family (Cohen et al., 2015) with two affected siblings showing ID, spasticity and dysmorphism. Subsequent work (e.g., Kojic et al., Nat Commun 2021) provided functional and mouse-model support, with an Elp2 mutant mouse recapitulating neurodevelopmental deficits and tRNA modification defects, but human genetic replication in additional independent probands remains sparse. Thus the human genetic evidence is credible but limited, best fitting "Existing," with some chance that additional reported families/exome cohorts have upgraded it toward "Established." Purely biological/animal support would only justify "Hypothesized," which retains modest weight; a complete absence of evidence ("Novel") is very unlikely given the recognized OMIM entry.

Familial hypertryptophanemia (OMIM 600627) is an extremely rare condition described in only a handful of siblings/families, and the biochemical phenotype (elevated plasma tryptophan with reduced kynurenine pathway metabolites) has long been attributed to deficient hepatic tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase (TDO2, tryptophan pyrrolase) activity, making TDO2 the obvious candidate gene on mechanistic grounds. However, to my knowledge no replicated, unambiguous pathogenic TDO2 variants have been documented in these probands; the gene assignment in databases is largely inferential, and Tdo2 knockout mice do show hypertryptophanemia, which is animal rather than human variant evidence. This places most weight on "Hypothesized," with meaningful probability on "Existing" in case a single human report or candidate-gene sequencing study (which I may not recall precisely) exists. "Established" is unlikely given the absence of multiple independent human families with confirmed variants, and "Novel" is improbable because the biological link is direct and well recognized.

Familial hypertryptophanemia (OMIM 600627) is a rare biochemical phenotype described in a small number of sibships (e.g., Snedden, Mellor and Martin, 1983), where deficient hepatic tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase activity was inferred from the metabolic profile rather than demonstrated by molecular analysis. TDO2 is the obvious candidate because it encodes the rate-limiting enzyme of tryptophan catabolism, and Tdo2-deficient mice display marked hypertryptophanemia, giving very strong biological/pathway and animal-model support. However, to my knowledge OMIM does not list a confirmed molecular basis, and there is little or no replicated human variant-level evidence (candidate TDO2 polymorphism studies exist mainly in autism/Tourette contexts, not in proven hypertryptophanemia families). Therefore most weight goes to "Hypothesized," with some probability reserved for a limited human report I may be underweighting, and only minimal probability for "Established."

TDO2 encodes tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase, the rate-limiting hepatic enzyme of tryptophan catabolism, so its deficiency is the obvious biochemical candidate mechanism for familial hypertryptophanemia (OMIM 600627), giving very strong biological plausibility and pathway relevance. However, the classic clinical reports (e.g., Snedden et al., Martin et al.) described affected families with elevated plasma tryptophan and inferred enzyme deficiency without identifying causative TDO2 sequence variants, so causality has not been molecularly proven. There is some human genetic literature implicating TDO2 polymorphisms in related tryptophan-metabolism phenotypes (e.g., autism with hypertryptophanemia, Nabi et al.), which supports a limited "Existing" level of human variant evidence. Gene–disease curations generally regard the TDO2–hypertryptophanemia relationship as limited or unconfirmed rather than definitive, so "Established" receives little weight, and "Novel" is essentially excluded given the direct enzymatic rationale.

Cantú syndrome (hypertrichotic osteochondrodysplasia) was shown in 2012 by two independent groups (Harakalova et al.; van Bon et al.) to be caused by heterozygous gain-of-function missense variants in ABCC9, encoding the SUR2 regulatory subunit of KATP channels. Numerous additional probands and families have since been reported, with recurrent variants such as p.Arg1154Gln/Trp and p.Ser1054Tyr, and genotype–phenotype correlations described. Functional studies confirm reduced ATP inhibition/increased KATP channel activity, and mouse models recapitulate cardiovascular and hypertrichosis features, supporting the human genetic data. A related gene, KCNJ8, accounts for a minority of cases, but ABCC9 is the major, definitively established cause.

Gain-of-function missense variants in ABCC9 (encoding the SUR2 subunit of KATP channels) were identified as the cause of Cantú syndrome (hypertrichotic osteochondrodysplasia) in 2012 by two independent groups (Harakalova et al., Nature Genetics; van Bon et al., AJHG), with subsequent replication in numerous independent probands and families worldwide. Recurrent variants such as p.Arg1154Gln/Trp and p.Ser1054Tyr have been reported repeatedly in humans, with clear genotype–phenotype correlations. Functional studies in heterologous systems and mouse models confirm KATP channel overactivity as the mechanism, and a small minority of cases are attributed to KCNJ8. ABCC9–Cantú syndrome is classified as "Definitive" by gene curation efforts (e.g., OMIM #239850, ClinGen-style evaluations), leaving essentially no doubt about causality.

Gain-of-function missense variants in ABCC9, encoding the SUR2 regulatory subunit of KATP channels, were identified as the cause of Cantú syndrome (hypertrichotic osteochondrodysplasia) in 2012 by two independent groups (Harakalova et al., Nature Genetics; van Bon et al., AJHG), each reporting multiple unrelated probands and families. Subsequent cohort studies and international registries have confirmed ABCC9 variants in the majority of clinically diagnosed patients, with recurrent hotspot mutations (e.g., p.Arg1154Gln/Trp, p.Cys1043Tyr). Functional electrophysiology and mouse models recapitulate the phenotype and support the gain-of-function mechanism, and KATP-channel inhibitors are being trialed therapeutically. This is an unambiguous, replicated human gene–disease relationship (also curated as definitive by ClinGen/OMIM #239850).

MT-TA encodes the mitochondrial tRNA-Alanine, and pathogenic variants in mt-tRNA genes are a well-recognized cause of mitochondrial disease through impaired mitochondrial translation and multiple respiratory chain complex deficiency. Specific MT-TA variants, notably m.5628T>C, have been reported in independent human probands with chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia and mitochondrial myopathy, with supporting single-fiber segregation studies and COX-deficient/ragged-red fibers; MITOMAP classifies m.5628T>C as a confirmed pathogenic variant. Additional variants such as m.5650G>A and m.5591G>A have been described in patients with myopathy/encephalopathy with functional corroboration. The main uncertainty is the relatively small number of independent families for any single variant, so some probability remains on "Existing" as evidence for this gene is less extensive than for MT-TL1 or MT-TK.

MT-TA encodes the mitochondrial tRNA-Alanine, and several pathogenic point variants have been reported in human patients with mitochondrial disease, most notably m.5628T>C (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia/mitochondrial myopathy) and m.5650G>A (myopathy with exercise intolerance), with supportive evidence from heteroplasmy segregation in single COX-negative muscle fibers, transmitochondrial cybrid/steady-state tRNA studies, and muscle biopsy findings. MITOMAP classifies at least one MT-TA variant as "confirmed" pathogenic, indicating replication or robust single-fiber/functional validation in humans. However, the total number of independent probands and families is modest compared with well-established mt-tRNA genes such as MT-TL1 or MT-TK, so the evidence sits at the boundary between definitive and limited. I therefore split points nearly evenly between Established and Existing, with little weight to Hypothesized or Novel, since direct human genetic evidence clearly exists.

MT-TA encodes the mitochondrial tRNA-Alanine, and pathogenic variants in mt-tRNA genes are a classic cause of mitochondrial disease through impaired mitochondrial translation. Several human variants have been reported, most notably m.5650G>A (mitochondrial myopathy with ragged-red/COX-deficient fibres, supported by single-fibre segregation and transmitochondrial/steady-state tRNA studies) and m.5628T>C (associated with CPEO and myopathy), with additional reported variants such as m.5591G>A and m.5636T>C in encephalomyopathy phenotypes. MITOMAP classifies at least one MT-TA variant as "confirmed" pathogenic, and functional evidence (heteroplasmy threshold, single-fibre segregation, reduced tRNA steady-state levels) supports causality in humans. However, the number of independent probands/families is relatively small compared with genes such as MT-TL1 or MT-TK, so some weight remains on "Existing" rather than firmly replicated "Established."

Revy et al. (Cell, 2000) identified biallelic AICDA mutations in multiple unrelated patients with autosomal recessive hyper-IgM syndrome, defining HIGM2 (OMIM 605258). Numerous subsequent human cohorts (Minegishi, Durandy, Quartier, Imai and others) have replicated this in independent probands, including dominant-negative C-terminal variants causing autosomal dominant HIGM with impaired class-switch recombination but preserved somatic hypermutation. Functional studies and Aicda-knockout mice corroborate the mechanism, but the causal evidence itself is robust human genetic data. This is a textbook, gene–disease relationship classified as definitive by ClinGen/IUIS inborn errors of immunity classifications.

Revy et al. (Cell, 2000) identified biallelic AICDA (AID) mutations in multiple unrelated patients from consanguineous families with autosomal recessive hyper-IgM syndrome, and this has been replicated in numerous independent cohorts worldwide, including dominant-negative C-terminal variants causing autosomal dominant HIGM2. OMIM designates HIGM2 (#605258) as caused by mutation in AICDA, and the gene–disease relationship is curated as definitive by ClinGen-type frameworks. The mechanism (loss of class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation) is supported by human patient B-cell studies and by Aicda-knockout mice recapitulating the phenotype. Evidence is therefore unambiguous and human-based, warranting near-complete confidence in the Established category.

Revy et al. (Cell, 2000) identified biallelic AICDA (AID) mutations as the cause of autosomal recessive hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 in multiple unrelated human patients, and this has been replicated in numerous independent cohorts worldwide (European, Japanese, Middle Eastern, Latin American registries). Both recessive loss-of-function and dominant-negative C-terminal AICDA variants have been described in humans with the characteristic phenotype of normal/elevated IgM, absent IgG/IgA, defective class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation, and lymphoid hyperplasia. Aicda-knockout mice recapitulate the phenotype, and functional assays confirm pathogenic mechanisms, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive. AICDA–HIGM2 is a canonical, OMIM-recognized (MIM 605258) gene–disease relationship classified as definitive by curation efforts such as ClinGen/IUIS.

phenotype: X-linked central congenital hypothyroidism with late-onset testicular enlargement
justification: Loss-of-function variants in IGSF1 were identified by Sun et al. (Nature Genetics, 2012) as the cause of an X-linked syndrome of central congenital hypothyroidism with macroorchidism (late-onset testicular enlargement), delayed pubertal testosterone rise, and variable prolactin/GH deficiency. This finding has been replicated in numerous independent kindreds and cohorts worldwide (e.g., Joustra et al. international IGSF1 Deficiency Consortium studies describing dozens of affected males and carrier females), with a defined OMIM entry (IGSF1 deficiency syndrome, MIM 300888). Functional work shows IGSF1 is expressed in pituitary thyrotropes and Leydig cells, and mutant proteins fail to traffic to the plasma membrane, providing a coherent mechanism, though the human genetic evidence alone is definitive.
