The gene–disease relationship is therefore firmly Established.

phenotype: X-linked central congenital hypothyroidism with late-onset testicular enlargement
justification: Loss-of-function variants in IGSF1 were identified by Sun et al. (Nature Genetics, 2012) in multiple unrelated families with X-linked central congenital hypothyroidism, prolactin deficiency, and macroorchidism (late-onset testicular enlargement), defining "IGSF1 deficiency syndrome" (OMIM 300888). This has been replicated in numerous independent human cohorts and case series (e.g., Joustra et al., Tenenbaum-Rakover et al., Nakamura et al.), with dozens of affected males and carrier females characterized clinically and molecularly. Functional studies (impaired membrane trafficking of mutant IGSF1, Igsf1-knockout mice with reduced pituitary TRH receptor expression) provide corroborating mechanistic support. The gene–disease relationship is therefore definitively established in humans, with essentially no residual probability for the lesser categories.

phenotype: X-linked central congenital hypothyroidism with late-onset testicular enlargement
justification: Loss-of-function variants in IGSF1 were identified by Sun et al. (Nature Genetics, 2012) as the cause of an X-linked syndrome of central congenital hypothyroidism with macroorchidism, delayed pubertal testosterone rise, and variable prolactin/GH deficiency, in multiple unrelated families. This was rapidly replicated and expanded by large international cohort studies (e.g., Joustra et al., JCEM 2013, describing dozens of affected males and carrier females across many independent families), and subsequent case series worldwide have added further pathogenic variants with consistent genotype–phenotype correlation. The gene is included in OMIM as IGSF1 deficiency syndrome (MIM 300888) and in diagnostic panels for congenital central hypothyroidism. Human genetic evidence is therefore strong, replicated, and definitive, supported additionally by mouse models and functional membrane-trafficking studies.

Biallelic ERCC6L2 variants were first reported by Tummala et al. (2014, AJHG) in consanguineous families with bone marrow failure, developmental delay and microcephaly, establishing "bone marrow failure syndrome 2" (OMIM 615715), which corresponds to the pancytopenia–developmental delay phenotype. Multiple independent human cohorts and case series have since replicated this (e.g., Zhang et al. 2016 in inherited bone marrow failure cohorts, Bluteau et al., Douglas et al. 2019 describing ERCC6L2-related BMF with progression to MDS/AML, and additional reports from Finnish and other populations), confirming causality across unrelated probands. Functional work supports a DNA repair/transcription-coupled repair defect consistent with the hematopoietic and neurodevelopmental features, but the human genetic evidence alone is replicated and definitive. A small residual weight is placed on "Existing" because the neurodevelopmental component is more variable than the marrow failure phenotype across reported patients.

Biallelic ERCC6L2 variants are the recognized cause of bone marrow failure syndrome 2 (OMIM 615715), described as pancytopenia with developmental delay/learning difficulties and microcephaly. The original report by Tummala et al. (2014, AJHG) identified homozygous loss-of-function variants in consanguineous families, and this has been replicated in multiple independent human cohorts (e.g., Zhang et al. 2016; Bluteau et al. 2018 in inherited bone marrow failure cohorts; Tummala et al. 2018 in Blood describing associated MDS/AML predisposition; Douglas et al. 2019). Functional work supports a DNA damage response/transcription-coupled repair mechanism consistent with marrow failure and neurodevelopmental features. Evidence is human, replicated across unrelated probands, so the relationship is Established, with only minor residual uncertainty about the consistency of the developmental-delay component across all reported patients.

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ERCC6L2 were first reported by Tummala et al. (2014, AJHG) in consanguineous families with bone marrow failure, microcephaly and developmental delay, defining bone marrow failure syndrome 2 (OMIM 615715), which corresponds to the pancytopenia–developmental delay phenotype. Multiple independent human cohorts and case series have replicated this (e.g., Zhang et al. 2016, Bluteau et al. 2018 in inherited bone marrow failure cohorts, Tummala et al. 2018 Blood, Douglas et al. 2019), including a recurrent founder variant and a strong predisposition to MDS/AML with TP53 mutations. Functional work supports a role in transcription-coupled DNA repair and the DNA damage response, consistent with the mechanism, but the classification rests on abundant human genetic evidence. Therefore the relationship is best considered Established, with only a small residual probability that specific nomenclature/phenotype matching could be judged more narrowly.

HEY2 (HRT2/CHF1/HESR2) is a Notch-pathway bHLH transcriptional repressor essential for ventricular chamber and outflow tract development; Hey2-null mice display ventricular septal defects, tetralogy-of-Fallot–like malformations, tricuspid atresia and cardiomyopathy, providing very strong biological/animal support (Hypothesized floor). In humans, candidate-gene resequencing studies (including Chinese cohorts with VSD/TOF and reports of somatic/germline variants in malformed hearts) have described rare HEY2 variants with in vitro loss of transcriptional repression, and 6q22 deletions encompassing HEY2 have been reported with cardiac defects, supporting the "Existing" tier. However, these reports are relatively few, often small, sometimes with limited segregation or replication, and the best-replicated human HEY2 genetic association is with Brugada syndrome/ECG repolarization rather than structural CHD. Therefore the evidence falls short of "Established," with most weight on limited-but-credible human evidence layered on robust model-organism biology.

HEY2 (CHF1/HERP1) is a Notch-effector bHLH transcription factor with strong developmental relevance: Hey2-null mice show ventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot-like malformations, valve anomalies and cardiomyopathy, providing robust biological/animal support (Hypothesized-level evidence at minimum). In humans, candidate-gene resequencing and association studies—including somatic/germline variant screens in septal defects and tetralogy of Fallot, and polymorphism association studies in Chinese cohorts—have reported rare variants and SNPs in HEY2 linked to congenital heart disease, and HEY2 locus variation is well established for Brugada syndrome/ECG traits, which is cardiac but not CHD. These human findings are limited in size, inconsistently replicated, and HEY2 is not a recognized definitive Mendelian CHD gene in curated resources such as ClinGen. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the human genetic reports are judged too weak, and only a small probability of "Established."

HEY2 (HESR2/HRT2/CHF1) is a Notch-pathway bHLH effector with a well-documented role in cardiac chamber, valve, septal and outflow-tract development; Hey2-null mice show ventricular septal defects, valve dysplasia and cardiomyopathy, providing strong biological/animal support (Hypothesized floor). In humans, rare germline and somatic HEY2 sequence variants have been reported in small cohorts with septal defects and tetralogy of Fallot (e.g., analyses of malformed heart tissue and candidate-gene screens in Chinese CHD cohorts), and HEY2 lies within 6q22 deletion intervals associated with congenital heart malformations; common variation at the HEY2 locus is also robustly linked to cardiac conduction/Brugada phenotypes, reinforcing human cardiac relevance. These human genetic data are limited in size, sometimes based on somatic variants, and not consistently replicated with segregation in multiple independent families, so the evidence best fits "Existing" rather than "Established." A modest allocation remains for "Established" given the recurrence across several small human reports, and little probability for "Novel" given the abundant mechanistic data.

Carney-Stratakis syndrome (the dyad of gastrointestinal stromal tumor and paraganglioma) was shown by McWhinney et al. (NEJM 2007) and Pasini et al. (Eur J Hum Genet 2008) to be caused by germline loss-of-function mutations in the succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes SDHB, SDHC, and SDHD, identified in multiple independent probands and affected families. Tumors from these patients show loss of heterozygosity and loss of SDHB immunostaining, supporting a two-hit tumor-suppressor mechanism in humans. Subsequent series and clinical guidelines (e.g., on SDH-deficient GIST and hereditary paraganglioma) consistently list SDHB among the established causal genes for this syndrome. The evidence is human, replicated, and mechanistically supported, so the relationship is Established, with only minor residual probability assigned to lower categories given that SDHB accounts for a subset of cases relative to SDHD/SDHC.

Carney-Stratakis syndrome (the dyad of gastrointestinal stromal tumor and paraganglioma) was shown by McWhinney et al. (NEJM 2007) and Pasini et al. (Eur J Hum Genet 2008) to be caused by germline loss-of-function mutations in the succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes SDHB, SDHC, and SDHD in multiple independent human families and probands. Subsequent human studies confirmed SDHB germline variants with loss of heterozygosity and loss of SDHB immunostaining in tumors, supporting causality and autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance. The gene is included in standard clinical diagnostic panels and OMIM/GeneReviews entries for the syndrome. Evidence is human, replicated, and mechanistically supported, so the relationship is clearly Established, with only a small residual probability reflecting that SDHB is somewhat less frequently implicated than SDHC in this specific dyad.

Carney-Stratakis syndrome (the dyad of gastrointestinal stromal tumor and paraganglioma) was shown by McWhinney et al. (NEJM 2007) and Pasini et al. (Eur J Hum Genet 2008) to result from germline inactivating mutations in the succinate dehydrogenase subunit genes SDHB, SDHC, and SDHD, identified in multiple independent human probands and families. SDHB mutations specifically have been reported in several affected individuals, with tumors showing loss of heterozygosity and loss of SDHB immunostaining, supporting a causal, two-hit tumor-suppressor mechanism. The gene–disease relationship is recognized in OMIM, GeneReviews, and clinical testing panels for hereditary paraganglioma/GIST syndromes. Evidence is human, replicated, and mechanistically coherent, so the association is Established; only a small residual probability reflects the rarity of the syndrome and the greater frequency of SDHB/SDHC involvement variation across series.

TAFAZZIN (formerly TAZ/G4.5) was identified by Bione et al. (1996) as the gene mutated in X-linked Barth syndrome, and hundreds of pathogenic variants have since been reported in independent human probands and families worldwide, catalogued in the Barth Syndrome Human TAZ Variants Database. The gene–disease relationship is mechanistically explained by defective cardiolipin remodeling (monolysocardiolipin/cardiolipin ratio), which serves as a diagnostic biomarker in patients. TAFAZZIN is the only known gene for Barth syndrome, and the association is classified as "Definitive" by ClinGen and gene curation efforts. Evidence derives overwhelmingly from human clinical genetic studies, supplemented by yeast, mouse, and iPSC models. This is an unambiguous, replicated causal relationship.

TAFAZZIN (formerly TAZ/G4.5) was identified by Bione et al. (1996) as the gene mutated in X-linked Barth syndrome, and hundreds of pathogenic variants have since been reported in independent probands and families worldwide, catalogued in the Barth Syndrome Registry and the Human Tafazzin Gene Variants Database. The gene–disease relationship is mechanistically explained by defective cardiolipin remodeling, with concordant biochemical evidence (monolysocardiolipin/cardiolipin ratio) used diagnostically in patients. Curation efforts (e.g., ClinGen, OMIM #302060) classify this as a definitive gene–disease association. This is unambiguously an Established relationship based on human genetic evidence.

TAFAZZIN (TAZ, G4.5) was identified by Bione et al. (1996) as the causative gene for X-linked Barth syndrome, and hundreds of pathogenic variants have since been reported in independent probands and families worldwide, catalogued in the Barth Syndrome Human TAZ Variants Database. The mechanism is well characterized: loss of tafazzin, a cardiolipin transacylase, causes abnormal monolysocardiolipin/cardiolipin ratios, a biochemical diagnostic marker in patient bloodspots. Clinical features—cardiomyopathy, neutropenia, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria, and skeletal myopathy—segregate with TAZ variants in an X-linked pattern across many pedigrees. Supporting functional data exist in yeast, Drosophila, and mouse models, but the human clinical genetic evidence alone is definitive. This is an unambiguous gene–disease relationship, classified as Definitive by ClinGen.

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in AP3B1, encoding the beta-3A subunit of the adaptor protein-3 complex, were first shown to cause Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 2 by Dell'Angelica et al. (1999) in a patient with oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding diathesis, and neutropenia. Subsequent reports (Huizing, Shotelersuk, Jung et al. 2006, Enders et al., and multiple later cohorts) identified additional independent probands and families with distinct AP3B1 mutations, including cases with immunodeficiency and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. The mechanism—defective AP-3-mediated cargo sorting to lysosome-related organelles—is well characterized in human patient cells, and the pearl mouse model recapitulates the phenotype. HPS-2 is by definition the AP3B1-related subtype, making this a textbook established gene–disease relationship.

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in AP3B1, encoding the beta-3A subunit of the adaptor protein complex 3, are the definitive cause of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 2, first reported by Dell'Angelica et al. (1999) in a patient with oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding diathesis, and neutropenia. Multiple independent probands and families have since been described (e.g., Huizing et al., Jung et al. 2006, Enders et al. 2006), including patients with immunodeficiency, congenital neutropenia, and impaired cytotoxic T-cell granule secretion. The gene–disease pair is codified in OMIM (HPS2, #608233) and is supported by concordant functional data (pearl mouse model, AP-3 trafficking defects) and clinical diagnostic testing. This is an unambiguous, replicated human gene–disease relationship.

AP3B1 encodes the beta-3A subunit of the adaptor protein-3 complex, and biallelic loss-of-function variants were first shown to cause Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 2 by Dell'Angelica et al. (1999) in a human patient with oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding diathesis, and neutropenia. Multiple independent probands and families have since been reported (e.g., Huizing et al., Jung et al. 2006, Enders et al., and subsequent cohorts), consistently demonstrating congenital neutropenia, immunodeficiency with impaired CTL cytotoxicity, and platelet dense-granule deficiency. HPS2 is defined by AP3B1 mutations in OMIM (#608233) and gene panels, with concordant functional data and the pearl mouse model supporting the mechanism. Evidence is replicated in humans, making this an unambiguous Established gene–disease relationship.

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in IL11RA are the recognized cause of craniosynostosis and dental anomalies (CRSDA, OMIM 614188), first reported by Nieminen et al. (2011, AJHG) in multiple consanguineous and unrelated families with homozygous/compound heterozygous IL11RA mutations, delayed tooth eruption, supernumerary teeth and craniosynostosis. Independent replication came from Keupp et al. (2013) and subsequent case reports in additional probands from different populations, supporting a clear autosomal recessive causal relationship in humans. Functional studies showing impaired IL-11/gp130-STAT3 signaling and Il11ra-null mouse models with craniosynostosis provide corroborating mechanistic support. This gene–disease pair is curated as definitive/strong in databases such as OMIM and gene curation panels, so the evidence is unambiguous.

Biallelic IL11RA loss-of-function variants cause an autosomal recessive syndrome of craniosynostosis with delayed tooth eruption, supernumerary teeth and maxillary hypoplasia (CRSDA, OMIM 614188), first reported by Nieminen et al. (AJHG 2011) in multiple consanguineous families with homozygous missense and truncating mutations. Independent replication came from Keupp et al. (2013) and subsequent case reports describing additional probands from different populations, plus functional studies showing impaired IL-11/STAT3 signaling. Il11ra-null mice recapitulate craniosynostosis and dental phenotypes, supporting the mechanism, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive. The gene–disease relationship is curated as definitive/strong in gene-disease validity resources, so points are concentrated in "Established."

Biallelic loss-of-function variants in IL11RA were identified by Nieminen et al. (2011, AJHG) as the cause of an autosomal recessive syndrome of craniosynostosis, delayed tooth eruption/supernumerary teeth, and maxillary hypoplasia in multiple consanguineous and non-consanguineous families. This was independently replicated and expanded by Keupp et al. (2013) and subsequent case reports, with additional homozygous/compound heterozygous mutations and functional evidence of impaired IL-11 signaling (STAT3 activation). The disorder is recognized in OMIM as craniosynostosis and dental anomalies (CRSDA, #614188), and Il11ra knockout mice recapitulate craniosynostosis, supporting the mechanism. Evidence is human, replicated across independent probands, and mechanistically supported, so the relationship is clearly Established.

Human piebaldism (OMIM 172800) is a well-known autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous loss-of-function and dominant-negative variants in KIT, first demonstrated by Giebel and Spritz (1991) and Fleischman et al., with subsequent reports of dozens of independent probands and families carrying missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice, and whole-gene deletion alleles. Genotype–phenotype correlations are established, with tyrosine kinase domain missense (dominant-negative) variants producing the most severe depigmentation and haploinsufficiency alleles milder phenotypes. Supporting mouse W (Kit) mutants show analogous white-spotting, and functional studies confirm impaired KIT signaling in melanoblast migration/survival, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive and replicated. Only SNAI2 explains a small minority of KIT-negative cases, which does not diminish KIT's established causal role.

Heterozygous loss-of-function and dominant-negative mutations in KIT (4q12) are the classic, well-replicated cause of autosomal dominant piebaldism, first reported by Giebel and Spritz and by Fleischman in 1991 in human families. Dozens of independent probands and pedigrees worldwide have since been reported with missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site mutations and whole-gene deletions, with genotype–phenotype correlations (kinase-domain missense causing the most severe depigmentation). This is supported by concordant mouse W (Kit) locus mutants producing white spotting, but the human genetic evidence alone is definitive. OMIM lists piebaldism (#172800) as a KIT-related Mendelian disorder, and gene curation efforts classify it as Definitive.

Human piebaldism (OMIM 172800) is a textbook autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in KIT, first demonstrated by Giebel and Spritz and by Fleischman and colleagues in 1991. Since then, dozens of independent probands and multigenerational families have been reported with missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, and whole-gene deletion mutations, with a well-described genotype–phenotype correlation (dominant-negative kinase-domain missense mutations producing severe depigmentation versus haploinsufficiency producing milder phenotypes). The mechanism is corroborated by the classic mouse dominant white spotting (W/Kit) model and by functional studies of KIT receptor signaling in melanoblast migration and survival, but the primary evidence base is human clinical genetics. This is an unambiguous, definitive gene–disease relationship curated as "Definitive" by ClinGen-type frameworks.

Lindhurst et al. (NEJM 2011) identified a somatic mosaic activating AKT1 mutation (c.49G>A, p.Glu17Lys) in affected tissues of 26 of 29 patients with Proteus syndrome, using exome sequencing of paired affected/unaffected tissue in human probands. This finding has been independently replicated in multiple subsequent human cohorts and is now used as a diagnostic molecular criterion for Proteus syndrome, with mutant allele fraction correlating with tissue involvement. The mechanism (mosaic gain-of-function PI3K/AKT pathway activation causing segmental overgrowth) is well supported functionally, and AKT inhibitors (e.g., miransertib) have been trialed in patients. This is a textbook example of an established, causal gene–disease relationship in humans, leaving negligible weight for lower-evidence categories.

Lindhurst et al. (NEJM, 2011) identified a somatic mosaic activating mutation in AKT1 (c.49G>A, p.Glu17Lys) in affected tissues from the large majority of patients with Proteus syndrome, using paired affected/unaffected tissue sequencing in human subjects. This finding has been independently replicated in multiple additional patient cohorts and is now used diagnostically, with the mutation detectable in lesional tissue and cell-free DNA. Functional studies confirm constitutive AKT1 activation and downstream PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway hyperactivity, and AKT inhibitors (e.g., miransertib) have been trialed clinically in Proteus syndrome. The mosaic AKT1 p.Glu17Lys variant is considered the definitive molecular cause of Proteus syndrome, satisfying the Established category with human genetic evidence in numerous independent probands.

Lindhurst et al. (NEJM 2011) identified a somatic mosaic activating AKT1 mutation (c.49G>A, p.Glu17Lys) in affected tissues from 26 of 29 patients with Proteus syndrome, using whole-exome sequencing of paired affected/unaffected tissue. This finding has been replicated in multiple independent human cohorts and case series worldwide, and mutant allele detection in lesional tissue is now used as a molecular diagnostic criterion in the clinical diagnostic guidelines for Proteus syndrome. Functional studies confirm constitutive AKT1 activation and downstream PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathway hyperactivity, providing mechanistic support, and AKT inhibitors (e.g., miransertib) have been trialed in patients. The evidence is human-based, replicated, and definitive, making "Established" overwhelmingly likely.

SLC24A5 is the recognized gene for oculocutaneous albinism type 6 (OCA6, OMIM 113750), first identified by Wei et al. (2013) via homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing in a consanguineous Chinese family, with functional support from the zebrafish "golden" mutant and known SLC24A5 involvement in human pigmentation variation. Subsequent independent reports (e.g., Morice-Picard et al., Mauri et al., and albinism cohort screens from India, Europe, and Japan) identified additional biallelic loss-of-function variants in unrelated probands with hypopigmentation, nystagmus, and foveal hypoplasia, satisfying replication in humans. The gene product is a melanosomal cation exchanger essential for melanin synthesis, providing a coherent mechanism. Although OCA6 is rare and accounts for a small fraction of albinism cases, the human genetic evidence across multiple independent families supports an Established classification, with a small residual probability reflecting the limited number of reported patients.

SLC24A5 is the recognized gene for oculocutaneous albinism type 6 (OMIM 113750), first identified by Wei et al. (2013) through homozygosity mapping/exome sequencing in a consanguineous Chinese family with biallelic loss-of-function variants. Subsequent independent reports (e.g., Morice-Picard et al. and albinism cohort screening studies in European, Indian, Chinese, and Middle Eastern patients) have identified additional unrelated probands with biallelic SLC24A5 variants, providing replication in humans. Supporting biological evidence includes the zebrafish "golden" mutant and the role of the NCKX5 cation exchanger in melanosome maturation, but the human genetic evidence is primary. Because the gene remains a rare cause of albinism with a relatively modest number of reported families, a small share of probability is retained for "Existing," though the causal relationship is widely accepted as established.

(2013) through homozygosity mapping in a consanguineous Chinese family with a homozygous loss-of-function variant. Supporting biology is strong: SLC24A5 encodes a melanosomal cation exchanger (NCKX5), the zebrafish golden mutant shows hypopigmentation, and the p.Ala111Thr polymorphism underlies human skin pigmentation variation. Because human genetic evidence is replicated across multiple independent families, the relationship is best classified as Established, though the relatively small number of reported cases leaves modest weight for "Existing."

phenotype: intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities
justification: FBXO11 is the established cause of intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (IDDFBA, OMIM 618089), an autosomal dominant condition caused by de novo loss-of-function and missense variants. Gregor et al. (2018, AJHG) reported ~20 unrelated individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants and a consistent phenotype of developmental delay/intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, and behavioral problems; Fritzen et al. (2018) and Jansen et al. (2019) independently replicated this in additional cohorts. The gene is also recurrently identified in large de novo mutation studies of developmental disorders (DDD/autism cohorts), providing statistical enrichment evidence in humans. Given multiple independent human probands, replication, and gene-level statistical support, the relationship is clearly Established, with only minimal residual probability assigned to lower categories.

phenotype: intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities
justification: FBXO11 is the established gene for intellectual developmental disorder with dysmorphic facies and behavioral abnormalities (IDDFBA; OMIM 618089), an autosomal dominant condition caused by de novo loss-of-function and missense variants. Gregor et al. (2018, AJHG) reported de novo FBXO11 variants in 20 individuals with a variable neurodevelopmental disorder, and Jansen et al. (2019) independently described additional patients with developmental delay, behavioral problems, and dysmorphic features. These human cohort studies represent multiple independent probands with consistent phenotypes and de novo occurrence, satisfying strong causal criteria. Supporting functional and animal data exist but are secondary to the robust human genetic evidence.

The evidence is human genetic, replicated, and curated as definitive by OMIM/ClinGen-type resources, so the relationship is clearly Established.

DCLRE1C encodes Artemis, essential for V(D)J recombination hairpin opening; null mutations cause T-B-NK+ radiosensitive SCID, while hypomorphic/leaky mutations permit oligoclonal T-cell expansion producing Omenn syndrome. Ege et al. (Blood, 2005) reported multiple unrelated human patients with Omenn syndrome caused by hypomorphic ARTEMIS/DCLRE1C mutations, and additional independent cohorts and case reports (e.g., Athabascan-descent and other SCID/Omenn registries, IUIS classifications) have replicated this in humans. Omenn syndrome is a recognized clinical phenotype listed for DCLRE1C in OMIM/ClinGen-type curations. Thus the evidence is human, replicated across independent probands, supporting an Established relationship, with only minor residual uncertainty about curation strength.

DCLRE1C encodes Artemis, essential for V(D)J recombination hairpin opening; null mutations cause radiosensitive T-B-NK+ SCID, while hypomorphic (leaky) mutations permit limited oligoclonal T-cell development and produce Omenn syndrome. Ege et al. (Blood, 2005) reported multiple human patients with Omenn syndrome due to ARTEMIS/DCLRE1C mutations, and subsequent independent cohorts (e.g., Athymic/radiosensitive SCID series, Navajo/Apache founder populations, and various SCID registries) have confirmed Omenn phenotypes in DCLRE1C-deficient probands. These are human clinical genetic studies in independent families, supported by functional recombination assays. This constitutes replicated, causal, human evidence, so the relationship is best classified as Established, with only minor residual probability for weaker categories.

DCLRE1C encodes Artemis, essential for V(D)J recombination hairpin opening; null mutations cause radiosensitive T-B-NK+ SCID, while hypomorphic mutations permit residual recombination and oligoclonal autoreactive T cells. Ege et al. (Blood, 2005) described multiple human patients with Omenn syndrome due to hypomorphic ARTEMIS/DCLRE1C mutations, and subsequent cohort studies (e.g., Athabascan-descent and other populations, IUIS/ESID registries) have reported additional independent probands with Omenn phenotype or atypical/leaky SCID. The mechanism is well understood and consistent with other Omenn-causing recombination genes (RAG1/RAG2, LIG4, NHEJ1, RAG-adjacent pathways). Gene curation efforts (e.g., ClinGen, gene panels for SCID/Omenn) list DCLRE1C among established Omenn syndrome genes. Only minor uncertainty remains because Omenn presentation is a less common manifestation of DCLRE1C deficiency than classic SCID.

LRPAP1 is the OMIM-designated gene for MYP23 (autosomal recessive high myopia), based principally on Aldahmesh et al. (2013, AJHG), who identified homozygous truncating variants segregating in consanguineous families with severe early-onset myopia, with functional support involving TGF-beta signaling via LRP1 chaperone function. A small number of subsequent reports/exome studies have described additional LRPAP1 variants in high-myopia probands, but replication across independent families is limited compared with classic well-established disease genes, and gene–disease validity curations tend toward "moderate/limited" rather than definitive. Thus the evidence is clearly human genetic and causal in nature (favoring Established), but the modest number of independent probands leaves substantial weight on Existing. Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are unlikely given direct human variant evidence.

LRPAP1 is the designated gene for MYP23 (autosomal recessive high myopia; OMIM 615431), based on Aldahmesh et al. (2013, AJHG), who identified a homozygous truncating LRPAP1 variant segregating in a consanguineous family with extreme axial myopia, alongside CTSH in a separate family. Additional human reports and cohort screens (including Asian high-myopia cohorts) have described further rare LRPAP1 variants, providing some replication, though the total number of independent probands remains modest and some variants are of uncertain significance. Supporting biology is strong—LRPAP1 chaperones LRP1 and modulates TGF-β signaling relevant to scleral extracellular matrix remodeling—and knockdown/animal data reinforce plausibility, but the human genetic evidence is the primary basis. Given the limited number of independent families, the evidence sits between "moderate/limited" and firmly established, so points are split mainly between Established and Existing.

LRPAP1 was identified as the gene for autosomal recessive high myopia (MYP23) by Aldahmesh et al. (AJHG 2013), who reported a homozygous truncating variant segregating in a consanguineous family with extreme early-onset myopia, alongside CTSH for a related locus. Subsequent human studies, including exome screening of large early-onset high myopia cohorts (e.g., Jiang et al., IOVS 2015) and additional consanguineous Middle Eastern patients described by Khan and colleagues, have reported further LRPAP1 variants, though some carriers show broader syndromic features and the total number of independent probands remains modest. This gives credible, human-based, at least partially replicated evidence, so the weight sits between "Established" and "Existing," with curation efforts often rating such gene–disease pairs as moderate rather than definitive. Purely biological/animal support (LRP1 chaperone function, TGF-β signaling in scleral remodeling) is supplementary rather than the primary evidence, so "Hypothesized" gets little weight and "Novel" is essentially excluded.

CHD2 is the recognized gene for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 94 (formerly "epileptic encephalopathy, childhood-onset," OMIM 615369). Multiple independent human studies, including Carvill et al. (2013), Suls et al. (2013), and Thomas et al. (2015), identified recurrent de novo loss-of-function and missense CHD2 variants in dozens of unrelated probands with myoclonic-atonic/photosensitive epilepsy, intellectual disability, and epileptic encephalopathy. The association has been replicated in large exome/gene-panel cohorts and is curated as Definitive by ClinGen for CHD2-related DEE. Supporting zebrafish and mouse models exist, but the causal evidence rests primarily on abundant human genetic data, firmly placing this pair in the Established category.

CHD2 is the gene assigned to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 94 (OMIM 615369, formerly "epileptic encephalopathy, childhood-onset"), and this designation reflects extensive human genetic evidence. Multiple large independent cohort and trio exome/gene-panel studies (e.g., Epi4K/EPGP, Carvill et al. 2013, Suls et al. 2013, and subsequent case series) identified recurrent de novo loss-of-function and missense CHD2 variants in dozens of unrelated probands with photosensitive myoclonic epilepsy, Lennox–Gastaut-like or Dravet-like phenotypes, and intellectual disability. The association has been replicated internationally, with genotype–phenotype series describing the "CHD2 encephalopathy" spectrum, and is curated as Definitive by ClinGen. Supporting zebrafish and mouse haploinsufficiency models add mechanistic support but are not needed to establish causation. Therefore the evidence overwhelmingly supports the Established category.

CHD2 is the well-recognized gene for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 94 (formerly "epileptic encephalopathy, childhood-onset," MIM 615369). Multiple independent human studies, including Carvill et al. (2013), Suls et al. (2013), and subsequent large epilepsy gene-panel and exome cohorts, identified numerous de novo loss-of-function and missense variants in unrelated probands with myoclonic-atonic/Lennox-Gastaut-like epilepsy, photosensitivity, and intellectual disability. The gene is curated as "Definitive" by ClinGen for this phenotype and is included in standard clinical epilepsy panels. Functional zebrafish and mouse models corroborate the mechanism, but the causal designation rests firmly on replicated human genetic evidence.

phenotype: congenital microcephaly - severe encephalopathy - progressive cerebral atrophy syndrome
justification: Biallelic ASNS variants cause asparagine synthetase deficiency (OMIM 615574), characterized precisely by congenital microcephaly, severe encephalopathy, intractable seizures and progressive cerebral atrophy. The condition was first defined by Ruzzo et al. (2013, Neuron) in multiple consanguineous families of different ancestries, with functional support, and has since been replicated in numerous independent probands and cohorts worldwide (e.g., Alfadhel, Palmer, Gataullina, Sun, Yamamoto reports), including diverse missense and truncating variants with segregation and biochemical/CSF asparagine evidence. This is a well-curated gene–disease relationship classified as Definitive by ClinGen/GeneReviews-type resources. Therefore the evidence overwhelmingly supports "Established," with only residual probability for a more conservative "Existing" classification.

phenotype: congenital microcephaly - severe encephalopathy - progressive cerebral atrophy syndrome
justification: Biallelic ASNS variants cause asparagine synthetase deficiency (OMIM 615574), whose cardinal features are congenital microcephaly, severe encephalopathy with intractable seizures, and progressive cerebral atrophy. The seminal report by Ruzzo et al. (Neuron, 2013) identified homozygous/compound heterozygous ASNS missense variants in multiple consanguineous and non-consanguineous families, supported by low CSF/plasma asparagine and functional studies. Numerous subsequent independent human cohorts and case series (from Saudi, European, Asian, and North American populations) have replicated the association with additional pathogenic alleles, and the gene–disease relationship is curated as definitive by clinical genetics resources. Animal/in vitro data (yeast complementation, ASNS knockdown models) provide supportive mechanistic evidence but are not required, given the robust human genetic replication.

The gene–disease relationship is curated as Definitive by ClinGen-type assessments, so essentially all probability belongs to "Established."

PPP1R13L encodes iASPP, and biallelic variants were reported by Falik-Zaccai et al. (EMBO Mol Med, 2017) in a consanguineous Arab Israeli kindred with a cardiocutaneous syndrome featuring woolly hair, keratoderma and severe, often fatal childhood dilated cardiomyopathy; subsequent case reports and small series in additional unrelated probands have supported this human genotype–phenotype link. Supporting evidence includes concordant naturally occurring animal models (Poll Hereford "woolly haircoat and cardiomyopathy" cattle and iASPP-deficient mice with cardiomyopathy) and functional data on desmosomal/intercalated disc integrity, which reinforce biological plausibility. However, the total number of independently reported human families remains modest and the cardiomyopathy is sometimes classified as arrhythmogenic/mixed rather than purely dilated, so gene-curation efforts may rate the evidence as moderate rather than definitive. Therefore probability is split mainly between Established and Existing, with a small allowance for a purely hypothesized (animal/functional-driven) classification.

PPP1R13L (iASPP) biallelic loss-of-function variants were reported by Falik-Zaccai et al. (EMBO Mol Med, 2017) in consanguineous families with a cardio-cutaneous syndrome featuring woolly hair, keratoderma and severe, often fatal dilated cardiomyopathy in childhood, and additional independent probands/families with PPP1R13L variants and DCM have since been described. Supporting non-human evidence is strong (iASPP mutations cause fatal dilated cardiomyopathy in Holstein cattle and Poodles, and iASPP-deficient mice develop cardiomyopathy), with plausible mechanism via desmosome/intercalated disc and p53-pathway regulation—but such animal data alone would only justify "Hypothesized." Because the human evidence includes multiple probands from more than one family with segregation and functional support, "Established" is plausible, though the number of independent human reports is still modest and curation bodies may rate it moderate/limited, so substantial weight also goes to "Existing." Very little probability is assigned to "Novel."

PPP1R13L (iASPP) biallelic variants were reported in humans by Falik-Zaccai et al. (2017) in consanguineous Israeli Arab families with a cardiocutaneous syndrome featuring severe childhood dilated cardiomyopathy, woolly hair, keratoderma and sudden cardiac death, and additional case reports of compound heterozygous/homozygous variants with pediatric DCM have since appeared. Supporting biology is strong: naturally occurring iASPP mutations cause cardiomyopathy and woolly haircoat in Poll Hereford cattle, and Ppp1r13l-null mice develop cardiac disease, with mechanistic links to desmosomal/NF-κB signaling. However, much of the human evidence derives from a founder variant in a limited number of families plus scattered reports, so gene–disease validity is often curated as limited-to-moderate rather than definitive. Therefore points concentrate on Existing with substantial weight on Established, a smaller share on Hypothesized (animal/functional data alone), and minimal on Novel.

MIRAGE syndrome (Myelodysplasia, Infection, Restriction of growth, Adrenal hypoplasia, Genital phenotypes, Enteropathy) was defined by Narumi et al. (Nature Genetics, 2016), who identified de novo gain-of-function missense variants in SAMD9 in multiple unrelated human probands. Numerous subsequent independent clinical reports and cohorts (including cases with monosomy 7/adaptive revertant mosaicism and somatic loss of the mutant allele) have replicated this association in humans. Functional studies confirm that mutant SAMD9 causes growth restriction/anti-proliferative effects consistent with the phenotype, and SAMD9 is the recognized disease gene in OMIM (#617053) and clinical gene panels. The evidence is human, replicated, and mechanistically supported, making this an unambiguously established gene–disease relationship.

MIRAGE syndrome (myelodysplasia, infection, restriction of growth, adrenal hypoplasia, genital phenotypes, enteropathy) was defined by Narumi et al. (Nature Genetics, 2016) who identified de novo gain-of-function missense variants in SAMD9 in multiple unrelated human probands. Numerous subsequent case reports and cohort studies from independent groups worldwide have replicated this association, expanding the phenotypic spectrum and documenting the characteristic somatic revertant mosaicism/monosomy 7 "adaptation by aneuploidy" mechanism in patient bone marrow. Functional studies in human cells confirm that the variants enhance SAMD9's growth-restricting activity, consistent with the growth-restriction and multisystem features. The gene–disease relationship is unambiguous and is curated as definitive in ClinGen/OMIM (OMIM 617053).

MIRAGE syndrome (Myelodysplasia, Infection, Restriction of growth, Adrenal hypoplasia, Genital phenotypes, Enteropathy) was defined by Narumi et al. (Nature Genetics, 2016), who identified de novo gain-of-function missense variants in SAMD9 in multiple unrelated human probands with this multisystem disorder. Subsequent independent human case series and cohorts (including patients with 46,XY disorders of sex development, adrenal hypoplasia, and monosomy 7-associated myelodysplasia) have replicated SAMD9 GOF variants, and adaptive somatic rescue events (monosomy 7, revertant mosaicism) provide strong mechanistic corroboration in patients. Functional studies show SAMD9 GOF suppresses cell growth, consistent with the growth-restriction phenotype. The gene–disease relationship is curated as definitive in OMIM/ClinGen-type resources, so essentially all weight belongs to Established.

Biallelic CRB2 variants are the recognized cause of ventriculomegaly with cystic kidney disease (OMIM 219730), first reported by Slavotinek and colleagues (2015) in multiple unrelated families/fetuses presenting with cerebral ventriculomegaly, cystic/echogenic kidneys, elevated alpha-fetoprotein, and a congenital nephrosis-like phenotype. Additional human reports link CRB2 to steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome/FSGS (NPHS9) and to prenatally detected renal cystic disease, providing independent replication of the renal phenotype. Zebrafish crb2b knockdown and podocyte functional data support the mechanism (slit diaphragm/apical polarity), but the primary evidence base is human genetic. Given replication across independent probands and formal OMIM disease-gene status, "Established" is strongly favored, with modest residual probability for "Existing" reflecting the relatively small number of reported families.

Biallelic CRB2 variants are the recognized cause of ventriculomegaly with cystic kidney disease (VMCKD, OMIM 219730), first delineated by Slavotinek et al. (2015) in multiple consanguineous and non-consanguineous families with fetal/neonatal ventriculomegaly and cystic/nephrotic kidney disease. Independent human reports (e.g., Ebarasi et al., 2015; subsequent case reports of prenatal presentations) confirm CRB2 mutations in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome/FSGS type 9 with overlapping cerebral ventriculomegaly, supporting replication across probands. Functional and zebrafish/mouse Crb2 data provide supportive mechanistic evidence (podocyte slit-diaphragm and apical polarity roles), but the core evidence is human genetic. Residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because the total number of reported families remains modest and some phenotypic overlap/variable expressivity persists.

Biallelic CRB2 variants are the recognized cause of ventriculomegaly with cystic kidney disease (OMIM #219730), first delineated by Slavotinek and colleagues (2015) in multiple consanguineous and non-consanguineous families with fetal/neonatal cerebral ventriculomegaly, cystic/echogenic kidneys, congenital nephrosis-like renal disease, and elevated alpha-fetoprotein. Independent reports (e.g., Ebarasi et al. 2015 and subsequent case series) confirmed CRB2 mutations in steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome/congenital nephrotic syndrome with overlapping renal cystic and ventriculomegaly features, providing replication across independent human probands. Functional data in zebrafish and mouse Crb2 models support the mechanism (podocyte slit diaphragm and apical polarity defects), but the causal evidence itself is human genetic. Residual probability is assigned to "Existing" only to account for the relatively small number of reported families and phenotypic heterogeneity.

Heterozygous truncating mutations clustered in the final exon (exon 34) of SRCAP were identified as the cause of Floating-Harbor syndrome by Hood et al. (2012, AJHG) using exome sequencing in affected probands, and this was rapidly replicated by Nikkel et al., Le Goff et al., and numerous subsequent cohorts and case reports worldwide. The mutational mechanism (dominant-negative/gain-of-function truncations in a narrow hotspot) is consistent across dozens of independent unrelated human probands, including de novo occurrences and rare familial transmissions. SRCAP is now the sole recognized gene for Floating-Harbor syndrome in OMIM, GeneReviews, and ClinGen curation. The evidence is unambiguously human clinical genetic data, so the relationship is Established with essentially no residual uncertainty.

Heterozygous truncating mutations clustered in the final exons (exon 33/34) of SRCAP were identified by exome sequencing as the cause of Floating-Harbor syndrome (Hood et al., AJHG 2012), and this was rapidly replicated in multiple independent cohorts (Nikkel et al. 2013, Le Goff et al. 2013, and subsequent case series worldwide). SRCAP is now the sole recognized disease gene for this disorder, with dozens of unrelated probands and de novo occurrences reported, and it is curated as definitive in OMIM/ClinGen-type resources. Molecular testing of SRCAP is standard clinical practice for diagnosing Floating-Harbor syndrome, and a distinct DNA methylation episignature further supports causality. All key evidence is human, so the relationship is Established.

Truncating mutations clustered in exons 33–34 of SRCAP were identified by exome sequencing as the cause of Floating-Harbor syndrome (Hood et al., AJHG 2012), and this was rapidly replicated in independent cohorts (e.g., Nikkel et al. 2013, Le Goff et al. 2013, and subsequent case series worldwide). Dozens of unrelated human probands with the characteristic facial gestalt, short stature, delayed bone age, and expressive language delay carry de novo SRCAP variants in this hotspot, with clear genotype–phenotype correlation. The gene–disease relationship is curated as "definitive" by ClinGen/OMIM (FLHS, OMIM 136140), and SRCAP testing is standard clinical practice for this syndrome. Evidence is entirely human-based and replicated, so essentially all weight belongs in the Established category.

MEND syndrome (Male EBP Disorder with Neurological Defects) is by definition caused by hemizygous, typically hypomorphic, variants in the X-linked EBP gene encoding emopamil-binding protein (sterol Δ8-Δ7 isomerase), the same gene whose loss-of-function causes X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata (CDPX2) in females. Multiple independent human reports (e.g., Arnold et al. 2012, Barboza-Cerda et al. 2014, Furtado et al. 2017, and additional case series) describe surviving males with missense EBP variants, characteristic 8(9)-cholestenol/8-dehydrocholesterol accumulation, and a consistent phenotype of intellectual disability, cataracts, digital anomalies, skin findings, and other malformations. Biochemical sterol profiling in patients provides functional confirmation of pathogenicity in humans. The gene–disease relationship is therefore definitive/established, with only minor residual weight for "existing" given the relative rarity and modest number of reported probands.

MEND syndrome (Male EBP Disorder with Neurological defects) is by definition caused by hemizygous, typically hypomorphic, variants in the X-linked EBP gene encoding emopamil-binding protein (sterol Δ8-Δ7 isomerase), the same gene whose loss-of-function causes X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata (CDPX2/Conradi–Hünermann–Happle) in females. Multiple independent male probands from unrelated families have been reported since the initial delineation (e.g., Arnold et al. 2012 and subsequent case series), with concordant biochemical confirmation showing elevated 8-dehydrocholesterol and 8(9)-cholestenol in plasma or tissues. The evidence is human-based, replicated, and mechanistically supported, and MEND is listed in OMIM/GeneReviews as an EBP-related disorder. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" only because the number of reported cases remains modest for a rare disorder.

MEND syndrome (Male EBP Disorder with Neurological Defects) is defined by its molecular cause: hemizygous, typically hypomorphic, missense variants in EBP (emopamil-binding protein, the 3β-hydroxysteroid-Δ8,Δ7-isomerase of cholesterol biosynthesis) in males, the same gene whose loss-of-function causes X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata (CDPX2/Conradi–Hünermann–Happle) in females. The condition was delineated by Arnold et al. (2012) and subsequently confirmed in multiple independent male probands and families with characteristic biochemical findings of elevated 8(9)-cholestenol and 8-dehydrocholesterol. Human genetic, biochemical, and clinical data are replicated across several reports and the gene–disease relationship is curated in OMIM/GeneReviews-type resources. Evidence therefore strongly supports the Established category, with only minor residual weight for "Existing" given the relative rarity and small number of published cases.

In 2013, several independent groups (Dyment et al., Thauvin-Robinet et al., Chudasama et al., Schroeder et al.) simultaneously reported heterozygous mutations in PIK3R1, predominantly clustering in the C-terminal SH2 domain (e.g., p.Arg649Trp), in unrelated probands and families with SHORT syndrome (Short stature, Hyperextensibility, Ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, Teething delay, with lipoatrophy and insulin resistance). Subsequent case series and cohorts have replicated these findings in many additional human patients, and the gene is listed in OMIM as the cause of SHORT syndrome (#269880). Functional studies in human fibroblasts confirm impaired PI3K/AKT signaling and insulin resistance, providing a coherent mechanism. The evidence is therefore definitively "Established" in humans, with negligible probability for the other categories.

In 2013, several independent groups (Dyment et al., Thauvin-Robinet et al., Chudasama et al., Schroeder et al.) simultaneously reported heterozygous mutations in PIK3R1, predominantly clustering in the C-terminal SH2 domain (notably the recurrent p.Arg649Trp), in multiple unrelated probands and families with SHORT syndrome (short stature, hyperextensibility, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, teething delay, lipoatrophy, insulin resistance). Numerous subsequent case series and cohort reports have replicated this finding in independent human probands, and functional studies confirm impaired PI3K/AKT signaling and insulin resistance consistent with the phenotype. PIK3R1 is the recognized disease gene for SHORT syndrome in OMIM (#269880) and ClinGen/GeneReviews. This constitutes definitive, replicated human genetic evidence for causation.

In 2013, multiple independent groups (Dyment et al., Thauvin-Robinet et al., Chudasama et al., Schroeder et al.) simultaneously reported heterozygous PIK3R1 mutations—most recurrently the p.Arg649Trp change in the C-terminal SH2 domain—in unrelated probands and families with SHORT syndrome (short stature, hyperextensibility, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, teething delay, lipoatrophy, insulin resistance). Subsequent case series and cohort studies have replicated these findings in many additional human patients, and functional work confirms impaired p85α-mediated PI3K/AKT signaling causing insulin resistance, consistent with the clinical phenotype. PIK3R1-SHORT syndrome is listed in OMIM (#269880) and is considered the definitive molecular cause of the disorder. The evidence base is human genetic, replicated, and mechanistically supported, so the relationship is firmly Established.

ZFTRAF1 (formerly C15orf39) was reported around 2023 in a multi-family study describing bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in consanguineous families with a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly and seizures, supported by segregation and functional/expression data. Because several independent probands/families were described in human patients, the evidence leans toward an established gene–disease relationship, though it largely stems from a single collaborative publication with limited independent replication, which keeps substantial weight on "Existing." Supporting functional work (expression in brain, loss-of-function modeling) reinforces plausibility but is secondary to the human genetic data. A "Novel" classification is very unlikely given the published human cohort.

ZFTRAF1 (formerly C15orf39) was reported around 2023 in a multi-center study describing bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in several consanguineous families with a recessive neurodevelopmental disorder featuring global developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly, seizures, and dysmorphism, with supporting functional/expression data. Because multiple independent human probands/families with segregating variants were reported in a single collaborative publication, the evidence leans toward "Established," though independent replication beyond that initial cohort is still limited, which keeps meaningful weight on "Existing." Animal/functional data alone would not suffice, but the core evidence here is human genetic. Very little probability remains for "Hypothesized" or "Novel," since a direct gene–disease report exists.

ZFTRAF1 (formerly C15orf39) has been reported in a multi-family cohort study describing bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in affected individuals with a neurodevelopmental phenotype including global developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly and seizures, with segregation in consanguineous families and supporting functional data. This constitutes human genetic evidence in multiple independent probands, favoring an "Established" classification, and the gene has been recognized in disease databases as a new NDD gene. However, the evidence base is relatively recent and derives largely from a single collaborative publication with limited independent replication, so substantial probability remains for "Existing." Purely biological/animal-model-only evidence (Hypothesized) or absence of any link (Novel) is unlikely given the published human variant data.

ATP2B1 encodes the plasma membrane calcium ATPase PMCA1, and OMIM designates "Intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 66" (MRD66) as caused by heterozygous ATP2B1 variants. This entry derives from a cohort report (Am J Hum Genet, ~2021) describing multiple unrelated individuals with de novo missense/loss-of-function ATP2B1 variants presenting with developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, and seizures, with supporting functional calcium-efflux assays. The presence of several independent human probands with de novo variants and concordant functional data supports an established gene–disease relationship, and additional case reports have since been added. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because the evidence base is relatively recent and largely stems from one primary multi-patient study rather than many fully independent replications.

ATP2B1 encodes the plasma membrane calcium ATPase PMCA1, and heterozygous de novo missense variants were reported in a multi-patient cohort (published in the American Journal of Human Genetics, ~2021) describing individuals with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and seizures, with functional assays showing impaired calcium extrusion. This entity was subsequently curated by OMIM as intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 66 (MRD66), indicating a defined gene–disease relationship. The original report included multiple unrelated probands with de novo variants plus supporting in vitro functional data, and additional case reports have expanded the phenotype. This satisfies criteria for an established, replicated human causal association, with a small residual probability that curation bodies consider the evidence still limited/moderate (Existing).

ATP2B1 encodes PMCA1, a plasma membrane calcium ATPase, and OMIM designates intellectual developmental disorder, autosomal dominant 66 (MRD66) as caused by heterozygous ATP2B1 variants. This designation followed a multi-center human cohort report (AJHG, ~2021) describing a series of unrelated probands with de novo missense/loss-of-function ATP2B1 variants presenting with developmental delay/intellectual disability, hypotonia, seizures, and dysmorphism, with functional calcium-efflux assays supporting pathogenicity. Multiple independent probands from different centers and subsequent case reports provide replication, satisfying criteria for an established gene–disease relationship. A small residual probability is retained for "Existing" given that the evidence base is relatively recent and derived largely from one main cohort publication plus scattered case reports.

CCDC88A encodes girdin (GIV), and Nahorski et al. (Brain, 2016) reported homozygous truncating CCDC88A variants segregating with a PEHO-like phenotype (progressive encephalopathy, severe developmental delay, seizures, brain atrophy) in consanguineous families, supported by a concordant Ccdc88a knockout mouse model. This gene–disease pair is recognized in OMIM/ClinGen-style curations as PEHO-like syndrome (autosomal recessive), and additional families/case reports have since been described, supporting replication in humans. The main residual uncertainty is the relatively small number of independent probands, which keeps some probability on "Existing" rather than fully established. Animal/functional data exist but are supplementary to direct human genetic evidence, so little weight goes to "Hypothesized" or "Novel."

CCDC88A encodes girdin (GIV), and biallelic loss-of-function variants were reported by Nahorski et al. (Brain, 2016) in consanguineous families with a PEHO-like syndrome phenotype (progressive encephalopathy with brain atrophy and thin corpus callosum, PEBAT; OMIM 615188), supported by a concordant Ccdc88a knockout mouse model. Subsequent independent case reports/families from different populations have described additional truncating variants with a consistent severe neurodevelopmental phenotype, providing replication in humans. This supports an Established relationship, though the total number of reported probands remains modest, leaving some probability that curators would consider the evidence only moderate/limited (Existing). Purely hypothesized or novel classifications are very unlikely given direct human genetic evidence.

CCDC88A encodes girdin (GIV/APE), and Nahorski et al. (Brain, 2016) reported a homozygous truncating CCDC88A variant segregating in a consanguineous human family with a PEHO-like phenotype (severe developmental delay, epileptic encephalopathy/hypsarrhythmia, optic atrophy, brain atrophy), supported by a concordant Ccdc88a knockout mouse model. Subsequent case reports of additional consanguineous families with biallelic loss-of-function CCDC88A variants have been described, and the gene–disease pair is recognized in OMIM as PEHO-like syndrome. However, the total number of independent probands remains small and largely from consanguineous pedigrees, so some curators would classify the evidence as moderate rather than definitive. This supports weighting mainly toward Established with substantial probability on Existing; purely biological/animal-only (Hypothesized) or no-evidence (Novel) classifications are unlikely given the human genetic data.

SLC38A3 encodes SNAT3, a system N glutamine transporter central to the glutamate–glutamine cycle in astrocytes, making it highly plausible biologically for epileptic encephalopathy. Beyond plausibility, human genetic evidence exists: biallelic loss-of-function/missense SLC38A3 variants were reported in multiple unrelated consanguineous families with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder featuring infantile-onset refractory seizures, microcephaly, hypotonia, and profound developmental delay (e.g., Marafi et al., Brain 2022), leading to the OMIM designation developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 102 (MIM 619881). Because several independent probands/families were described with supporting functional data, the evidence best fits "Established," though the relative recency and limited number of subsequent replication reports leave some probability on "Existing."

SLC38A3 encodes SNAT3, a system N glutamine/sodium-coupled amino acid transporter central to the glutamate–glutamine cycle, providing strong biological plausibility for an epileptic encephalopathy. A multi-family study (Marafi et al., Brain 2022) reported biallelic loss-of-function and missense SLC38A3 variants in around ten affected individuals from several unrelated, consanguineous families with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, microcephaly, hypotonia and brain abnormalities, with supporting functional/transport assays. On this basis OMIM created the specific phenotype entry "developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 102" linked to SLC38A3, indicating curated gene–disease validity. Because the evidence largely derives from a single (though multi-family, multi-proband) human cohort with additional subsequent case reports, most weight goes to Established with meaningful residual probability for Existing if one demands independent replication.

SLC38A3 encodes SNAT3, a system N glutamine/glutamate transporter central to the glutamate–glutamine cycle in astrocytes, giving strong biological plausibility for epilepsy. Human genetic evidence exists: biallelic loss-of-function and missense variants in SLC38A3 have been reported in multiple unrelated consanguineous families with a severe neurodevelopmental disorder featuring early-onset refractory seizures, microcephaly, hypomyelination and developmental arrest, leading to the OMIM designation DEE102. Because this rests largely on a single multi-family cohort report (with supporting functional/transport assays and mouse data), some curators would classify the evidence as moderate rather than definitively replicated across independent publications. I therefore weight Established most heavily, with substantial residual probability on Existing, and little on Hypothesized or Novel since human variant-level evidence clearly exists.

CFAP43 encodes a cilia- and flagella-associated protein best known for biallelic loss-of-function causing multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella (MMAF). Morimoto et al. (Neurology, 2019) reported a homozygous nonsense CFAP43 variant segregating in a Japanese family with autosomal recessive normal pressure hydrocephalus, supported by Cfap43-knockout mice that developed communicating hydrocephalus with abnormal ependymal ciliary beating — providing direct human genetic evidence plus a concordant animal model. However, the human evidence largely rests on one family/small cohort with limited independent replication in other iNPH populations, so the association is credible but not definitively established. Accordingly, most weight falls on "Existing," with some probability on "Established" (if additional familial iNPH cohorts have replicated it) and a residual share on "Hypothesized" (if one considers the mouse ciliary/hydrocephalus data the strongest support).

Morimoto et al. (Neurology, 2019) reported a homozygous nonsense variant in CFAP43 segregating in a Japanese family with autosomal recessive normal pressure hydrocephalus, and Cfap43 knockout mice recapitulated the ventriculomegaly/hydrocephalus phenotype with abnormal ependymal ciliary function, providing direct human genetic plus supportive animal evidence. CFAP43 is otherwise well established as a MMAF/male-infertility gene, and its ciliary/flagellar biology (ependymal motile cilia driving CSF flow) makes the mechanism highly plausible. However, human evidence for NPH rests largely on a small number of families/probands from one population, with limited independent replication in larger idiopathic NPH cohorts, so the association falls short of firmly established. Accordingly, most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful probability for "Established" if subsequent cohort sequencing studies are counted as replication, and a smaller share for "Hypothesized" if the human data are judged too preliminary.

CFAP43 encodes a cilia- and flagella-associated protein best known for biallelic loss-of-function causing multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagella, but a human study (Morimoto et al., Neurology 2019) reported nonsense/loss-of-function CFAP43 variants segregating in Japanese families with familial idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, supported by Cfap43-knockout mice developing ventriculomegaly and abnormal ependymal ciliary beating. This provides credible human genetic evidence plus a plausible mechanism (ependymal motile ciliopathy impairing CSF flow), placing the pair firmly at least in "Existing." Replication in independent, well-powered NPH cohorts remains limited and some reports have not consistently confirmed enrichment, so "Established" is possible but not clearly met. A minority of weight goes to "Hypothesized" in case the main support is judged to rest chiefly on the mouse/ciliary functional data, and essentially none to "Novel."

phenotype: epidermolysis bullosa simplex 6, generalized, with scarring and hair loss
justification: Two landmark 2016 human genetic studies (Lin et al., Nature Genetics; He et al., American Journal of Human Genetics) identified de novo and inherited start-codon (p.Met1) mutations in KLHL24 in multiple independent probands and families with a distinctive epidermolysis bullosa simplex characterized by generalized skin fragility, atrophic scarring, alopecia and nail dystrophy, corresponding to OMIM 617294 (EBS6). The mechanism—translation reinitiation producing an N-terminally truncated KLHL24 protein that gains stability and leads to excessive ubiquitin-mediated degradation of keratin 14 (and later shown to affect keratin 5 and cardiac desmin)—has been functionally validated in patient keratinocytes and mouse models. Numerous subsequent case reports and cohorts worldwide have replicated the recurrent p.Met1 variants, including associations with dilated cardiomyopathy. The gene–disease relationship is definitive by ClinGen-style criteria, leaving essentially no weight for lower-evidence categories.

phenotype: epidermolysis bullosa simplex 6, generalized, with scarring and hair loss
justification: Two independent 2016 papers (He et al. and Lin et al., Am J Hum Genet) reported heterozygous start-codon (p.Met1) mutations in KLHL24 in multiple unrelated families with a distinctive epidermolysis bullosa simplex characterized by neonatal blistering, skin scarring/atrophy, alopecia, and nail dystrophy; this entity is catalogued as EBS6 (OMIM 617294). The mechanism—N-terminally truncated KLHL24 escaping autoubiquitination and causing excessive degradation of keratin 14—has been validated in patient keratinocytes and confirmed by subsequent reports, including associated dilated cardiomyopathy. Numerous additional probands from diverse populations have been described, satisfying replication in humans. Evidence is therefore unambiguous and causal, warranting near-complete weight on "Established."

phenotype: epidermolysis bullosa simplex 6, generalized, with scarring and hair loss
justification: Heterozygous start-codon (p.Met1) mutations in KLHL24 were reported in 2016 by two independent groups (He et al. and Lin et al., Am J Hum Genet) in multiple unrelated families with generalized epidermolysis bullosa simplex featuring skin fragility, scarring, and alopecia, establishing OMIM entry EBS6 (#617294). The mechanism—translational reinitiation producing an N-terminally truncated KLHL24 that escapes autoubiquitination and leads to excessive CUL3-mediated degradation of keratin 14—has been functionally validated in patient keratinocytes. Subsequent human reports have replicated the same recurrent start-codon variants in additional probands worldwide, some with associated dilated cardiomyopathy. This constitutes strong, replicated human genetic and functional evidence for causation.

Lassuthová et al. (Am J Hum Genet, 2018) reported heterozygous missense variants in ATP1A1 segregating with autosomal dominant axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy in multiple independent families, with supporting functional data showing impaired Na+/K+-ATPase pump activity and altered intracellular sodium homeostasis. This formed the basis for the OMIM entry CMT2DD (618036). Additional case reports and diagnostic panel/exome cohorts have subsequently identified further ATP1A1 variants in patients with axonal neuropathy, some with additional features (e.g., intellectual disability, hypomagnesemia, refractory seizures from other ATP1A1 alleles). The evidence is human-based, replicated across independent probands, and mechanistically supported, so "Established" is most likely; residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because the total number of reported CMT2DD families remains modest and some variants are of uncertain significance.

ATP1A1 was identified as the cause of autosomal dominant axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2DD in a 2018 American Journal of Human Genetics study (Lassuthova et al.), which reported multiple independent families with segregating missense variants and supporting functional data on Na+/K+-ATPase pump activity. OMIM assigns CMT2DD (#618036) to ATP1A1, and additional case reports/cohorts have since described further probands with ATP1A1 variants and axonal neuropathy, sometimes with additional features such as hypomagnesemia or intellectual disability. The evidence therefore comes from multiple human families with segregation and functional corroboration, meeting criteria for an established gene–disease relationship. A small residual probability is left for "Existing" because the total number of independent reported probands remains modest compared with classic CMT genes.

ATP1A1 was identified as a cause of autosomal dominant axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT2DD, OMIM 618036) by Lassuthova et al. (Am J Hum Genet, 2018), who reported heterozygous missense variants segregating in multiple independent families of different ancestries, with supporting functional studies showing impaired Na+/K+-ATPase pump activity. Subsequent case reports and gene-panel/exome studies in additional CMT probands have confirmed pathogenic ATP1A1 variants, and the gene is included in standard inherited neuropathy diagnostic panels. The evidence is human, replicated across independent families, and mechanistically supported, meeting criteria for an Established gene–disease relationship. A small residual probability is assigned to "Existing" given the relatively small total number of reported families and the recognition of allelic ATP1A1 phenotypes (hypomagnesemia, seizures, intellectual disability) that broaden the phenotypic spectrum.

Cousin syndrome (pelviscapular dysplasia with epiphyseal dysplasia and craniofacial anomalies) was shown by Lausch et al. (2008, AJHG) to result from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in TBX15 in affected human patients, with supporting evidence from the mouse droopy ear (de) Tbx15-null model that phenocopies scapular and pelvic hypoplasia. Subsequent case reports have described additional patients with homozygous TBX15 variants and the characteristic phenotype, and OMIM lists Cousin syndrome as a TBX15-related autosomal recessive disorder. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence, supporting "Established," though the total number of independent probands is small given the extreme rarity of the condition, leaving some weight on "Existing." Functional/animal data alone would only support "Hypothesized," so little weight is placed there, and "Novel" is essentially excluded.

Cousin syndrome (pelviscapular dysplasia with epiphyseal dysplasia and abnormal facies, OMIM 260660) was shown by Lausch et al. (2008, AJHG) to result from biallelic loss-of-function TBX15 mutations in affected human probands, with subsequent case reports adding independent patients. This is supported by the Tbx15-deficient droopy ear mouse, which recapitulates scapular and pelvic girdle hypoplasia, providing strong functional corroboration. Because the causal evidence comes from human families with segregating homozygous variants and has been replicated in additional independent cases, the relationship is best regarded as established, though the total number of reported probands is relatively small, leaving some probability on "Existing."

Cousin syndrome (pelviscapular dysplasia with epiphyseal and vertebral anomalies, OMIM 260660) is a recognized autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TBX15, first demonstrated by Lausch et al. (2008, Am J Hum Genet) in affected human patients, with subsequent additional case reports of homozygous TBX15 mutations in consanguineous families. The human genetic evidence is supported by the well-characterized droopy ear (de) mouse model, which carries Tbx15 mutations and shows skeletal/scapular defects that phenocopy the human condition, providing strong functional corroboration. Because the disorder is ultra-rare, the number of independent probands remains small, so some probability is retained for "Existing" rather than fully replicated "Established" status. There is essentially no scenario in which this pairing is merely hypothesized or novel, since the causal variants were identified directly in humans.

ANE syndrome (alopecia, neurologic defects, and endocrinopathy; OMIM 612079) was first linked to a homozygous missense variant (p.Leu351Pro) in RBM28 by Nousbeck et al. (2008, AJHG) in a consanguineous Israeli Arab family with multiple affected individuals, with functional work showing reduced RBM28 (nucleolar protein, yeast Nop4 homolog) expression in patient hair follicles and pituitary. RBM28 is currently the only gene known to cause this ultra-rare disorder, and subsequent case reports/small series in additional unrelated patients have described further biallelic RBM28 variants, supporting replication in humans. The main caveat is the very small number of reported probands, so some curation frameworks might rate the gene–disease validity as moderate rather than definitive, which justifies a substantial share for "Existing." Purely biological/animal-model-only evidence (Hypothesized) or absence of evidence (Novel) are clearly inconsistent with the human genetic data.

ANE syndrome (alopecia, neurologic defects, and endocrinopathy; OMIM 612079) was linked to RBM28 by Nousbeck et al. (J Clin Invest, 2008), who identified a homozygous missense mutation (p.Leu351Pro) segregating in a large consanguineous Israeli Arab family, with supporting functional work on the nucleolar protein and its yeast ortholog Nop4. Subsequent human reports (e.g., Spiegel et al., describing combined pituitary hormone deficiency in ANE syndrome with the same RBM28 variant, and later additional patients/families) reinforce causation, so the evidence is human-based and clinically replicated. However, ANE syndrome is ultra-rare and the number of truly independent probands/families is small, with some sharing a founder allele, which keeps the gene–disease validity closer to moderate rather than unequivocally definitive. Hence most weight goes to Established, with substantial residual probability on Existing, and little on Hypothesized or Novel since human genetic evidence clearly exists.

ANE syndrome (alopecia, neurologic defects, and endocrinopathy; OMIM 612079) was defined molecularly by Nousbeck et al. (2008, AJHG), who identified a homozygous RBM28 missense variant (p.Leu351Pro) segregating in a consanguineous family, with functional data supporting reduced nucleolar RBM28 and impaired ribosome biogenesis. Subsequent human reports (e.g., additional affected individuals/families, including patients sharing the same or other biallelic RBM28 variants) have supported the association, and RBM28 is the sole recognized gene for this ultra-rare recessive disorder in OMIM and clinical panels. However, the total number of independent probands remains small, so some curation frameworks might classify the evidence as moderate rather than definitive, which justifies substantial weight on "Existing." Animal/in vitro data (yeast Nop4 orthology, ribosomopathy mechanism) are supportive but secondary to the human genetic evidence, so little weight goes to "Hypothesized" or "Novel."

phenotype: cerebellar dysfunction with variable cognitive and behavioral abnormalities
justification: CAMTA1 haploinsufficiency is the recognized cause of "cerebellar dysfunction with variable cognitive and behavioral abnormalities" (CECBA; OMIM 614756), an autosomal dominant condition.
