Several case reports and cohort studies of intragenic CAMTA1 deletions/de novo variants describe patients with intellectual disability, developmental delay, and autism spectrum traits, and the gene appears in autism candidate gene lists (e.g., SFARI) with suggestive rather than strong evidence. However, ASD is generally a secondary/comorbid feature rather than a replicated primary phenotype attributed specifically to CAMTA1, so "Established" is unlikely. Supporting mouse models (Camta1 knockout with cerebellar/behavioral phenotypes) add biological plausibility but are non-human, supporting some weight on "Hypothesized." Given the human genetic evidence linking CAMTA1 variants to neurodevelopmental phenotypes including autistic features, "Existing" is the most probable category.

POU3F3 (BRN1) de novo variants and 2q12.1 deletions have been reported in humans to cause Snijders Blok–Fisher syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder with developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and behavioral abnormalities, with autistic features/ASD diagnoses documented in a subset of the reported probands. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence linking the gene to a phenotype spectrum that includes autism, supporting the "Existing" category, and POU3F3 has been flagged in autism gene resources through large-scale de novo variant studies. However, ASD is not the core or consistently replicated phenotype, and the evidence base is dominated by syndromic NDD cohorts rather than dedicated, replicated ASD association studies, so "Established" is unlikely. Supporting biology (POU-domain transcription factor essential for cortical neuron migration and upper-layer neurogenesis, with informative mouse models) would independently justify at least "Hypothesized." Minimal probability is assigned to "Novel" given the clear human clinical reports.

WDFY3 (ALFY) is a well-recognized autism/neurodevelopmental candidate gene, carrying a high-confidence SFARI classification, with recurrent de novo loss-of-function and damaging missense variants reported across independent large-scale human exome sequencing studies of ASD probands (e.g., Iossifov, De Rubeis, Sanders, Satterstrom cohorts). Additional human clinical case series describe WDFY3 haploinsufficiency causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome with intellectual disability, altered head circumference (micro/macrocephaly), and autistic features, supporting causality in independent probands. Strong supporting mechanistic work exists in mouse and cellular models (Wdfy3/Alfy roles in autophagy, cortical neurogenesis, and neuronal connectivity), which reinforces but does not by itself establish the association. The main uncertainty is whether the human phenotype is best framed as a broader NDD with variable autism features rather than ASD specifically, so some weight remains on "Existing." Very little probability is warranted for "Novel" given the substantial human genetic evidence.

KMT2E (MLL5) emerged as an exome-wide significant autism risk gene in large-scale human sequencing studies (e.g., Satterstrom et al. 2020, ASC/SPARK cohorts), with recurrent de novo protein-truncating variants in independent ASD probands, and it is classified as a high-confidence gene in SFARI. Independently, O'Donnell-Luria et al. (2019) described ~38 individuals with heterozygous KMT2E variants causing a neurodevelopmental spectrum including developmental delay, epilepsy, macrocephaly, and autistic features, providing replication across independent human cohorts. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence, favoring "Established," though some may argue ASD is one component of a broader KMT2E-related NDD phenotype rather than a specific ASD-causing gene, which supports assigning substantial weight to "Existing." Supporting functional/expression data (chromatin regulation, high brain expression, mouse models) are consistent but are not the primary basis of the association, so little weight goes to "Hypothesized" and essentially none to "Novel."

ZBTB20 is the gene underlying Primrose syndrome (de novo missense variants) and is contained in the 3q13.31 microdeletion region, both human neurodevelopmental conditions in which autistic features, intellectual disability, and macrocephaly are frequently described. ZBTB20 also appears in SFARI Gene and in de novo variant lists from human exome studies of autism/neurodevelopmental disorder cohorts, providing credible but not definitive gene-specific evidence for ASD as the primary phenotype. Most reported ASD is a secondary feature of a broader syndromic presentation rather than replicated, well-powered case-control association specifically for idiopathic autism, which argues against "Established." Supporting mouse and expression data (ZBTB20 role in hippocampal/cortical development) reinforce biological plausibility, so some weight remains on "Hypothesized," while "Novel" is very unlikely given the human syndromic data.

CSNK2A1 de novo missense variants cause Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS), a human condition in which autism or prominent autistic features are reported in a substantial fraction of probands across multiple independent cohorts and case series. In addition, CSNK2A1 has been recovered as a de novo mutation target in large-scale autism exome sequencing studies (e.g., ASC/Satterstrom-type analyses) and is curated in SFARI Gene as an ASD-risk gene, supporting replicated human genetic evidence. Some uncertainty remains because ASD is one variable feature of a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than an isolated, consistently penetrant outcome, which supports substantial weight on "Existing" as well. Supportive functional and mouse/neuronal data on CK2α in synaptic signaling reinforce biological plausibility but are secondary to the human variant evidence, so little weight goes to "Hypothesized" and essentially none to "Novel."

PHF21A (BHC80) is a component of the LSD1–CoREST chromatin-repressor complex at 11p11.2 and is disrupted in Potocki–Shaffer syndrome; human studies (e.g., translocation/deletion cases and later cohorts of de novo point variants) describe intellectual disability, craniofacial anomalies, and behavioral features including autism or autistic traits. De novo damaging PHF21A variants have also been reported in large ASD/NDD exome sequencing cohorts, and the gene is listed among SFARI candidate ASD genes, supporting at least one credible human genetic link. However, the phenotype is predominantly a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder in which ASD is a variable feature rather than a replicated, primary ASD diagnosis, so evidence falls short of unambiguous "Established" status for ASD specifically. Its chromatin-regulatory biology, shared with many high-confidence ASD genes, provides additional mechanistic plausibility, warranting some weight on "Hypothesized." Very little probability is assigned to "Novel" given the documented human variant-phenotype reports.

SMARCA4 (BRG1) encodes the ATPase subunit of the BAF/SWI-SNF chromatin remodeling complex, a pathway strongly and repeatedly implicated in autism spectrum disorder (e.g., ARID1B, ARID1A, SMARCC2, ADNP-related chromatin regulators). Germline de novo SMARCA4 variants cause Coffin–Siris syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring intellectual disability and, in a subset of patients, autistic features, providing human genetic evidence for a syndromic ASD link. Large-scale ASD exome sequencing studies have reported occasional de novo damaging SMARCA4 variants in probands, and SFARI Gene includes SMARCA4 as a candidate ASD gene, but it has not reached exome-wide significance in the major ASD gene-discovery analyses (e.g., Satterstrom et al.). Thus the evidence is credible and human-based but limited and not definitively replicated as a primary ASD gene, best fitting "Existing," with residual probability for "Established" (given syndromic overlap) and "Hypothesized" (given the strong pathway/functional rationale from BAF complex biology and mouse models).

GRIN1 encodes the obligatory GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor, and de novo missense and loss-of-function variants are a well-documented cause of a human neurodevelopmental disorder (GRIN1-related encephalopathy) in which autistic features, stereotypies, and intellectual disability are frequently described (e.g., Lemke et al., Ohba et al., Fry et al.). De novo GRIN1 variants have also been reported in autism/developmental disorder exome sequencing cohorts, and GRIN1 is catalogued as an ASD candidate gene in SFARI Gene, supporting at least "Existing" human genetic evidence. However, GRIN1 has generally not reached exome-wide significance as an ASD risk gene in large case-control studies (e.g., the ASC 102-gene list), and its core phenotype is epileptic encephalopathy/ID with autism as a comorbid feature rather than isolated ASD, which tempers an "Established" designation. Extensive mouse (Grin1 knockdown, hypomorph) and in vitro receptor-function data provide strong mechanistic plausibility but count toward "Hypothesized" rather than human causal proof. Thus most weight falls on Existing, with substantial residual probability for Established.

SIN3A haploinsufficiency causes Witteveen–Kolk syndrome (OMIM 613406), a human neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by mild intellectual disability, microcephaly, dysmorphism, and frequently autistic features/behavioral problems, described in multiple independent probands with de novo truncating variants and 15q24 microdeletions. De novo loss-of-function SIN3A variants have also been recovered in large autism/NDD exome sequencing cohorts, and SIN3A is annotated in SFARI Gene as an ASD-associated gene, consistent with a chromatin/transcriptional-corepressor mechanism shared with other high-confidence ASD genes. However, the core, most consistently reported phenotype is syndromic intellectual disability with autistic traits rather than idiopathic ASD per se, so replicated causal evidence specifically for ASD is somewhat less definitive. This supports strong weighting toward "Existing," with substantial probability for "Established" given multiple independent human probands, and only residual weight for hypothesized or novel.

KCNQ2 is definitively established as a cause of benign familial neonatal epilepsy and KCNQ2-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE7), in which autistic features, intellectual disability, and global developmental delay are frequently described in human patients — a phenotype strongly linked to and often overlapping ASD. KCNQ2 is included in the SFARI autism gene database with suggestive/limited evidence, and de novo or rare variants have been reported in a small number of individuals ascertained for ASD or with ASD as part of a broader neurodevelopmental presentation. However, ASD is not a core, replicated primary outcome of KCNQ2 variation, and large ASD exome studies have not identified KCNQ2 as an exome-wide significant risk gene, so "Established" is unlikely. Strong mechanistic plausibility (M-current regulation of neuronal excitability, Kcnq2 mouse models with behavioral/cognitive deficits) supports at least a hypothesized relationship if human variant-level evidence is discounted. The weight therefore falls mainly on "Existing," with meaningful residual probability on "Hypothesized."

RFX3, a ciliogenesis-related transcription factor, emerged as an exome-wide significant autism risk gene in large sequencing studies (e.g., the Autism Sequencing Consortium analysis of >35,000 samples), driven by recurrent de novo loss-of-function variants in independent probands. A dedicated clinical cohort study (Harris et al., Genetics in Medicine, 2021) described multiple unrelated individuals with RFX3 haploinsufficiency presenting with autism, ADHD, intellectual disability, and behavioral dysregulation, supporting replication across independent human cohorts. RFX3 is classified as a high-confidence ASD gene in curated databases such as SFARI Gene. Some residual uncertainty remains because the phenotype is a broad neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated ASD and the number of published probands is still moderate, so a portion of probability is retained for "Existing." Supporting mouse and cilia-biology data reinforce but are not the primary basis for the human genetic evidence.

PTPN11 is the major gene for Noonan syndrome and related RASopathies, and human studies (e.g., Adviento et al., 2014; Alfieri et al.) document elevated autistic traits and ASD diagnoses in individuals with PTPN11 mutations, which supports at least the "Existing" category through a well-recognized syndromic route to ASD. Additional human evidence comes from large autism sequencing/de novo variant studies and SFARI Gene, which lists PTPN11 as a syndromic ASD-associated gene with suggestive-to-moderate scoring, and from Ras/MAPK signaling being a convergent ASD pathway. However, PTPN11 variants are not consistently or highly penetrant for ASD, and the association is largely secondary to the Noonan/RASopathy phenotype rather than replicated ASD-specific causal findings, so full "Established" status is uncertain. Mouse models of Ptpn11 mutation show social and cognitive deficits, but these animal data alone would only support "Hypothesized," leaving a modest weight there. "Novel" is essentially excluded given the substantial human literature co-implicating PTPN11 and autistic features.

TCF12 (HEB) is a class I bHLH transcription factor best established as a cause of coronal craniosynostosis (haploinsufficiency), and a subset of these patients show developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autistic features, which supports a human variant–phenotype link to neurodevelopmental outcomes. De novo and loss-of-function TCF12 variants have appeared in large exome sequencing studies of autism and developmental disorders (e.g., DDD, ASC/SPARK-type cohorts), and TCF12 is catalogued in SFARI Gene with a suggestive/moderate score rather than as a high-confidence ASD gene. Its biology—dimerization with TCF4 (a Pitt–Hopkins/ASD-relevant gene), regulation of neurogenesis and cortical development—provides strong mechanistic plausibility, supporting substantial weight for Hypothesized as well. Evidence is not yet replicated at the level of clearly causal, recurrent ASD probands with consistent phenotype, so Established receives limited weight. Novel is unlikely given multiple human co-segregating neurodevelopmental reports.

TUBB2A is a well-established tubulinopathy gene, with de novo missense variants causing complex cortical dysplasia with other brain malformations (CDCBM5), polymicrogyria, developmental delay, epilepsy and intellectual disability — phenotypes that frequently co-occur with autistic features, making a neurodevelopmental link biologically compelling. However, I am not aware of dedicated, replicated ASD cohort studies establishing TUBB2A as an autism risk gene; any autism mention is typically incidental within broader tubulinopathy or developmental-disorder (e.g., DDD, large de novo NDD sequencing) case series. Microtubule dynamics, neuronal migration and cortical patterning are strongly implicated ASD-relevant mechanisms, and related tubulin genes (TUBA1A, TUBB2B, TUBGCP5) appear in neurodevelopmental/ASD literature, supporting a hypothesized biological relationship. A small number of human probands with TUBB2A variants may have documented autistic features, which would justify some weight for "Existing," but the evidence is sparse and not definitive. Established status is very unlikely given the absence of replicated ASD-specific genetic evidence.

FOXP2 is definitively established as causal for childhood apraxia of speech/developmental verbal dyspraxia (KE family, 7q31 deletions, point mutations), but its role in autism specifically is much weaker. Human candidate-gene association studies have reported associations of FOXP2 variants with autism or with language/communication phenotypes within ASD cohorts (e.g., Chinese Han samples, some family-based studies), while several other studies (e.g., Newbury et al., Wassink et al.) failed to replicate; rare 7q31 deletions and occasional de novo/rare FOXP2 variants have been observed in ASD probands, and SFARI lists FOXP2 with only suggestive-level evidence. Strong supporting biology exists—FOXP2 transcriptionally regulates CNTNAP2 and other neurodevelopmental targets, and mouse Foxp2 mutants show altered vocalization and social behavior—which supports at least a hypothesized mechanism. Because the human genetic evidence is credible but inconsistent and not replicated at a causal level, "Existing" is the best fit, with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized" (much of the support being functional/animal or via the related paralog FOXP1) and only a small probability of "Established."

SPEN (SHARP/MINT) harbors de novo loss-of-function and truncating variants identified in large-scale autism and neurodevelopmental sequencing cohorts (e.g., Iossifov, De Rubeis, Satterstrom/ASC exome studies), and it is listed as a high-confidence ASD risk gene in SFARI Gene. Independently, Radio, Tartaglia and colleagues (2021, AJHG) delineated a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by heterozygous SPEN haploinsufficiency (Radio–Tartaglia syndrome) in a large multi-center cohort, in which autism spectrum disorder/autistic features were a recurrent phenotype across unrelated probands. These are human genetic data from multiple independent studies with de novo occurrence and statistical enrichment, supporting a causal role, so "Established" carries most weight. Some residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because ASD is one feature of a broader syndromic presentation rather than an isolated, fully replicated ASD-only association, and gene-level statistical significance in ASD-specific cohorts has been borderline in some analyses. Minimal weight goes to Hypothesized/Novel given the strong human variant-level evidence.

QRICH1 de novo loss-of-function variants cause Ververi-Brady syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech delay, mild dysmorphism, and in a substantial subset, autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis; several independent probands have been described in DDD, exome cohorts, and dedicated case series. QRICH1 has also appeared among genes with de novo variants in large autism/NDD sequencing studies and is catalogued in ASD gene databases, supporting a human genetic link. However, the core phenotype is syndromic developmental delay rather than isolated/idiopathic ASD, and autism is reported as a variable associated feature, so evidence for ASD specifically is credible but not definitive. This places most weight on "Existing," with some probability on "Established" given repeated human observations, and residual weight on purely biological/hypothesized support.

ZMYM2 (ZNF198) encodes a transcriptional corepressor within the LSD1/CoREST complex, and de novo loss-of-function variants have been reported in humans causing a syndromic disorder with congenital anomalies of the kidney/urinary tract accompanied by developmental delay, intellectual disability, and in some probands autistic features (Connaughton et al., AJHG 2020), plus sporadic occurrences in large developmental-disorder and neurodevelopmental exome cohorts. This supports at least "Existing" evidence — a human gene–variant link to a neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly associated with ASD — but ZMYM2 is not a well-replicated, high-confidence autism risk gene in the major ASD sequencing consortia analyses, so "Established" is unlikely. Substantial weight also goes to "Hypothesized," since much of the mechanistic support comes from chromatin-regulatory biology (LSD1/CoREST, ZMYM family paralogs such as the X-linked ZMYM3 implicated in ID/ASD) and model-system data rather than ASD-specific human genetic association. A small residual probability remains that documented associations are incidental to ASD specifically rather than to general neurodevelopmental impairment.

RFX7 belongs to the regulatory factor X family of transcription factors, several members of which (RFX3, RFX4, RFX7) have been directly implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders. A multi-center human cohort study (Harris et al., Genetics in Medicine 2021) described individuals with de novo/rare loss-of-function variants in RFX3, RFX4 and RFX7 presenting with autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability and ADHD, providing patient-level genetic evidence. RFX7 has also appeared among candidate/high-confidence ASD risk genes in large-scale exome sequencing meta-analyses and is curated in ASD gene databases, supporting replication beyond a single report. However, the number of independent RFX7-specific probands is smaller than for RFX3, and functional validation is limited, so the evidence sits between "Existing" and "Established" rather than being unequivocally causal. Purely biological/pathway arguments (ciliary and neuronal transcriptional regulation) would only support "Hypothesized," which is why a small share of probability remains there.

ANK2 (ankyrin-B) is one of the high-confidence autism risk genes identified through large-scale human exome sequencing studies of simplex and multiplex ASD cohorts (e.g., Sanders et al., Iossifov et al., De Rubeis et al., and Satterstrom et al. 2020), where recurrent de novo loss-of-function variants reached exome-wide significance and it is classified as SFARI category 1. Independent replication across multiple cohorts and consortia supports a causal contribution of rare damaging ANK2 variants to ASD, often with associated developmental delay. Supporting mouse models with Ank2 giant-isoform disruption show axon branching abnormalities and autism-like behaviors, reinforcing biological plausibility, though the human genetic data alone are sufficient. Residual probability is assigned to "Existing" because ANK2 variants are incompletely penetrant, phenotypically variable, and part of a polygenic/neurodevelopmental spectrum rather than a classic Mendelian ASD syndrome.

SPTBN1 (β-II spectrin) has been established as a neurodevelopmental disorder gene through Cousin et al. (2021, Nature Genetics), which reported de novo and inherited pathogenic variants in ~29 unrelated individuals with developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and a substantial proportion with autism spectrum disorder or autistic features. Additional support comes from large-scale exome sequencing of autism/developmental disorder cohorts (e.g., ASC/SPARK and DDD analyses), where SPTBN1 emerges among genes enriched for de novo damaging variants, and it is curated in SFARI Gene. These are human proband-based studies in independent families, supporting an Established causal role, although ASD is one component of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated autism, which tempers certainty somewhat toward "Existing." Supporting mechanistic work (axonal cytoskeleton, neuronal morphology, mouse and in vitro models) reinforces biological plausibility but is not the primary evidence. Very little probability remains for "Novel."

NSD1 haploinsufficiency (point mutations and 5q35 microdeletions) causes Sotos syndrome, a well-characterized human overgrowth–intellectual disability disorder in which autism spectrum features are frequently reported; multiple independent cohort studies (e.g., behavioral phenotyping of Sotos patients by Lane, Tatton-Brown and colleagues) document high rates of ASD diagnoses, supporting a syndromic causal link. In addition, de novo loss-of-function NSD1 variants have been identified in probands from large ASD/neurodevelopmental exome sequencing studies, and NSD1 is curated as a syndromic ASD gene in SFARI Gene. Evidence is therefore human-based and replicated, though ASD is part of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than isolated autism, which leaves some ambiguity between "Established" and "Existing." Supporting chromatin-regulatory biology (H3K36 methyltransferase affecting neurodevelopmental gene networks) and mouse models provide mechanistic plausibility but are not the primary evidence. Essentially no basis for considering this relationship novel.

SETD1A is a well-established human neurodevelopmental gene: de novo loss-of-function variants are robustly linked to schizophrenia (Singh et al., SCHEMA) and to a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, speech delay, epilepsy, and prominent autistic features (Kummeling et al., 2021, multiple unrelated probands). It is catalogued in SFARI Gene and has appeared among candidate/risk genes in large autism exome sequencing studies (Autism Sequencing Consortium/Fu et al.), with de novo LoF variants reported in ASD probands. However, ASD is often part of a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than an isolated, definitively replicated SETD1A-specific outcome, so evidence sits between "existing" and "established." Supporting mouse and neuronal models (Setd1a haploinsufficiency causing synaptic and cognitive deficits) reinforce biological plausibility but are non-human and thus only support the hypothesized tier. Overall, human variant-level evidence exists and is fairly strong, making "Existing" most probable with meaningful weight on "Established."

KCNB1 (Kv2.1) de novo variants are firmly established as a cause of developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE26) and intellectual disability in humans, and multiple published patient cohorts (e.g., de Kovel et al., Bar et al., Marchese/ Bar-Yosef series) describe autism or prominent autistic features in a substantial fraction of affected individuals, indicating credible human genetic evidence linking the gene to ASD phenotypes. KCNB1 is also curated in SFARI Gene, and rare de novo variants have appeared in neurodevelopmental/ASD sequencing cohorts. However, ASD in these patients is generally part of a broader encephalopathy phenotype rather than isolated, non-syndromic autism, and dedicated replication in independent ASD-specific cohorts is limited, so the evidence falls short of "Established" for ASD per se. Strong supporting biology (Kv2.1 role in neuronal excitability, synaptic/somatic clustering, and mouse models with behavioral abnormalities) additionally supports a hypothesized mechanistic link. Hence the bulk of probability sits on "Existing," with meaningful weight on "Established" and "Hypothesized."

PACS1 is best known for the recurrent de novo missense variant p.Arg203Trp causing Schuurs-Hoeijmakers syndrome (PACS1 neurodevelopmental disorder), first described in 2012 and replicated in many independent probands worldwide, including a large multicenter cohort of ~180 individuals. Autism spectrum disorder or autistic features are reported in a substantial fraction (roughly 40–60%) of these patients, providing human genetic evidence for a causal contribution to an ASD phenotype within a syndromic context. PACS1 is also curated in autism gene databases (e.g., SFARI) and has appeared in de novo variant analyses of neurodevelopmental/ASD cohorts, and zebrafish/neuronal models support a functional role in neurodevelopment. The main uncertainty is whether the evidence establishes PACS1 as an "autism gene" per se versus a syndromic ID gene in which ASD is a frequent comorbid feature, so points are split mainly between Established and Existing.

PRR12 is a chromatin-associated nuclear protein in which de novo loss-of-function variants and translocations have been reported in humans with a neuro-ocular syndrome comprising intellectual disability, ocular anomalies, and neuropsychiatric features, with autism or autistic traits described in a subset of probands (e.g., Leduc et al. 2018; Chowdhury et al. 2021). PRR12 has also emerged as a candidate in large-scale de novo variant studies of neurodevelopmental disorders/ASD and is catalogued in autism gene databases such as SFARI. However, ASD is typically a variable accompanying feature of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than a replicated, specifically established ASD-causing association, and case numbers remain modest. This supports strong "Existing" evidence in humans with a reasonable but lesser chance the field would consider it "Established." Purely biological/animal-model-only support would be insufficient here, so few points go to Hypothesized and almost none to Novel.

NR2F1 (COUP-TFI) heterozygous loss-of-function and missense variants cause Bosch-Boonstra-Schaaf optic atrophy syndrome (BBSOAS), a human neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism spectrum disorder or autistic features are reported in a substantial minority (roughly 30–50%) of probands across multiple independent cohorts and case series (Bosch et al., Chen et al., Rech et al.). NR2F1 is also curated in ASD gene databases (e.g., SFARI) as a syndromic ASD gene, and de novo variants have been noted in neurodevelopmental/ASD sequencing cohorts. This constitutes credible, replicated human genetic evidence that NR2F1 variants contribute to ASD, though mostly as one feature of a broader syndrome rather than isolated idiopathic autism, which tempers a fully "Established" designation. Supporting mouse and cortical patterning/neurogenesis data provide mechanistic plausibility but are secondary to the human evidence. Hence most weight goes to Existing, with meaningful probability on Established.

GRIA2 encodes the AMPA receptor GluA2 subunit, a core component of excitatory synaptic transmission, making it highly plausible biologically for ASD. Human genetic evidence exists: Salpietro et al. (2019, Nat Commun) reported ~28 unrelated patients with de novo GRIA2 variants presenting with intellectual disability, developmental delay, epilepsy, and autism spectrum disorder or autistic features, with functional validation of receptor dysfunction. Additional de novo variants have appeared in large ASD/NDD sequencing cohorts, and GRIA2 is curated as a candidate ASD gene in SFARI. However, ASD in these patients is typically part of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated ASD, and GRIA2 has not clearly reached exome-wide significance in dedicated ASD cohorts, so the evidence is credible and replicated but arguably not definitive for ASD specifically. This places most weight between "Existing" and "Established," with only residual probability on purely biological/hypothesized status.

VEZF1 (ZNF161) is a zinc-finger transcription factor best characterized in vascular/endothelial development, angiogenesis, and as a chromatin insulator/boundary-associated factor; it is not a recognized autism risk gene and does not appear among high-confidence SFARI/ASD sequencing consortium genes. Its role as a DNA-binding transcriptional regulator makes it biologically plausible that disruption could affect neurodevelopment, and rare de novo or CNV events at 17q22 could have been incidentally reported in large ASD exome/CNV screens, which supports some weight for "Hypothesized" and a smaller amount for "Existing." However, I am not aware of any replicated human genetic study, case series, or association analysis implicating VEZF1 variants in ASD, so "Established" is very unlikely. The bulk of probability therefore falls on "Novel," with meaningful residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the gene's transcription-regulatory biology and possible expression in the developing brain.

TRIO encodes a RhoGEF regulating RAC1 signaling, actin dynamics, and synaptic development, and recurrent de novo variants have been identified in humans with neurodevelopmental disorders (MRD44/MRD63) that frequently include autistic features. TRIO was among the 102 high-confidence ASD risk genes reported in large-scale exome sequencing meta-analyses (e.g., Satterstrom et al. 2020), with multiple independent de novo damaging variants in ASD probands, and it carries a high-confidence SFARI gene score. Additional human cohort studies and case series (Pengelly et al., Barbosa et al., Ba et al.) report ASD/ID phenotypes with functionally validated GEF-domain variants. Some uncertainty remains because the core phenotype is often intellectual disability/developmental delay with variable autism, so a portion of probability is retained for "Existing." Animal and in vitro work supports the mechanism but is not the primary basis for the human genetic evidence.

WDR26 haploinsufficiency (de novo loss-of-function variants and 1q41q42 microdeletions) causes Skraban-Deardorff syndrome, a human neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, seizures, speech delay and distinctive facies; several reported probands display autistic features or a formal autism diagnosis, and WDR26 has appeared among de novo variant genes in large neurodevelopmental/ASD sequencing cohorts. This provides credible human genetic evidence linking WDR26 variation to a phenotype strongly overlapping with and encompassing ASD, favoring "Existing." However, ASD is not the defining or consistently replicated phenotype—autism appears as a variable comorbid feature within a broader syndromic ID picture—so "Established" for ASD specifically is less supported. Some weight remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the mechanistic support (CTLH E3 ligase complex, neuronal development, mouse/functional models) is non-human, and minimal weight for "Novel" given the clear human clinical genetic data.

SETD1B encodes a COMPASS-family H3K4 methyltransferase, and de novo loss-of-function/missense variants have been repeatedly reported in humans with a neurodevelopmental syndrome comprising intellectual disability, myoclonic absence epilepsy, language delay, and autistic features (e.g., Hiraide et al., Krzyzewska et al., Roston et al., and the larger Weerts et al. cohort delineating the SETD1B-related syndrome, in which a substantial proportion of patients meet ASD criteria). SETD1B is also curated in SFARI Gene and has appeared in large-scale de novo variant analyses of NDD/ASD cohorts, and a specific DNA methylation episignature supports pathogenicity of its variants. The main uncertainty is whether ASD is a core causal outcome versus a frequent comorbid feature of a broader syndromic NDD phenotype, which keeps meaningful weight on "Existing" alongside "Established." Purely biological/animal-model-only evidence is not the primary basis here, so "Hypothesized" receives limited weight and "Novel" is essentially excluded.

GRIN2A encodes the GluN2A NMDA receptor subunit and is definitively established as a cause of epilepsy-aphasia spectrum disorders (Landau-Kleffner, CSWS, rolandic epilepsy) and developmental/epileptic encephalopathy with intellectual disability and speech impairment—phenotypes frequently accompanied by autistic features. In human ASD cohorts, rare de novo and inherited GRIN2A variants have been reported in exome-sequencing and CNV studies, and the gene is curated in ASD gene databases (e.g., SFARI), supporting a credible human genetic contribution. However, ASD is generally a variable, secondary feature of GRIN2A-related neurodevelopmental disorder rather than a replicated, gene-specific primary phenotype, so the evidence falls short of the "Established" bar for autism per se. Supporting mechanistic data (glutamatergic synaptic dysfunction, mouse Grin2a models with social/communication deficits) reinforce plausibility but are non-human and thus contribute to the hypothesized weight. On balance, "Existing" best captures the current human evidence, with meaningful residual probability for "Established."

CSNK1E encodes casein kinase 1 epsilon, a core circadian clock regulator, and the "clock genes/social timing" hypothesis of autism has motivated candidate-gene studies (e.g., Nicholas et al. 2007 and subsequent Asian cohort studies) that genotyped panels of circadian genes including CSNK1E, PER1, PER2, NPAS2 and TIMELESS in ASD probands; in those studies the strongest signals were generally for PER1/NPAS2, with CSNK1E showing weak or inconsistent findings, so any human genetic support is limited and unreplicated. CSNK1E is also plausibly linked to ASD biology through sleep disturbance (a very common ASD comorbidity), Wnt/β-catenin and DVL phosphorylation signaling, and dopaminergic/behavioral phenotypes in Csnk1e mutant mice—supporting a "Hypothesized" designation. It is not a recognized SFARI high-confidence ASD gene, and no recurrent de novo or rare damaging variants have established causation, so "Established" is very unlikely. The distribution therefore favors Hypothesized, with meaningful weight on Existing given the human candidate-gene/circadian association literature and some weight on Novel because CSNK1E-specific human associations may be entirely null.

FBXW11 encodes β-TrCP2, an F-box component of SCF ubiquitin ligase complexes regulating Wnt/β-catenin, Hedgehog and NF-κB signaling, pathways repeatedly implicated in neurodevelopment. De novo missense and loss-of-function FBXW11 variants have been reported in humans with a neurodevelopmental syndrome featuring developmental delay, brain, eye and digit anomalies, with several probands showing autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis (e.g., Holt et al., 2019), and the gene appears in large-scale exome studies of ASD/DD cohorts and in SFARI gene curation. However, ASD is not the core or consistently replicated phenotype, and most affected individuals present with broader syndromic neurodevelopmental disease, so causal evidence specific to ASD remains limited rather than definitive. This supports "Existing" as most likely, with some probability for "Established" given the accumulating de novo human data, and residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the ASD link rests mainly on pathway biology and model systems.

ATAT1 encodes the major alpha-tubulin acetyltransferase, and microtubule acetylation is a well-studied mechanism in neuronal migration, axonal transport, dendritic spine formation, and cilia function—processes broadly implicated in autism pathophysiology; Atat1 knockout mice show altered neuronal morphogenesis and behavioral phenotypes, and the ATAT1/HDAC6 acetylation balance has been discussed in neurodevelopmental disease models. However, I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies identifying ATAT1 variants as causal or significantly associated with ASD, and ATAT1 is not among the well-recognized ASD risk genes (e.g., SFARI high-confidence categories). At most, isolated de novo or rare variants might appear incidentally in large exome/genome sequencing datasets without statistical support, which would only weakly support the "Existing" category. Because the supporting evidence is largely mechanistic and animal/in vitro based, the bulk of probability belongs to "Hypothesized," with a substantial residual possibility that the pairing is essentially unstudied ("Novel").

ZNF865 (19q13.42) has been reported in human genetics as a novel neurodevelopmental disease gene: a multi-center cohort described de novo/rare deleterious variants in a small number of probands presenting with global developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, seizures, and, in several individuals, autistic features or a formal autism diagnosis. This supports at least "Existing" evidence, since ASD appears as part of a syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than as an independently replicated isolated ASD association. The gene's proposed role in cell-cycle progression and DNA damage response provides plausible biological relevance to neurodevelopment, which also supports a "Hypothesized" contribution. Evidence falls short of "Established" for ASD specifically because ASD is a variable secondary feature in a small case series, without large-scale ASD cohort replication (e.g., it is not a high-confidence SFARI/ASC exome gene). "Novel" retains a small weight in case my recollection of the ASD phenotypic overlap is overstated.

YWHAG (14-3-3 gamma) is a well-documented human disease gene: recurrent de novo missense variants cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy 56 (DEE56), and published patient cohorts describe intellectual disability with autistic features/ASD diagnoses in a subset of individuals, which supports at least "Existing" evidence for a link to autism as part of a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype. YWHAG also lies at 7q11.23, a region whose duplications are strongly associated with ASD, and the gene appears in autism candidate gene resources (e.g., SFARI) largely on the basis of rare de novo variants in NDD/ASD exome cohorts. However, evidence that YWHAG variants specifically and causally produce isolated ASD—rather than ASD as a secondary feature of epileptic encephalopathy/ID—is not replicated at the level required for "Established." Strong biological plausibility (14-3-3 scaffolding of synaptic and signaling proteins, mouse knockdown/knockout showing neuronal migration and behavioral deficits) supports substantial weight on "Hypothesized." Very little probability is given to "Novel," since co-mentions are far from incidental.

TCF7L2 encodes a key Wnt/β-catenin pathway transcription factor, a pathway repeatedly implicated in autism and neurodevelopment, providing a strong biological rationale. Beyond biology, there is human genetic evidence: de novo and rare loss-of-function TCF7L2 variants have been reported in cohorts with syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder featuring developmental delay, intellectual disability, ADHD and autistic features (e.g., multi-individual case series describing TCF7L2 haploinsufficiency), and the gene appears in autism gene curation resources such as SFARI. However, most reports describe ASD as one component of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated autism, and independent replication specifically for ASD is still relatively limited, so the evidence sits between "existing" and "established." Supportive mouse and expression data (thalamic/neuronal development) reinforce plausibility but would only count toward "hypothesized." Novel is essentially excluded given documented human variant data.

CREBBP haploinsufficiency causes Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome type 1, a human neurodevelopmental disorder in which autistic features/ASD diagnoses are frequently reported, and the Menke–Hennekam variants (exons 30–31) are also associated with autistic behavior. De novo damaging CREBBP variants have additionally been reported in large exome-sequencing cohorts of autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, and the gene is curated in SFARI Gene as a syndromic/high-confidence ASD candidate. This human genetic evidence in independent probands supports an Established or at least strongly Existing classification, with the main caveat being that ASD occurs as part of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than isolated autism, and CREBBP did not reach exome-wide significance in some ASD-specific gene lists. Supporting mouse and chromatin/CBP-histone-acetylation pathway data provide mechanistic plausibility, but the primary evidence is human, so few points go to Hypothesized and essentially none to Novel.

SKI is best known in human genetics as the gene for Shprintzen–Goldberg syndrome (gain-of-function missense variants), a connective tissue disorder that frequently includes developmental delay and intellectual disability, with occasional reports of autistic features/behavioral abnormalities; it also lies within the 1p36 deletion critical region, a CNV strongly associated with ID and ASD-like phenotypes. These links provide plausible but indirect, non-specific human evidence rather than replicated demonstration that SKI variants cause idiopathic ASD. SKI is not an established or high-confidence ASD gene in large de novo/exome sequencing studies, and it is not a strongly scored SFARI gene. Biologically, SKI represses TGF-β/SMAD signaling and is expressed in the developing brain with roles in neural development, supporting a hypothesized mechanistic relevance. Therefore most weight falls on Hypothesized, with meaningful probability for Existing (via syndromic/contiguous-gene human phenotypes) and little support for Established.

NSD2 (WHSC1/MMSET) lies in the Wolf–Hirschhorn critical region, and haploinsufficiency due to de novo truncating/missense variants causes Rauch–Steindl syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autistic features/ASD diagnoses are reported in a subset of patients across multiple independent case series. De novo loss-of-function NSD2 variants have also been recovered in large autism/developmental-disorder exome sequencing cohorts (Simons Simplex/ASC/DDD-type studies), and NSD2 is catalogued as an autism candidate gene in SFARI. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence linking NSD2 variation to ASD, though ASD is typically one feature of a broader syndromic NDD rather than the definitive replicated primary phenotype, so "Existing" is favored over "Established." Chromatin-modifier biology (H3K36 methyltransferase, convergent with other ASD chromatin genes) provides additional mechanistic support, but human variant data make purely hypothesized status unlikely. Novel is essentially excluded.

NBEA (neurobeachin) has been an autism candidate since Castermans et al. (2003) reported a de novo balanced translocation disrupting the gene in a patient with autism, followed by additional cytogenetic disruptions and rare deletions/variants in ASD cohorts. Subsequent large-scale exome studies (e.g., Mulhern et al. 2018 and de novo variant analyses in NDD/ASD trios) identified de novo loss-of-function variants in patients with developmental delay, epilepsy, and autistic features, and NBEA is listed as a high-confidence gene in curated ASD databases such as SFARI. However, much of the human evidence links NBEA primarily to a broader neurodevelopmental/epilepsy phenotype in which autism is a frequent but not obligate feature, so a strictly ASD-specific causal claim is somewhat less definitive. Strong supporting biology (synaptic receptor trafficking, Nbea knockout mouse synaptic transmission deficits) reinforces plausibility but is animal/in vitro. Therefore the weight sits between "Existing" and "Established," with little probability for Hypothesized or Novel.

EEF1A2 is a well-recognized human disease gene in which de novo missense variants (e.g., G70S, E122K, D252H) cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE33) and intellectual disability, and autism or prominent autistic features are frequently described in these probands. EEF1A2 has also been reported as a de novo variant target in large autism exome-sequencing cohorts (e.g., Simons/ASC studies) and is catalogued in SFARI Gene, supporting human genetic evidence beyond mere biological plausibility. However, autism in most reported cases occurs in the context of a broader neurodevelopmental/epileptic syndrome rather than as isolated, replicated non-syndromic ASD, so the causal link specific to ASD is credible but not definitively established. Supporting rodent (wasted mouse) and functional translation-elongation data add mechanistic plausibility but are non-human and thus only reinforce the Hypothesized tier. Consequently, most weight falls on Existing, with substantial residual probability for Established.

ARF3 (ADP-ribosylation factor 3) has been implicated in human neurodevelopmental disease: de novo missense variants (e.g., Sakamoto et al., 2022, and subsequent case reports) cause a syndrome with developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy and brain malformations, and some reported probands display autistic features, placing it within the broad NDD/ASD-associated gene space rather than as a specific, replicated ASD gene. ARF3 is highly expressed in brain and functions in Golgi/vesicular trafficking and neurite outgrowth, a pathway shared with several established ASD genes, and supporting zebrafish/in vitro functional work exists—this underpins a substantial "Hypothesized" weight. However, I am not aware of large ASD cohort studies (e.g., ASC/SPARK exome analyses) identifying ARF3 as an exome-wide significant ASD risk gene with independent replication, so "Established" is unlikely. The most probable classification is "Existing" (human variants linked to an NDD phenotype strongly overlapping ASD), with meaningful residual probability on "Hypothesized" if the ASD-specific human evidence is judged too indirect.

TNRC6B (a GW182-family gene central to miRNA-mediated silencing) has recurrent de novo loss-of-function/truncating variants identified in large human autism and neurodevelopmental sequencing cohorts (e.g., Autism Sequencing Consortium/Satterstrom et al. exome analyses, where it reached exome-wide significance among ASD risk genes), and it is curated as a high-confidence ASD gene by SFARI. A dedicated clinical case series (Granadillo et al., 2020) described ~17 unrelated individuals with de novo TNRC6B variants presenting with developmental delay, intellectual disability, ADHD, and autistic features, providing independent proband-level replication in humans. This combination of statistical enrichment of de novo variants in ASD cohorts plus a multi-proband clinical phenotype series supports an Established causal role, though some may argue the core phenotype is a broader NDD with variable autism penetrance, which keeps meaningful weight on Existing. Purely biological/animal-model support (miRNA pathway relevance) is secondary given the direct human genetic data, so Hypothesized and Novel receive little weight.

KCNMA1 (BK potassium channel) has a well-known human report by Laumonnier et al. (2006) describing a de novo translocation disrupting the gene in a child with autism plus a rare hemizygous variant with reduced channel function in another ASD case, and subsequent rare variant/CNV findings have been reported in ASD and neurodevelopmental cohorts. KCNMA1 channelopathy series (paroxysmal dyskinesia, epilepsy, developmental delay) include patients with autistic features, supporting association with a phenotype spectrum overlapping ASD. However, replication in large ASD sequencing studies is weak and the gene has not reached definitive/established causal status (SFARI lists it at a suggestive/limited evidence level rather than high confidence). Strong supporting biology (BK channel role in neuronal excitability, Fmr1/FXS-related BK dysfunction, and mouse models with social/behavioral deficits) underpins a hypothesized mechanism, so some weight remains there. Established is unlikely given the small number of independent probands and lack of robust replication.

MSL2 encodes the E3 ligase subunit of the MSL histone acetyltransferase complex, whose other members (KAT8, MSL3) are well-established neurodevelopmental disorder genes (e.g., MSL3-related Basilicata-Akhtar syndrome features autistic behavior), providing strong biological plausibility. Beyond pathway inference, human genetic evidence exists: heterozygous de novo MSL2 variants have been reported in cohorts with developmental delay/intellectual disability, epilepsy, dysmorphism and a distinct DNA methylation episignature, with autistic features described in a subset of probands, and MSL2 appears among candidate genes from large exome sequencing studies of autism/NDD. However, the reported phenotype is a broad neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than autism specifically, and replication across independent autism-focused cohorts is limited, so the evidence falls short of "Established" for ASD as the primary phenotype. Therefore most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful residual probability on "Hypothesized" if one judges the human data to be primarily about syndromic NDD rather than ASD.

BRD4 is best established in humans as a cause of a Cornelia de Lange–like neurodevelopmental syndrome (Olley et al., de novo/deleted BRD4 variants disrupting the NIPBL–BRD4 interaction), a phenotype that includes intellectual disability and autistic features, which supports at least "Existing" evidence for a link to ASD-related neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Additional support comes from BRD4 appearing occasionally in de novo variant lists from large developmental disorder/ASD sequencing cohorts, though it is not a replicated, high-confidence ASD gene comparable to CHD8 or SCN2A. Much of the ASD-specific evidence is biological/animal-based: pharmacological BET inhibition (JQ1) in mice produces autism-like social and repetitive behaviors, and BRD4 regulates neuronal transcriptional programs and chromatin, which justifies substantial weight on "Hypothesized." Because direct, replicated human genetic evidence for BRD4 variants causing idiopathic ASD is lacking, "Established" receives little weight, and "Novel" is essentially excluded given the clear mechanistic and syndromic links.

FOXG1 is a well-established disease gene in humans: loss-of-function point mutations and 14q12 deletions cause the congenital variant of Rett syndrome (FOXG1 syndrome), and 14q12 duplications encompassing FOXG1 have been reported in patients with developmental delay, epilepsy, and autistic features—Rett-like phenotypes being widely recognized as ASD-related conditions, and FOXG1 is catalogued as a syndromic ASD gene in SFARI Gene. However, most FOXG1 patients present with severe encephalopathy and intellectual disability where autistic behaviors are a secondary feature, and FOXG1 is not a recurrently implicated gene in large idiopathic ASD sequencing cohorts, so causality for ASD per se is supportive rather than definitive. Additional human mechanistic evidence comes from iPSC-derived organoids from individuals with idiopathic ASD showing FOXG1 overexpression driving GABAergic imbalance, which supports biological relevance but does not involve FOXG1 variants. This mix justifies most weight on "Existing," with meaningful shares to "Established" (syndromic ASD gene with replicated human cases) and "Hypothesized" (expression/functional and mouse-model data).

HIVEP2 (Schnurri-2/MIBP1) de novo truncating and missense variants have been reported in multiple unrelated human probands with intellectual disability and developmental delay (MRD43, OMIM 616977; Srivastava et al. 2016, Steinfeld et al. 2016), and a substantial fraction of these patients display autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis. HIVEP2 has also been flagged as a candidate risk gene in autism/developmental disorder exome-sequencing cohorts and is curated on the SFARI gene list, supporting more than a purely hypothetical link. However, the core, replicated human phenotype is ID/DD with variable autistic behavior rather than isolated ASD, so causality specifically for ASD is suggestive but not definitively established. Supporting biology (Shn2 knockout mice with abnormal social behavior, immature dentate gyrus, NF-κB pathway involvement) is animal-based and reinforces plausibility but cannot itself elevate the category. Accordingly, most weight falls on "Existing," with meaningful probability for "Established" and residual weight for "Hypothesized."

ZMYND8 (PRKCBP1/RACK7) is a chromatin reader involved in transcriptional regulation and DNA damage response, a functional class heavily enriched among autism risk genes. De novo and rare heterozygous ZMYND8 variants have been reported in human neurodevelopmental cohorts (exome/trio sequencing of ASD, DD/ID, and DDD-type series), and a case series describing a ZMYND8-related neurodevelopmental phenotype with developmental delay, intellectual disability, autistic features and occasional congenital anomalies has been published; the gene is also catalogued in SFARI Gene. This human genetic evidence supports at least "Existing," with some probability of "Established" given multiple independent probands, though replication specifically for ASD (rather than broader NDD) is still relatively limited and statistical exome-wide significance for autism is not firmly established. Supporting mouse/cellular data on Zmynd8 in neuronal chromatin regulation strengthens biological plausibility, so some weight remains on "Hypothesized," while "Novel" is very unlikely.

PTPRS encodes a presynaptic receptor-type tyrosine phosphatase that acts as a synaptic organizer, binding trans-synaptic partners (Slitrks, TrkC, NGL-3, IL1RAP-family proteins) that are themselves implicated in neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders; PTPRS-null mice show altered synapse development and behavioral abnormalities, giving strong biological plausibility (Hypothesized). Human genetic evidence is comparatively sparse: PTPRS has been noted as a candidate in copy-number variant regions (19p13.3) and occasional rare/de novo variants in autism and neurodevelopmental exome cohorts, but replication in independent probands is limited and it is not a high-confidence ASD gene (unlike its paralog PTPRD, which has clearer association data). Therefore an "Existing" level of limited human evidence is plausible but not certain, and "Established" is very unlikely. A modest probability remains that all connections are purely mechanistic/animal-based, which would place it in Hypothesized, or that co-mentions are incidental (Novel).

ZBTB34 encodes a poorly characterized BTB/POZ zinc-finger transcriptional regulator, and unlike related family members (ZBTB18, ZBTB20, ZBTB16) it is not a recognized neurodevelopmental disease gene and does not appear among the high-confidence ASD risk genes from large exome sequencing consortia (e.g., Satterstrom/ASC, SPARK) or as a scored SFARI gene to my knowledge. At most, it may appear incidentally as a single de novo or rare variant in variant databases (denovo-db) or in large candidate lists from ASD cohorts, which would constitute only weak, non-replicated human evidence. Its general biology as a transcription factor expressed in brain provides a plausible but generic mechanistic rationale, supporting a modest probability for "Hypothesized." There is no evidence of replicated, causal human variants, so "Established" is very unlikely, and the most probable classification is "Novel" with some chance of a single limited human report.

PBX1 is a TALE-class homeobox transcription factor whose de novo loss-of-function and missense variants cause CAKUTHED syndrome (congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract with hearing loss, external ear abnormalities, and developmental delay), a phenotype that frequently includes intellectual disability and, in some reported patients, autistic features; 1q23.3 deletions encompassing PBX1 have also been described with neurodevelopmental impairment. PBX1 appears on autism candidate gene lists (e.g., SFARI) largely on the basis of rare de novo variants observed in developmental-disorder/ASD sequencing cohorts, which supports "Existing" rather than "Established" evidence, since replication specifically for ASD as the primary phenotype is limited. Biologically, PBX1 partners with MEIS/HOX and PAX proteins in neural patterning, midbrain dopaminergic neuron development, and cortical neurogenesis, giving a plausible mechanistic basis that supports at least "Hypothesized." Because much of the strongest mechanistic support comes from mouse models and the human variant data are dominated by syndromic renal/DD phenotypes rather than idiopathic autism, the probability mass is split mainly between Existing and Hypothesized. Established is unlikely given the absence of multiple independent ASD-focused replications, and Novel is improbable given the clear neurodevelopmental involvement.

GABRB3 lies within the 15q11-q13 region whose maternal duplication is one of the best-known cytogenetic causes of autism, and numerous human association/linkage studies (e.g., Cook et al., Buxbaum et al., Menold et al., Delahanty et al. with the P11S variant) have reported associations of GABRB3 markers or rare variants with ASD, though replication has been inconsistent. Rare de novo and inherited GABRB3 variants have also been reported in ASD sequencing cohorts, and GABRB3 is a recognized SFARI autism candidate gene, while clearly pathogenic GABRB3 variants more definitively cause epileptic encephalopathies with frequent comorbid autistic features. Supporting biology (GABA-A receptor subunit expression in brain, Gabrb3 knockout mice showing autism-like behaviors) reinforces plausibility but is animal/in vitro and thus counts toward Hypothesized. Because the human genetic evidence is credible and repeated but not consistently replicated at genome-wide significance for ASD specifically, "Existing" is most appropriate, with meaningful weight on "Established" given the 15q11-13 duplication and epileptic-encephalopathy-with-ASD literature.

De novo heterozygous loss-of-function variants and deletions in USP7 cause Hao-Fountain syndrome (MIM 616863), a neurodevelopmental disorder delineated in multiple independent human cohorts (Hao et al. 2015; Fountain et al. 2019 and subsequent expanded series), in which autism spectrum disorder or prominent autistic features are reported in a substantial fraction of probands. USP7 also regulates MAGEL2, a gene implicated in Schaaf-Yang syndrome and Prader-Willi-related autism phenotypes, providing a mechanistic link. USP7 is curated in SFARI Gene as a high-confidence ASD-associated gene, and multiple large-scale de novo variant/sequencing studies in ASD and NDD cohorts have implicated it. The main caveat is that ASD is one feature within a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental presentation rather than isolated autism, which leaves some probability on "Existing." Little weight belongs to Hypothesized or Novel given the replicated human genetic evidence.

CNOT1 encodes the scaffold subunit of the human CCR4-NOT complex, and de novo loss-of-function/missense variants have been reported in cohorts of patients with neurodevelopmental disorder (Vissers et al., AJHG 2020, ~39 individuals; "Vissers-Bodmer syndrome"), where autism/autistic features were described in a subset alongside developmental delay, intellectual disability and holoprosencephaly. CNOT1 has also appeared as a candidate/risk gene in large autism exome sequencing efforts and is catalogued in SFARI Gene, supporting human genetic evidence. However, ASD is a variable, secondary feature of a broader syndromic NDD rather than a replicated, well-delineated autism phenotype, so the association falls short of "Established" for ASD specifically. Supporting biology (translational/mRNA-decay regulation, overlap with other CCR4-NOT subunits such as CNOT3 implicated in ASD) reinforces plausibility, giving some weight to Hypothesized, while Novel is very unlikely.

SOX11 is an established human disease gene: de novo loss-of-function and missense variants cause a Coffin-Siris–like neurodevelopmental disorder (Tsurusaki et al. 2014; Hempel et al. 2016; Al-Jawahiri et al. 2019), and autistic features/ASD diagnoses have been reported in a subset of these probands. It has also appeared in large-scale de novo variant analyses of neurodevelopmental disorders (DDD, ASD/DD sequencing cohorts) and is downstream of the BAF/SWI-SNF complex, a pathway strongly implicated in autism, supporting biological plausibility. However, the evidence base is dominated by syndromic ID/DD with ASD as a variable comorbid feature rather than replicated ASD-specific association studies, so the relationship falls short of "Established" for ASD per se. Mouse and neurogenesis expression data add mechanistic support but would only justify "Hypothesized" on their own. Therefore most weight goes to "Existing," with meaningful residual probability on "Established" and "Hypothesized."

SETBP1 haploinsufficiency (heterozygous loss-of-function variants and 18q12.3 deletions) causes a well-characterized human neurodevelopmental disorder featuring expressive speech and language impairment, intellectual disability, ADHD, and autistic features/ASD diagnoses in a substantial subset of patients, documented across multiple independent cohorts. Large-scale exome sequencing studies of autism (e.g., Autism Sequencing Consortium/Satterstrom et al. and related de novo variant analyses) have identified recurrent de novo damaging SETBP1 variants in ASD probands at exome-wide significance, and SFARI classifies SETBP1 as a high-confidence autism gene. This human genetic evidence is replicated across independent probands, supporting the Established category, though some weight remains for Existing because ASD is a variable rather than obligate feature of SETBP1 disorder and much of the phenotypic emphasis is on speech/language and ID. Supporting mouse and neuronal model data exist but are not the primary basis for the association, so only limited weight goes to Hypothesized, and essentially none to Novel.

YLPM1 (YLP motif containing 1) has emerged in recent human exome/genome sequencing studies of neurodevelopmental disorders, with de novo and loss-of-function variants reported in probands with developmental delay, intellectual disability, hypotonia, and autistic features, including at least one multi-patient case series delineating a YLPM1-related neurodevelopmental syndrome. It has also appeared among candidate genes in large autism and developmental-disorder cohorts (e.g., ASC/DDD-type analyses), which supports human genetic evidence for a contribution to ASD-related phenotypes, though ASD itself is usually a comorbid feature rather than the primary reported phenotype. Because replication specifically for autism spectrum disorder as the core phenotype is still limited, "Existing" is the most likely category, with some probability that curators consider the accumulating human de novo variant data sufficient for "Established." A smaller share remains for "Hypothesized," reflecting the possibility that support rests mainly on its transcription-regulatory/spliceosome-associated biology and brain expression rather than robust ASD-specific case data, and minimal weight for "Novel" given documented human NDD associations.

TUBB3 is a well-established disease gene for tubulinopathies (CFEOM3, cortical dysgenesis/polymicrogyria-like malformations) in which patients frequently have intellectual disability, developmental delay and sometimes autistic features, which provides a plausible but indirect human link to ASD. Its biology—neuronal-specific beta-tubulin essential for microtubule dynamics, neuronal migration, axon guidance and cortical development—is directly relevant to neurodevelopmental mechanisms implicated in autism, strongly supporting at least a "Hypothesized" relationship. Direct genetic evidence is sparse: occasional de novo or rare TUBB3 variants have appeared in large autism exome/trio sequencing datasets and case reports of tubulinopathy patients with autistic behavior, but TUBB3 is not a high-confidence ASD gene and replication in independent ASD probands is lacking. Therefore the weight falls mainly on Hypothesized with meaningful probability for Existing, minimal for Established, and a small residual for Novel given the possibility that all co-mentions are incidental.

KCND3 encodes the Kv4.3 A-type potassium channel, and its established human disease associations are spinocerebellar ataxia 19/22, Brugada syndrome, and early-onset cerebellar ataxia with intellectual disability—phenotypes that sometimes include cognitive and behavioral abnormalities but not ASD as a core feature. The strongest ASD link in this channel family is for the paralog KCND2 (Kv4.2), where a de novo variant was reported in autism with epilepsy; KCND3 itself appears only sporadically in large ASD exome/CNV datasets and in gene lists as a low-confidence candidate, so any human genetic evidence is limited and unreplicated. The biological rationale is nonetheless strong: Kv4.3 shapes dendritic excitability and cerebellar/interneuron function, pathways repeatedly implicated in ASD, supporting a "hypothesized" classification. I therefore weight Hypothesized highest, allow meaningful probability for Existing given possible single-case or cohort reports of rare KCND3 variants in ASD probands, and assign little weight to Established since no replicated causal evidence exists.

H1-4 (HIST1H1E) frameshift variants in the C-terminal tail cause Rahman syndrome, a human overgrowth–intellectual disability disorder in which autistic features and formal ASD diagnoses are reported in a subset of probands, and de novo H1-4 variants have appeared in large human neurodevelopmental/autism sequencing cohorts (DDD, ASC/ASD trio studies). This provides credible human genetic evidence linking the gene to a phenotype closely tied to ASD, supporting "Existing." Full "Established" status is less certain because ASD is a variable secondary feature of a broader syndromic epilepsy/ID/overgrowth presentation rather than a consistently replicated primary ASD phenotype, and the gene is not a top-tier, high-confidence ASD gene. Supporting biology (chromatin/linker histone regulation of neurodevelopment, epigenetic aging signature) also fits the "Hypothesized" mechanism tier, so some weight is retained there. Very little probability is assigned to "Novel" given the documented human variant-level findings.

PPP2CA encodes the catalytic Cα subunit of PP2A, and de novo missense/loss-of-function variants have been reported in humans (notably Reynhout et al., AJHG 2019) to cause a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, hypotonia, epilepsy, and in a subset of probands autistic features/ASD diagnoses. This places PPP2CA within the PP2A-related NDD family alongside PPP2R1A and PPP2R5D, the latter being a well-recognized ASD-associated gene, supporting biological plausibility and shared mechanism. PPP2CA also appears in curated neurodevelopmental/autism gene lists with de novo variants observed in NDD/ASD sequencing cohorts, but ASD is a variable secondary feature rather than the core, replicated phenotype. Therefore the evidence is human-based and credible but not definitive for ASD causation, favoring "Existing," with some weight on "Established" (multiple probands with autistic features) and residual weight on "Hypothesized" (pathway/functional inference from PP2A biology).

EP400 encodes a large chromatin-remodeling ATPase of the NuA4/TIP60 complex, a functional class (chromatin regulators) strongly enriched for de novo variants in autism spectrum disorder. Large-scale exome sequencing efforts (e.g., Simons Simplex Collection, ASC, DDD) have reported rare de novo loss-of-function and missense variants in EP400 in ASD/neurodevelopmental probands, and it appears on candidate lists such as SFARI Gene with a suggestive (not high-confidence) score. However, EP400 is an unusually large gene with a high background mutation rate, so statistical significance has not been robustly achieved and replication in independent human cohorts is limited, precluding an "Established" designation. Thus the human genetic evidence is real but preliminary, favoring "Existing," with meaningful residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the association is judged to rest mainly on pathway/chromatin biology rather than validated variant-level findings.

KCNA2 (Kv1.2) is a well-established disease gene in humans for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE32) and episodic ataxia type 1-like phenotypes, and case series of KCNA2-related encephalopathy frequently describe intellectual disability with autistic features or formal ASD diagnoses in a subset of probands, which supports "Existing" (ASD as part of a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype). However, ASD is not a core or consistently replicated phenotype attributed to KCNA2 variants, and large ASD cohort/de novo sequencing studies have not identified KCNA2 as a genome-wide significant risk gene, so "Established" is unlikely. Strong biological plausibility exists—Kv1.2 regulates axonal excitability, neurotransmitter release, and cerebellar/interneuron function, with mouse models showing seizures and behavioral abnormalities—supporting substantial weight on "Hypothesized" if human ASD-specific reports are considered too sparse. A small residual probability remains that co-mentions are incidental and no meaningful ASD link exists.

ZNF536 encodes a brain-enriched zinc-finger transcription factor that negatively regulates neuronal differentiation, giving it strong biological plausibility for neurodevelopmental phenotypes (supporting at least a "Hypothesized" relationship). In human genetics, ZNF536 is best known for association with schizophrenia (19q13 GWAS signals, particularly in Chinese cohorts) and alcohol dependence; several ASD/neurodevelopmental sequencing and CNV studies have reported rare or de novo variants in ZNF536, and it appears in candidate-gene compilations for autism, which supports limited "Existing" evidence. However, the ASD-specific signal has not reached exome-wide significance in the large ASC/SPARK analyses, and no replicated proband/family-based causal demonstration exists, so "Established" is very unlikely. A modest probability remains that all ASD co-mentions are incidental and the gene is effectively novel for this specific phenotype.

SCAF1 (SR-related CTD-associated factor 1) is an RNA polymerase II CTD-binding splicing regulator on 19q13.33; related family members SCAF4 and SCAF8 have documented links to neurodevelopmental disorders, which lends biological plausibility for a transcription/splicing-related mechanism relevant to autism. For SCAF1 itself, I am not aware of replicated, statistically robust human genetic evidence establishing causation in ASD; at most it may appear as a rare de novo or candidate variant in large exome/whole-genome sequencing cohorts or in low-confidence candidate lists, which would support only "Existing." Because such incidental candidate-list appearances are common and often do not survive replication, substantial probability remains that the gene–phenotype link is essentially incidental (Novel). The pathway-level plausibility (CTD-associated splicing regulation, brain expression) justifies meaningful weight on Hypothesized, while Established is very unlikely given the absence of multiple independent proband/family studies.

EMC7 encodes a subunit of the ER membrane protein complex, a chaperone/insertase for tail-anchored and multipass membrane proteins; other members of this complex (EMC1, EMC10) are implicated in human neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability and occasional autistic features, which provides a plausible biological rationale rather than direct evidence. I am not aware of EMC7 being listed as an ASD risk gene in SFARI Gene, nor of replicated de novo or rare-variant findings in large autism exome/genome sequencing cohorts (ASC, SPARK, SSC). It lies at 15q14, near regions (15q13.3–15q14) with recurrent CNVs linked to neurodevelopmental phenotypes, so incidental co-mention in CNV or candidate-region papers is possible but would not constitute gene-specific evidence. Therefore most weight falls between Novel and Hypothesized, with a modest allowance for a single unreplicated human report placing it in Existing, and essentially no support for Established.

De novo missense variants in PPP2R1A are well-established causes of a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder (intellectual developmental disorder 36, Houge–Janssens syndrome) featuring intellectual disability, hypotonia, corpus callosum abnormalities, and in a subset of patients autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis, which supports at least "Existing" evidence in humans. PPP2R1A has also appeared as a de novo variant gene in large-scale exome sequencing of ASD/developmental disorder cohorts and is catalogued in autism gene resources, though it is not among the highest-confidence ASD-specific genes from cohorts such as Satterstrom/Fu. Related PP2A subunits (notably PPP2R5D) have stronger direct ASD associations, and shared PP2A biology in synaptic signaling provides plausible mechanistic support, reinforcing the hypothesized tier. Because ASD in PPP2R1A patients is typically part of a broader syndromic ID phenotype rather than replicated non-syndromic ASD, full "Established" status is less certain. Very little probability is assigned to "Novel" given the multiple human reports linking the gene to neurodevelopmental phenotypes including autistic behavior.

NR4A2 (NURR1) haploinsufficiency, via 2q24.1 microdeletions and de novo truncating/missense variants, has been reported in human patients with a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring developmental delay, epilepsy, language impairment, and in several cases autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis (e.g., Lévy et al., Singh et al., Ansari et al.). NR4A2 is also listed as a candidate gene in autism gene databases (SFARI) based on rare de novo variants identified in ASD/NDD sequencing cohorts. However, the core phenotype is a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than isolated ASD, and ASD-specific replication across independent autism probands is limited, so the evidence falls short of "Established." Strong supporting biology exists (dopaminergic neuron differentiation, midbrain development, Nurr1 knockout/heterozygous mouse behavioral phenotypes), which underpins a substantial "Hypothesized" weight, but human variant-level data justify placing most probability on "Existing."

REV3L encodes the catalytic subunit of DNA polymerase zeta, central to translesion DNA synthesis and genome stability; it is a very large gene, so it frequently appears incidentally in exome/CNV screens of neurodevelopmental cohorts, and it has been proposed as a candidate gene disrupted in Möbius syndrome (a condition with elevated autism comorbidity), which provides a weak indirect human link. However, I am not aware of REV3L being a replicated, exome-wide significant ASD risk gene in the major sequencing consortia analyses (e.g., Satterstrom/SPARK/ASC), nor of it being a high-confidence SFARI gene, so an "Established" designation is very unlikely. Evidence at best consists of isolated de novo or rare variant reports and pathway-level plausibility (DNA damage response and mutational burden in neurons), which fits "Hypothesized" or a marginal "Existing" claim. Because the human genetic evidence is sparse and possibly incidental, I split weight roughly evenly between limited human association, biological plausibility, and the possibility that co-mention is essentially incidental.

DHDDS encodes a subunit of cis-prenyltransferase involved in dolichol synthesis and N-glycosylation; biallelic K42E variants cause retinitis pigmentosa 59, while de novo missense variants (e.g., R37H, R211Q) cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, hypotonia and a hyperkinetic movement disorder (Hamdan et al., 2017 and subsequent case series). Some of these human patients are reported with autistic features or an ASD diagnosis, and DHDDS has appeared among de novo variant genes in broad neurodevelopmental/ASD sequencing cohorts, supporting "Existing" evidence via a strongly linked neurodevelopmental phenotype. However, there is no replicated, ASD-specific association across independent autism probands, so "Established" is unlikely. Substantial weight remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the mechanistic support (glycosylation, synaptic/neuronal function, mouse and Drosophila models) is non-human and the human link to autism per se is largely incidental to a broader NDD phenotype.
