FBXO11 de novo loss-of-function and missense variants have been repeatedly identified in large-scale human exome sequencing studies of autism and neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., Simons Simplex Collection/Autism Sequencing Consortium analyses), and the gene is classified as a high-confidence ASD risk gene in SFARI Gene. Gregor et al. (2018, AJHG) reported a cohort of individuals with de novo FBXO11 variants presenting intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, and behavioral abnormalities including autistic traits, establishing OMIM entry IDDFBA (#618089). These findings derive from independent human probands and have been replicated across cohorts, supporting an "Established" designation, though some ambiguity remains because the core phenotype is a broader neurodevelopmental/ID syndrome with autism as a frequent but not obligate feature, which supports substantial weight on "Existing." Animal and functional work (ubiquitin ligase substrate regulation, neurodevelopmental expression) provides mechanistic support but is not the primary basis for the association. Very little probability remains for "Novel."

SETD2 encodes the H3K36 trimethyltransferase and is a recognized chromatin-regulator gene in neurodevelopmental disorders; de novo loss-of-function and damaging missense variants have been recurrently reported in large human ASD/NDD exome sequencing cohorts (e.g., Simons Simplex Collection and Autism Sequencing Consortium analyses), and it is classified as a high-confidence ASD risk gene by SFARI. Heterozygous SETD2 variants also cause Luscan-Lumish syndrome (overgrowth, macrocephaly, intellectual disability), in which autism spectrum disorder is a frequently described feature across independent probands. This gives strong human genetic evidence, supporting an "Established" classification, though some may argue ASD is a variable feature of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than a specific, replicated ASD-causing association, warranting substantial weight on "Existing." Supportive mouse and neuronal chromatin studies add mechanistic plausibility but are not needed for the human genetic case, so only modest weight goes to "Hypothesized," and essentially none to "Novel."

LMTK3 (lemur tyrosine kinase 3/AATYK3) is a brain-enriched serine/threonine kinase involved in neuronal vesicle trafficking, neurite outgrowth, and regulation of dopaminergic/monoaminergic signaling, and Lmtk3-knockout mice exhibit hyperactivity, reduced anxiety, and abnormal social/exploratory behaviors—strong biological and animal-model support consistent with the "Hypothesized" tier. Human genetic evidence is sparse: LMTK3 has been listed among candidate genes with rare or de novo variants in some autism/neurodevelopmental exome datasets and appears in low-confidence candidate gene lists, but no replicated, well-powered human association or multiple independent probands convincingly implicate it. Because the most compelling data are murine and in vitro, most weight belongs in Hypothesized, with a moderate allowance for limited human variant reports (Existing). An Established causal role is very unlikely given the absence of replicated clinical case series, and some probability remains that co-mentions are incidental (Novel).

NCKAP1 encodes NAP1, a component of the WAVE regulatory complex controlling actin dynamics in neurons, and it emerged as a recurrent de novo loss-of-function target in large-scale ASD exome sequencing efforts (Iossifov, De Rubeis, Sanders, and the Satterstrom 2020 list of 102 ASD-associated genes, exome-wide significant). A dedicated human cohort study (Guo et al., Genetics in Medicine 2020) reported ~20 unrelated individuals with de novo or inherited NCKAP1 variants presenting with autism and/or developmental delay, providing replication across independent probands. SFARI classifies NCKAP1 as a high-confidence (category 1) ASD gene. Supporting functional and model-organism data (WAVE complex, dendritic/synaptic phenotypes) reinforce but are not the primary evidence. Remaining uncertainty reflects the still-modest number of independently reported families and variable, syndromic-leaning phenotypes, which some might judge as "Existing" rather than fully established.

PHF12 (Pf1) encodes a PHD-finger protein in the SIN3B/MRG15/HDAC chromatin-repressor complex, a class of chromatin regulators heavily enriched among autism and neurodevelopmental risk genes, giving a strong biological rationale (Hypothesized). My recollection is that PHF12 has appeared as a candidate carrying de novo or rare loss-of-function variants in large human ASD/developmental-disorder exome cohorts (e.g., Simons/ASC/DDD-type datasets) and may be listed in SFARI Gene at a low-confidence score, which would support "Existing" evidence but not replication-level proof. I am not aware of multiple independent clinical reports or a defined PHF12-related syndrome with ASD as a core feature, so "Established" is unlikely. Some probability remains that any co-mentions are incidental and the gene is essentially uncharacterized for ASD (Novel). Overall, the evidence most plausibly sits between limited human genetic association and purely mechanistic plausibility.

CACNA1A encodes the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel Cav2.1, and pathogenic variants cause episodic ataxia type 2, familial hemiplegic migraine, SCA6, and early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathy — phenotypes in which autistic features, intellectual disability, and neurodevelopmental impairment are frequently co-reported in human patients. De novo CACNA1A variants have been identified in large autism exome sequencing cohorts (e.g., Simons Simplex/ASC datasets), and the gene is catalogued in SFARI Gene, supporting more than purely biological plausibility. However, CACNA1A is not among the high-confidence, replicated ASD risk genes (unlike CHD8, SCN2A, or ADNP), and the ASD phenotype usually appears as part of a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental presentation rather than isolated autism. Calcium-channel biology and Cacna1a mouse models add mechanistic plausibility but constitute non-human support. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Established" and "Hypothesized."

XPO1 (CRM1) lies within the 2p15–p16.1 microdeletion region, a recurrent CNV associated with intellectual disability, microcephaly, and autistic features, and it has been discussed as one of the candidate driver genes (alongside BCL11A, USP34, REL) in that interval—this provides human, but non-gene-specific, association evidence. XPO1 is also highly constrained (high pLI) and occasional de novo variants have been reported in large autism/neurodevelopmental sequencing cohorts, which would support a "candidate/limited evidence" listing rather than a definitive causal gene. There is no replicated, gene-specific, multi-proband clinical evidence establishing XPO1 variants as a cause of ASD, so Established is unlikely. Substantial weight also goes to Hypothesized, since much of the rationale is biological (nuclear export of synaptic and neurodevelopmental regulators, constraint metrics, model-system data) rather than variant-level human proof. A modest Novel weight reflects the possibility that XPO1–ASD co-mentions are incidental to the CNV region and cancer literature.

ARID1A encodes a BAF (SWI/SNF) chromatin-remodeling subunit; de novo loss-of-function and missense variants cause Coffin-Siris syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which autistic features and intellectual disability are frequently reported, making it a recognized syndromic route to ASD. Human de novo variants in ARID1A have also been reported in large autism/NDD exome sequencing cohorts (e.g., Simons Simplex Collection, Autism Sequencing Consortium, DDD), and SFARI Gene lists ARID1A as a candidate ASD gene, though with weaker support than its paralog ARID1B, which is an established ASD gene. The evidence is therefore human-based and credible but the number of ASD-specific probands with ARID1A variants is modest and the phenotype is often broader NDD rather than core ASD, so "Existing" receives most weight. Some probability is retained for "Established" given replicated de novo findings across independent cohorts and syndromic overlap, and a smaller share for "Hypothesized" reflecting the strong supporting BAF-complex biology and mouse models. "Novel" is essentially excluded.

ITSN1 (intersectin-1) is a synaptic endocytosis/clathrin-mediated vesicle recycling scaffold located in the Down syndrome region of chromosome 21, giving it strong biological plausibility for neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Human genetic data exist: rare de novo and loss-of-function ITSN1 variants have been reported in autism/neurodevelopmental exome and CNV cohorts, and the gene appears among candidate ASD risk genes (e.g., SFARI-listed at a moderate, non-syndromic confidence score); recent large rare-variant burden studies (notably in Parkinson's disease) explicitly noted prior ITSN1 associations with autism. However, the evidence is not replicated at the level of high-confidence ASD genes such as CHD8 or SCN2A, and no clear gene-level exome-wide significance in independent ASD cohorts has been firmly established. Therefore "Existing" is the most likely category, with substantial residual weight on "Hypothesized" if the human variant evidence is judged too sparse and the case rests mainly on synaptic biology and model systems.

ZFHX3 (ATBF1) has emerged as a neurodevelopmental disorder gene: a recent multi-center human cohort reported dozens of individuals with de novo loss-of-function/truncating variants or 16q22 deletions encompassing ZFHX3, presenting with developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autism or autistic features in a substantial proportion. ZFHX3 also appears among candidate genes in large-scale autism/NDD exome sequencing efforts (e.g., DDD, SPARK/ASC datasets) and in SFARI-type curated gene lists, supporting replicated human genetic evidence in independent probands. Whether this rises to "Established" specifically for ASD is arguable, since autism is one feature within a broader syndromic NDD phenotype rather than the primary indication. Supporting biology (high neuronal expression, transcriptional regulation of neurodevelopment, mouse models) reinforces plausibility but is secondary to the human variant data. I therefore weight Existing slightly above Established, with modest residual probability for Hypothesized and minimal for Novel.

RAB14 encodes a small GTPase involved in endosomal/Golgi vesicular trafficking, a broad cellular process with plausible but non-specific relevance to synaptic function; other RAB family members (RAB39B, RAB11FIP5, RAB2A) have documented neurodevelopmental or autism links, but RAB14 itself is not a recognized ASD gene and does not appear among high-confidence SFARI or large-scale de novo variant discovery genes (ASC/SPARK/SSC). At most, it may appear incidentally in sequencing or CNV datasets or in network/pathway analyses of trafficking genes, which would not constitute definitive human genetic evidence. There is no replicated human evidence establishing causality, so Established is essentially excluded. The balance of probability lies between Novel (no meaningful evidence) and Hypothesized (generic trafficking biology and family-level analogy), with a small allowance for a single weak human association report.

NRXN3 belongs to the neurexin family, whose members (especially NRXN1) are strongly implicated in autism and neurodevelopmental disorders through synaptic adhesion and neuroligin/SHANK pathway biology, giving a strong mechanistic rationale. For NRXN3 specifically, there is direct human genetic evidence, most notably Vaags et al. (2012) reporting rare exonic deletions at the NRXN3 locus in ASD probands, plus additional CNV, rare-variant, and candidate-gene association reports in ASD and related neurodevelopmental/behavioral phenotypes. However, these findings involve small numbers of probands, incomplete segregation/penetrance, and inconsistent replication, and NRXN3 has not reached genome-wide significance or high-confidence status comparable to NRXN1 in large sequencing consortia. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing" (credible human but limited), with modest probability for "Established" and some weight on "Hypothesized" if one discounts the small human studies in favor of model/functional data.

De novo variants in GNB1 are a well-documented cause of a neurodevelopmental syndrome (GNB1 encephalopathy / MRD42) featuring global developmental delay, hypotonia, epilepsy, and, in a subset of patients, autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis (e.g., Petrovski et al. 2016; Hemati et al. 2018; Revah-Politi cohorts). GNB1 has also appeared among genes carrying de novo damaging variants in large autism/NDD sequencing cohorts and is catalogued in ASD candidate-gene databases, though it was not among the high-confidence exome-wide significant ASD genes in the largest ASD-specific analyses (e.g., Satterstrom 2020). Thus human genetic evidence links GNB1 variants to a broad NDD phenotype that frequently includes ASD traits, supporting "Existing" most strongly, with some possibility that curators consider the replicated multi-proband human data sufficient for "Established." Biological plausibility (G-protein β subunit in GPCR/GIRK signaling, neuronal excitability) further supports a mechanistic link, keeping "Hypothesized" nontrivial. "Novel" is very unlikely given repeated human co-occurrence reports.

CGREF1 (cell growth regulator with EF-hand domain 1, 2p23.3) is a secreted calcium-binding protein studied mainly in cell-cycle regulation and cancer contexts, with no recognized role in neurodevelopment. It is not a SFARI autism gene and I am unaware of replicated de novo or rare-variant findings implicating it in ASD; at most it could appear incidentally in large CNV or exome datasets or within a broader 2p23 deletion region, which would be weak, non-specific evidence. Some points are allotted to "Hypothesized" because calcium-signaling and EF-hand proteins are broadly relevant to synaptic and neuronal biology, providing a plausible but indirect mechanistic rationale. The bulk of probability sits on "Novel" since no credible human genetic association specific to CGREF1 and ASD is documented.

PCLO encodes Piccolo, a core presynaptic active-zone scaffolding protein, so its biology is directly relevant to the synaptic dysfunction hypothesis of autism, supporting at least a "Hypothesized" relationship. In humans, biallelic PCLO loss-of-function causes pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 3 with intellectual disability, seizures and microcephaly, and PCLO has been reported as a candidate/suggestive gene in autism exome and rare-variant studies and appears on curated ASD candidate gene lists (e.g., SFARI, with a low-confidence score), which supports "Existing" as the most probable category. However, PCLO is a very large gene prone to incidental rare variants, and it has not reached exome-wide significance in large ASD cohorts (Iossifov, De Rubeis, ASC/SPARK), so "Established" is unlikely. A modest probability remains for "Novel" if the co-mentions are judged incidental or driven mainly by its stronger association with major depressive disorder rather than ASD.

KBTBD6 encodes a BTB-Kelch protein that, with its paralog KBTBD7, acts as a CUL3 substrate adaptor targeting TIAM1 for degradation, thereby regulating Rac1 signaling, neurite outgrowth and dendritic spine morphology — a pathway directly relevant to autism, since CUL3 is a high-confidence ASD gene and Rac1/TIAM1 signaling underlies synaptic phenotypes. This provides strong biological/mechanistic plausibility, favoring the "Hypothesized" category, though much of that evidence comes from cell-based and rodent studies rather than human genetics. I am not aware of replicated human genetic findings implicating KBTBD6 variants in ASD; it is not a well-established SFARI high-confidence gene, and any occurrence would likely be as an incidental de novo variant or within 13q14 copy-number changes that encompass many genes. There remains some chance that a single de novo/rare-variant report or a CNV case series has linked it to neurodevelopmental phenotypes, which would support "Existing." "Established" is very unlikely given the absence of multiple independent proband-based confirmations.

MTOR is the central node of a pathway (TSC1/TSC2, PTEN, DEPDC5) repeatedly implicated in syndromic autism, and germline gain-of-function MTOR variants cause Smith-Kingsmore syndrome (macrocephaly/megalencephaly, intellectual disability, seizures), in which autism spectrum features are reported in a substantial fraction of independent probands. Somatic/mosaic MTOR variants also cause focal cortical dysplasia and hemimegalencephaly, brain phenotypes linked to epilepsy and neurodevelopmental impairment. De novo MTOR variants have additionally been reported in large ASD/NDD exome sequencing cohorts, and MTOR is curated in ASD gene databases such as SFARI. However, the ASD phenotype is usually part of a broader syndromic presentation with ID and megalencephaly rather than isolated autism, so some curators would consider the evidence supportive but not definitive for ASD per se. Rich supporting mouse and cellular data (mTOR hyperactivation, aberrant synaptic pruning, macrocephaly models) reinforce biological plausibility but are secondary to the human genetic findings.

PTK2 (focal adhesion kinase, FAK) is a well-studied regulator of integrin/cytoskeletal signaling, neurite outgrowth, dendritic spine morphogenesis and synaptic plasticity, and it lies downstream of pathways (e.g., ECM/integrin, PI3K–mTOR, NMDA receptor signaling) implicated in autism, so a biologically plausible, mechanism-based link is well supported—largely from rodent and in vitro work—favoring "Hypothesized." PTK2 is not an established monogenic autism gene; it is not a high-confidence SFARI gene and there is no replicated set of pathogenic variants in independent ASD probands, so "Established" is very unlikely. Some points go to "Existing" because rare de novo or CNV events involving 8q24.3/PTK2 may appear incidentally in large ASD exome/CNV datasets, and the paralog PTK2B has human neuropsychiatric association data that could be conflated, but such findings for PTK2 itself would be sparse and non-definitive. A moderate share remains for "Novel," reflecting the possibility that any co-mention is incidental with no direct human genetic evidence.

YY1 haploinsufficiency in humans causes Gabriele-de Vries syndrome (Gabriele et al., 2017, AJHG), a de novo variant neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability, developmental delay, and behavioral abnormalities that include autistic features in a subset of probands. YY1 has also appeared as a candidate in large-scale de novo variant studies of neurodevelopmental/ASD cohorts and is catalogued among autism candidate genes (e.g., SFARI), supporting a credible human genetic link. However, the core phenotype is a broader ID/NDD syndrome rather than ASD specifically, and dedicated replicated ASD-focused cohorts are limited, so "Established" for ASD proper is not fully met. Strong supporting biology (YY1 as a transcription factor/chromatin looping regulator essential for neurodevelopment, mouse models) reinforces plausibility, warranting some weight on "Hypothesized." Essentially no basis for "Novel."

Truncating variants on the paternal allele of MAGEL2 cause Schaaf-Yang syndrome (Schaaf et al., Nature Genetics 2013), which was first identified in individuals ascertained partly for autism and Prader-Willi-like features. Multiple independent human cohorts and case series (dozens of probands across several countries) have replicated the finding, with autism spectrum disorder reported in roughly 75% of affected individuals, and MAGEL2 is classified as a high-confidence/syndromic ASD gene by SFARI. The evidence is human, genetic, and replicated in independent probands, supporting the Established category. Some residual weight goes to Existing because ASD occurs as one feature of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than as isolated idiopathic autism, and because common-variant/nonsyndromic association evidence is limited. Mouse Magel2-null models showing social behavior deficits provide supporting biology but are not the primary basis for the classification.

KANSL1 haploinsufficiency (via 17q21.31 microdeletion or intragenic loss-of-function variants) causes Koolen-de Vries syndrome, a human neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism spectrum features, intellectual disability, and hypotonia are frequently reported across multiple independent cohorts. In addition, de novo loss-of-function KANSL1 variants have been recurrently identified in large-scale exome sequencing studies of autism and neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., ASC/Satterstrom-type analyses), and KANSL1 is a high-confidence SFARI autism gene. This constitutes replicated human genetic evidence, supporting "Established," though some would argue ASD is one variable feature of a broader syndromic phenotype rather than a specific KANSL1-linked outcome, which keeps meaningful weight on "Existing." Mouse and functional chromatin-regulation (NSL complex) data provide supporting mechanism but are not the primary basis, so "Hypothesized" receives little weight and "Novel" essentially none.

SMARCB1 encodes a core subunit of the BAF (SWI/SNF) chromatin-remodeling complex, a pathway repeatedly implicated in autism and neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., ARID1B, SMARCC2, SMARCA4), providing strong biological plausibility. In humans, de novo SMARCB1 variants cause Coffin-Siris syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder in which intellectual disability, developmental delay, and autistic features/ASD diagnoses are frequently reported, making it a well-recognized syndromic context linked to ASD. SMARCB1 has also appeared in SFARI Gene and in some large-scale de novo variant/exome studies of NDD cohorts that include ASD probands, but the number of probands with a primary ASD diagnosis attributable to SMARCB1 is small and not robustly replicated. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing" (credible human genetic data, largely syndromic/limited), with meaningful residual weight on "Hypothesized" (much of the mechanistic support is pathway- and model-based) and a smaller chance that curators would call it "Established" via the Coffin-Siris route.

NFIB haploinsufficiency (deletions and de novo loss-of-function point variants at 9p23–p22.2) has been reported in humans to cause intellectual disability with macrocephaly (e.g., Schanze et al., AJHG 2018), and a subset of these probands display autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis. NFIB has also appeared among de novo variant genes in large developmental-disorder and neurodevelopmental/ASD sequencing cohorts, and it is listed as a candidate ASD risk gene in curated databases. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence linking NFIB variation to a neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly overlapping ASD, but ASD itself is not the primary or consistently replicated phenotype, so the evidence falls short of "Established." Supporting biology (NFIB's role in cortical and cerebellar neurogenesis, glial differentiation, and mouse Nfib knockout brain phenotypes) reinforces plausibility and justifies residual weight on "Hypothesized." Very little probability is given to "Novel" since the gene–phenotype co-occurrence is not incidental.

PSMC5 encodes the 19S proteasome ATPase subunit Rpt6, and recent human genetics work (e.g., cohorts describing de novo PSMC5 variants causing a proteasomopathy/neurodevelopmental disorder with developmental delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphism and immune dysregulation) reports autistic features in a subset of probands, which supports at least "Existing" evidence and links PSMC5 to a phenotype strongly associated with ASD. However, these reports are recent, involve small numbers of patients, and ASD is a secondary rather than the primary described phenotype, so replicated causal evidence specifically for Autism Spectrum Disorder is lacking, making "Established" unlikely. Substantial weight remains on "Hypothesized" because much of the mechanistic rationale comes from proteasome biology, synaptic protein degradation (Rpt6 phosphorylation in synaptic plasticity), and rodent/in vitro work, and because other proteasome genes (PSMD12, PSMC3) are the better-documented NDD/ASD links. "Novel" retains only modest weight given the plausible but not incidental biological and clinical connections.

LEMD3 (MAN1) is an inner nuclear membrane protein and antagonist of BMP/TGF-β signaling whose loss-of-function variants cause osteopoikilosis, Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome, and melorheostosis — skeletal/skin phenotypes with no established neurodevelopmental component. It is not a recognized autism risk gene in large sequencing consortia or SFARI high-confidence lists, and I am unaware of replicated case–control or de novo variant evidence linking it to ASD. Some weak, non-gene-specific support could come from 12q14 microdeletion syndrome, which spans LEMD3 and HMGA2 and includes developmental delay and occasionally autistic features, but the neurodevelopmental phenotype is generally attributed to other genes in the interval (e.g., HMGA2, GRIP1). Biological plausibility exists through BMP/TGF-β signaling and nuclear envelope function in neurodevelopment, supporting a modest hypothesized weight. Overall, the evidence best fits "Novel," with some probability mass allotted to "Existing" (contiguous-gene deletion cases) and "Hypothesized."

SYT1 (synaptotagmin-1) encodes the principal presynaptic calcium sensor for fast synchronous neurotransmitter release, making it highly plausible biologically for synaptic neurodevelopmental disorders. De novo missense variants in SYT1 in humans cause Baker–Gordon syndrome (SYT1-associated neurodevelopmental disorder), characterized by global developmental delay, hyperkinetic movement disorder, ophthalmic abnormalities, and behavioral features that in several probands include autistic traits or a formal autism diagnosis, and SYT1 appears in curated autism gene resources. However, ASD is a variable, secondary feature rather than the core, replicated phenotype, and large ASD exome/GWAS studies have not independently established SYT1 as an autism risk gene. This supports "Existing" (human genetic evidence linking SYT1 variants to a neurodevelopmental phenotype that overlaps/includes autism) more than "Established." Some probability remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the mechanistic support comes from mouse and in vitro synaptic-release studies rather than ASD-specific human association.

CHD7 is the established cause of CHARGE syndrome, a human condition in which autistic features/ASD diagnoses are common (reported in roughly 15–50% of patients), making it a well-recognized syndromic context strongly linked to ASD. In addition, de novo loss-of-function and damaging missense CHD7 variants have been reported in probands from large ASD exome-sequencing cohorts (Simons Simplex Collection, Autism Sequencing Consortium/ASC-DDD analyses), and CHD7 is annotated in SFARI Gene as a high-confidence/syndromic ASD gene, alongside its chromatin-remodeler paralogs CHD8 and CHD2. This constitutes credible, human, partially replicated genetic evidence, though CHD7 variants more consistently produce CHARGE/developmental delay phenotypes than isolated ASD, and gene-level statistical significance for ASD specifically is less definitive than for CHD8. Supporting mouse and neural-progenitor functional work (Chd7 in neurogenesis, cerebellar development, social behavior) reinforces biological plausibility but would only justify "Hypothesized" on its own. Therefore the weight falls mainly on "Existing," with substantial probability for "Established."

MAP1A encodes a microtubule-associated protein highly expressed in neurons and involved in dendritic/axonal cytoskeletal organization and synaptic scaffolding (interactions with CASK, neurobeachin, and postsynaptic complexes), giving it strong biological plausibility for neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Large-scale exome sequencing efforts in ASD cohorts (e.g., Simons Simplex/ASC studies) have reported rare de novo and damaging missense/LoF variants in MAP1A, and the gene appears in candidate gene resources such as SFARI Gene with only suggestive-level scoring, supporting "Existing" rather than "Established" evidence. There is no replicated, statistically robust exome-wide significance or multiple independent families establishing causation, so "Established" is unlikely. A substantial share of remaining weight goes to "Hypothesized," since much of the support is derived from expression, pathway/interactome data, and mouse cytoskeletal studies rather than definitive human genetic association.

GABBR2 encodes the GABA-B receptor subunit 2, and de novo variants in this gene are established causes of neurodevelopmental disorders (Rett-like syndrome, epileptic encephalopathy/EIEE59) that frequently include autistic features, and de novo missense variants have been reported in ASD probands in large exome sequencing cohorts, with the gene appearing in SFARI's autism gene list. Human postmortem studies (e.g., Fatemi and colleagues) also show altered GABA-B receptor subunit expression in autistic brain, and GABAergic signaling imbalance is a leading mechanistic hypothesis for ASD, supporting strong biological plausibility. However, evidence specifically linking GABBR2 variants to idiopathic ASD as a discrete phenotype is limited to a small number of de novo events and candidate-gene association findings rather than robust, replicated statistical or segregation evidence. Therefore "Existing" is most appropriate, with meaningful weight on "Hypothesized" (biology/expression/animal data) and only modest weight on "Established."

GSE1 (16q24.3) encodes a component of the BRAF35/HDAC (CoREST) chromatin-remodeling complex, a pathway repeatedly implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, and it lies near ANKRD11 in a region where microdeletions are linked to intellectual disability and autistic features. Human case reports and small cohorts describe de novo/heterozygous loss-of-function GSE1 variants in patients with developmental delay, speech impairment, ADHD and autistic traits, which supports at least "Existing" evidence, though the number of independent probands with a formal ASD diagnosis is limited and ASD is not the core phenotype. The evidence has not reached the level of multiple independent, replicated clinical studies establishing GSE1 variants as a cause of ASD specifically, so "Established" receives modest weight. A substantial share remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the support is biological (chromatin regulation, brain expression, animal/functional data) or derived from contiguous-gene deletions where causality is ambiguous. "Novel" is unlikely given the gene's inclusion in neurodevelopmental gene panels and candidate ASD gene lists.

PTPRT encodes a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase of the type IIB (LAR-like) family that is highly expressed in brain and regulates synapse formation and dendritic arborization, making it biologically plausible for ASD, and related family members (e.g., PTPRD) have documented neurodevelopmental associations. Human genetic support is limited but present: rare/de novo missense and loss-of-function variants in PTPRT have been reported in large ASD exome sequencing cohorts, and the gene appears in autism gene curation resources (e.g., SFARI) with only suggestive/low-confidence scoring. No replicated, well-powered family or case series has demonstrated that PTPRT variants cause ASD, so "Established" is unlikely. Much of the supporting evidence is functional/animal (knockout mouse synaptic and behavioral phenotypes), which supports "Hypothesized" as a strong alternative. Therefore probability is concentrated between Existing and Hypothesized, with little weight on Novel given the clear biological and sporadic genetic co-occurrence.

CAMK2A is a well-documented human neurodevelopmental disorder gene: de novo missense variants (e.g., Küry et al. 2017 AJHG; Stephenson et al. 2017; Chia et al.) cause intellectual disability (MRD53) with frequent autistic features, and CAMK2A variants have been reported in large autism/NDD exome cohorts, giving it a listing in the SFARI gene database. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence linking the gene to ASD-related phenotypes, supporting at least "Existing," with a reasonable share for "Established" since multiple independent probands/families exist—though most are primarily ID/NDD cases with ASD as a comorbid feature rather than ASD-specific replicated causation. Substantial supporting evidence also comes from Camk2a mouse models showing social and repetitive behavior deficits and from synaptic plasticity/pathway biology, which alone would only warrant "Hypothesized." Given the mix of strong human variant data with imprecise ASD-specific attribution, most weight falls on "Existing," with meaningful probability on "Established" and residual weight on "Hypothesized."

JARID2 (6p22.3), a PRC2 accessory subunit, has human genetic evidence linking haploinsufficiency to neurodevelopmental disease: 6p22–p24 microdeletions encompassing JARID2 were reported in patients with intellectual disability and autistic features, and a multi-patient cohort study (Verberne et al., Genetics in Medicine, 2021) described de novo JARID2 truncating variants and deletions causing a distinct neurodevelopmental syndrome in which autism/autistic behaviors are a frequent feature. JARID2 is also catalogued in SFARI Gene, and de novo variants have appeared in large ASD/DD sequencing datasets. However, ASD is typically a comorbid feature of a broader ID/dysmorphism syndrome rather than an isolated, replicated ASD phenotype, so the evidence is credible and human-based but not definitive for ASD specifically. Supporting chromatin-regulation biology and mouse Jarid2 neurodevelopmental models add mechanistic plausibility but would only justify "hypothesized" on their own.

CHAMP1 (ZNF828) de novo truncating variants are a well-replicated cause of a neurodevelopmental disorder (CHAMP1 disorder) characterized by intellectual disability, hypotonia, severe speech impairment, and frequently autism or prominent autistic features, reported across multiple independent human cohorts (e.g., Hempel et al. 2015, Isidor et al. 2016, Tanaka et al. 2016, and later phenotypic series). CHAMP1 has also been recovered as a de novo mutated gene in large autism/developmental-disorder sequencing studies (DDD, SSC/ASC exome analyses) and is included in curated autism gene resources such as SFARI Gene. The main ambiguity is whether ASD is a core causal phenotype or a frequent comorbid feature of a broader ID/NDD syndrome, which keeps substantial weight on "Existing" rather than fully on "Established." Evidence is human-genetic rather than only functional/animal, so little weight goes to Hypothesized, and essentially none to Novel.

CAPRIN1 encodes an RNA-binding protein that partners with FMRP and G3BP1 in neuronal RNA granules and stress granules, giving strong biological plausibility for a role in neurodevelopment. Human genetic evidence exists: Pavinato et al. (Brain, 2022) reported a series of unrelated individuals with heterozygous loss-of-function/de novo CAPRIN1 variants presenting a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring language impairment, ADHD, intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder in a substantial subset, and additional de novo variants have been noted in large autism/NDD sequencing cohorts (leading to SFARI gene listing). This constitutes multiple independent human probands, supporting an Established or near-Established causal role, though ASD is one component of a broader NDD phenotype rather than the exclusively replicated outcome, which tempers full confidence. Supporting functional and knockout-mouse data reinforce but are not the primary basis for the human association, so only modest weight goes to Hypothesized and essentially none to Novel.

EGR3 is an activity-dependent immediate-early transcription factor whose biology (synaptic plasticity, activity-regulated gene programs shared with ARC, BDNF, MEF2, and regulation by/of neurodevelopmental factors) is highly relevant to autism pathophysiology, and altered EGR-family expression has been reported in postmortem brain and in rodent models of neurodevelopmental disorders — this supports a strong "Hypothesized" weighting. Direct human genetic evidence for EGR3 is concentrated in schizophrenia (Japanese and other case–control association studies), not autism, and I am not aware of replicated ASD-specific variant associations or recurrent de novo/rare damaging EGR3 variants in large ASD sequencing cohorts. There may be isolated candidate-gene or expression-based reports touching on ASD, which leaves modest probability for "Existing," but nothing approaching established causality. EGR3 is not on high-confidence ASD gene lists (e.g., SFARI high-scoring categories), so "Established" is very unlikely, while a small chance remains that any co-mention is incidental ("Novel").

DSCAM (21q22.2) has been repeatedly identified in large-scale human exome sequencing studies of autism, with recurrent de novo loss-of-function and damaging missense variants in independent probands (e.g., Iossifov et al., De Rubeis et al., Sanders et al., Satterstrom et al. 2020), and it is classified as a high-confidence (SFARI category 1) ASD risk gene meeting genome-wide FDR thresholds. This supports either "Established" or strong "Existing" status, with the ambiguity arising because the evidence is statistical enrichment of de novo variants across cohorts rather than classical Mendelian segregation in families, and carriers often show variable phenotypes including intellectual disability and epilepsy. Supporting biology is also strong—DSCAM encodes a neural cell adhesion molecule critical for axon guidance, dendrite self-avoidance, and synaptogenesis, and Dscam mutant mice show social and behavioral abnormalities—but this animal/functional evidence only reinforces the human genetic findings rather than substituting for them. There is essentially no basis for classifying the relationship as Novel.

KMT2D (MLL2) is the major cause of Kabuki syndrome, a human developmental disorder in which autistic features and formal ASD diagnoses are frequently reported, making it a recognized syndromic ASD gene. De novo loss-of-function and damaging missense variants in KMT2D have been identified in probands from large autism sequencing cohorts (e.g., Simons Simplex Collection, ASC/De Rubeis and related exome studies), and the gene appears on the SFARI Gene list as a syndromic/candidate ASD gene. Evidence is therefore human-based and replicated across multiple independent cohorts, favoring Established or Existing; however, ASD is typically one feature of a broader neurodevelopmental syndrome rather than an isolated, definitively attributed phenotype, and KMT2D has not reached genome-wide exome significance for ASD as robustly as genes like CHD8 or SCN2A. Supporting chromatin-remodeling biology and mouse models add mechanistic plausibility but are secondary to the human genetic data. Hence probability mass is concentrated on Existing with substantial weight on Established.

TLE3 encodes a Groucho/TLE family transcriptional corepressor that partners with FOXG1, TCF7L2, HES/Notch effectors and NR2F/RUNX factors — pathways strongly implicated in cortical neurogenesis and in recognized ASD/neurodevelopmental genes — giving a solid biological rationale for a hypothesized link. I am not aware of any replicated human genetic studies establishing TLE3 variants as a cause of ASD; it is not among the high-confidence ASD genes from large exome consortia (e.g., Satterstrom/Fu lists). There may be sporadic de novo or rare variant reports in ASD/developmental-disorder cohorts and inclusion in candidate gene panels or 15q23 CNV discussions, which would support limited "Existing" evidence, but I cannot recall a definitive single credible association study. Consequently, most weight falls on Hypothesized, with meaningful probability for Existing, some chance the relationship is purely incidental (Novel), and very little for Established.

UBR5 encodes a HECT-domain E3 ubiquitin ligase, a gene class (like UBE3A, HUWE1, HERC2) repeatedly implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, giving strong biological plausibility. De novo and rare loss-of-function UBR5 variants have been reported in large exome sequencing cohorts of neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., DDD/ASD trio studies), and a recent multi-proband series described heterozygous UBR5 variants causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome with developmental delay, speech impairment and autistic features, supporting at least "Existing" human genetic evidence. However, ASD is typically a secondary/variable feature rather than the primary reported phenotype, and UBR5 has not reached genome-wide significance as an ASD risk gene in the major ASD exome analyses, so "Established" specifically for ASD is less likely. Substantial probability remains for "Hypothesized" if the strongest support derives from pathway membership, brain expression, and model-organism data rather than replicated human ASD-specific findings. Very little weight goes to "Novel" given multiple credible co-occurrence reports.

EFTUD2 encodes a core U5 snRNP spliceosomal GTPase, and heterozygous loss-of-function variants/deletions at 17q21.31 cause mandibulofacial dysostosis with microcephaly (Guion-Almeida type), a syndrome consistently featuring microcephaly, developmental delay and intellectual disability, with autistic features/ASD diagnoses reported in a subset of patients — a well-recognized syndromic route to ASD, supporting "Existing." De novo EFTUD2 variants have also appeared in large developmental-disorder/neurodevelopmental exome cohorts, though EFTUD2 is not a robustly replicated primary ASD risk gene in dedicated autism sequencing studies (e.g., not a high-confidence ASD gene in ASC/SPARK analyses). Zebrafish and mouse models show neural crest and neurodevelopmental defects and impaired splicing/p53 activation, providing biological plausibility that underpins a "Hypothesized" contribution. Because direct, replicated human genetic evidence linking EFTUD2 specifically to ASD (rather than to syndromic ID/microcephaly with autistic traits) is limited, "Established" receives little weight, and complete absence of any logical link ("Novel") is also unlikely but retains some probability.

TRIM8 is an established human disease gene for a distinct neurodevelopmental disorder—epileptic encephalopathy with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis—caused by de novo truncating variants in the last exon, and affected individuals frequently show global developmental delay, intellectual disability, and behavioral features that can include autistic traits, which supports at least limited human evidence linking TRIM8 to an ASD-related phenotype. However, TRIM8 is not a well-replicated, primary ASD risk gene; it does not appear as a high-confidence ASD gene with multiple independent ASD probands carrying damaging variants, so "Established" is unlikely. Some de novo variant reports from broad developmental disorder/NDD sequencing cohorts may include children with autistic features, giving partial support for "Existing." Its biology (regulation of STAT3, TAK1/NF-κB, p53 signaling, and expression in brain) provides a plausible mechanistic rationale, favoring "Hypothesized" as a strong alternative. A small residual probability remains that the gene–ASD link is essentially incidental.

LRRC4 encodes NGL-2, a postsynaptic leucine-rich repeat adhesion molecule that binds netrin-G2 and PSD-95 and regulates excitatory synapse development, placing it squarely in the synaptic-adhesion pathway (neuroligins, neurexins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs) repeatedly implicated in autism. The strongest direct evidence is from mouse work: Lrrc4/Ngl-2 knockout mice display autistic-like social and repetitive behaviors that respond to NMDAR modulation, which supports the "Hypothesized" category rather than human genetic proof. LRRC4 also maps to 7q31–32, within the classic AUTS1 autism linkage region, and paralogs such as LRRC4C (NGL-1) have human deletion/variant evidence in ASD, but such paralog and locus data do not establish LRRC4 itself. Some rare or de novo variants may have been reported in ASD sequencing cohorts or curated in SFARI-type databases, giving modest weight to "Existing," but replicated human causal evidence is lacking, so "Established" is very unlikely. Given the clear mechanistic and animal-model relevance, a fully "Novel" classification is also improbable.

ADGRB1 (BAI1) is a brain-enriched adhesion GPCR with strong synaptic biology directly relevant to ASD: it is a MEF2 target, binds MAGI/PSD-95 scaffolds and the ELMO/DOCK180-Rac pathway, and Bai1 knockout mice show dendritic spine, synaptic plasticity, and behavioral deficits — this alone justifies substantial weight on "Hypothesized." In humans, rare de novo and rare inherited/biallelic ADGRB1 variants have been reported in autism and neurodevelopmental disorder cohorts, and the gene appears on candidate ASD gene lists (e.g., SFARI), which supports "Existing," though such reports are few and often in mixed NDD phenotypes. Evidence falls short of "Established," since there is no large set of independent probands with replicated, statistically robust exome-wide significance for ASD specifically. "Novel" is very unlikely given the extensive mechanistic and candidate-gene literature linking this gene to synapse development and autism-related pathways.

HNRNPD (AUF1) is an RNA-binding protein of the hnRNP family, several members of which (HNRNPU, HNRNPH2, HNRNPK, HNRNPR, HNRNPUL2) are firmly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders including autism, making a biologically plausible, pathway-level case for HNRNPD involvement in mRNA stability and neuronal gene regulation. However, unlike those paralogs, HNRNPD has not been established as an autism gene: I am not aware of replicated clinical reports or a defined HNRNPD-related neurodevelopmental syndrome. Sporadic de novo or rare variants in HNRNPD may appear in large ASD exome/SPARK-type datasets or low-confidence SFARI-type curations, which would support only limited "Existing" evidence. The bulk of support is therefore indirect (family membership, expression in brain, potential FMRP-target/RBP network overlap), favoring "Hypothesized," with some residual probability that essentially no relevant evidence exists ("Novel").

RALGAPB encodes the beta subunit of the Ral GTPase-activating protein complex and has appeared as a candidate risk gene in large-scale exome sequencing studies of autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, where recurrent de novo loss-of-function/missense variants have been reported in probands (e.g., Simons Simplex/ASC cohorts), and it is catalogued in SFARI Gene as a lower-confidence candidate. This supports human genetic evidence that is credible but not yet definitively replicated across multiple independent clinical cohorts with well-characterized phenotypes, favoring the "Existing" category. It falls short of "Established" because there is no clearly delineated RALGAPB-associated syndrome with multiple independent families and functional validation. Some probability remains for "Hypothesized" (support largely from Ras/Ral signaling biology and statistical enrichment rather than confirmed causal variants) and a smaller chance that the association is essentially incidental/underpowered ("Novel").

MEIS2 haploinsufficiency (point variants and 15q14 microdeletions) causes a well-described human neurodevelopmental syndrome with intellectual disability, speech delay, cleft palate and cardiac defects, and several reported patients display autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis. De novo MEIS2 variants have appeared in large developmental disorder and autism/NDD sequencing cohorts, and the gene is catalogued among candidate ASD risk genes (e.g., SFARI-type curation), which supports human genetic evidence at the "Existing" level. However, ASD is not a consistent or defining outcome of MEIS2 variants, and the number of independent probands with rigorously ascertained autism is small, so "Established" causality specifically for ASD is not supported. Supporting biology—MEIS2 is a TALE homeobox transcription factor important in forebrain and striatal/GABAergic interneuron development, with relevant mouse models—also justifies substantial weight on "Hypothesized." Very little probability is assigned to "Novel" given the clear neurodevelopmental phenotype overlap.

SCN8A is a well-known neurodevelopmental disease gene (developmental and epileptic encephalopathy type 13, intellectual disability, movement disorders), and autistic features/ASD diagnoses are frequently reported among patients with pathogenic SCN8A variants. Human genetic evidence includes de novo and inherited SCN8A variants identified in ASD/neurodevelopmental sequencing cohorts (e.g., the Trudeau et al. family with a truncating variant and an autistic proband, and de novo variants in large autism exome studies), and SFARI curates SCN8A as an autism candidate gene with suggestive-to-strong evidence. However, most ASD presentations occur in the context of broader epileptic encephalopathy or intellectual disability rather than isolated, replicated ASD causation, so the evidence falls short of "Established" by strict criteria. Supporting mouse Scn8a models and channel-biology/E-I balance data further motivate the link but count toward hypothesized rather than human evidence.

ZBTB7A (LRF/Pokemon, 19p13.3) has been implicated in a human syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder: a 2022 cohort report described de novo loss-of-function and missense variants causing developmental delay, macrocephaly, obesity, and behavioral problems, with autistic features/ASD diagnoses in a subset of probands. De novo variants in ZBTB7A have also appeared in large NDD/autism sequencing datasets (DDD, ASC-type cohorts), and the gene is highly loss-of-function intolerant, supporting a candidate role, and it is listed among SFARI candidate genes at a modest confidence score. However, the evidence for ASD specifically is secondary to a broader NDD phenotype and has not been replicated in multiple independent ASD-focused studies, so "Established" for autism per se is unlikely. Substantial residual probability goes to "Hypothesized," since much of the supporting mechanistic work (transcriptional repression, chromatin/BTB-ZF biology, mouse models) is non-human and the human ASD link may be judged indirect. "Novel" is small but nonzero given the recency and limited literature.

MAF (16q23) is best known in human genetics for de novo missense variants in its transactivation domain causing Ayme-Gripp syndrome (congenital cataract, sensorineural hearing loss, intellectual disability, seizures, distinctive facies) and for isolated cataract; phenotype-expansion reports of Ayme-Gripp have noted behavioral abnormalities and occasionally autistic features, which provides limited, non-definitive human evidence linking MAF variants to a syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype that can include ASD traits. MAF is not, to my knowledge, a well-supported autism risk gene in large exome/genome sequencing studies (e.g., ASC/SPARK/SSC) nor a high-confidence SFARI gene, so an "Established" causal role for ASD is unsupported. Biologically, large Maf transcription factors participate in neuronal differentiation, sensory/lens and interneuron development, giving a plausible but indirect mechanistic rationale, supporting a substantial "Hypothesized" weight. A meaningful probability remains for "Novel," since any co-mention of MAF with ASD may be incidental to its cataract/ID syndrome rather than reflecting a specific autism association.

SLTM (SAFB-like transcription modulator) has been reported in recent human genetic studies of neurodevelopmental disorders, with de novo and loss-of-function variants described in cohorts of individuals presenting developmental delay, intellectual disability, and autistic features, and it has appeared among candidate genes in large-scale autism/NDD exome sequencing efforts. This supports at least "Existing" evidence, since autism is typically a component feature of the broader SLTM-related neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than the primary replicated diagnosis. Whether the evidence rises to "Established" specifically for Autism Spectrum Disorder is uncertain, as the published case series emphasize a syndromic NDD rather than isolated ASD, so some probability is retained there. A smaller share goes to "Hypothesized," reflecting the gene's plausible biology (transcriptional/RNA regulation, broad neuronal expression) if human variant evidence is judged insufficient. "Novel" is unlikely given the documented human variant reports.

PSMD12 haploinsufficiency (de novo truncating variants and microdeletions) was shown by Küry/Stankiewicz and colleagues (AJHG 2017) to cause Stankiewicz–Isidor syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder featuring intellectual disability, developmental delay, and autistic features/ASD in a subset of the multiple independent human probands reported. Subsequent case series expanded the cohort and confirmed autism or autistic traits as a recurrent component of the phenotype, and PSMD12 is listed as an ASD-associated gene in curated databases (e.g., SFARI), partly from de novo variants identified in large ASD/NDD sequencing studies. Thus there is clear human genetic evidence linking PSMD12 variants to a syndromic phenotype that includes ASD, though ASD is not fully penetrant and PSMD12 is best characterized as a broader neurodevelopmental gene rather than a specific, replicated ASD-causing gene. This supports strong weighting toward "Existing," with substantial probability for "Established" given multiple independent probands, and little support for "Novel."

GNAI1 (G protein subunit alpha i1) has emerged from large-scale human exome sequencing of autism cohorts, notably being included among the ~102 ASD-associated genes identified by the Autism Sequencing Consortium (Satterstrom et al., 2020) based on recurrent de novo damaging variants, and it carries a high-confidence SFARI gene score. Additional human case series (e.g., Muir et al., 2021) describe de novo GNAI1 missense/loss-of-function variants causing a neurodevelopmental syndrome with developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures, and autistic features, providing independent proband-level support. This constitutes credible, replicated human genetic evidence, though most reports frame the phenotype as a broader neurodevelopmental disorder in which ASD is one variable feature rather than a specific, well-delineated GNAI1–autism syndrome. Supporting biology (Gi signaling in neurons, GPCR modulation of synaptic transmission) reinforces plausibility. Therefore most weight falls on Existing, with substantial weight on Established and a smaller residual for Hypothesized.

GSK3B is a well-studied node in Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/AKT/mTOR and FMRP-related signaling, pathways strongly implicated in autism, and GSK3 inhibition (e.g., lithium) rescues phenotypes in Fmr1-knockout and other ASD mouse models — this animal/pathway-level evidence supports a strong "Hypothesized" weighting. There are a few small human candidate-gene/expression studies (e.g., promoter variant rs334558 and altered GSK3B protein/activity or expression in blood of ASD children) suggesting association, which justifies meaningful weight on "Existing," though these are underpowered, mostly non-replicated, and not supported by large ASD exome/GWAS datasets. GSK3B is not a recognized high-confidence ASD risk gene in SFARI or de novo variant studies, so "Established" is very unlikely. "Novel" is nearly excluded because the biological relevance is direct and extensively discussed rather than incidental.

TOP3B lies in the distal 22q11.2 region, and human studies (e.g., Stoll et al., Nat Neurosci 2013) reported rare TOP3B deletions enriched in individuals with schizophrenia and cognitive/neurodevelopmental impairment, with some cases including autism or autistic features; additional rare variant reports in neurodevelopmental cohorts exist. These human genetic findings are suggestive but modest in size, incompletely replicated for ASD specifically, and often confounded by larger CNVs encompassing neighboring genes, so the evidence falls short of established causality. Strong supporting biology comes from non-human work: TOP3B is an RNA topoisomerase that complexes with FMRP (the fragile X protein, a major ASD gene) to regulate synaptic mRNAs, and Top3b-knockout mice/Drosophila show synaptic and behavioral abnormalities—this supports Hypothesized rather than Existing. Overall, the balance favors "Existing" with substantial weight on "Hypothesized," and little support for "Established" or "Novel."

DIP2C lies within the 10p15.3 region, and terminal deletions of this region (typically encompassing both ZMYND11 and DIP2C) have been reported in patients with intellectual disability, developmental delay, and autistic features (e.g., DeScipio et al. and subsequent case series), providing human but non-gene-specific evidence. Most of the causal weight in that interval has been attributed to ZMYND11, an established ASD/ID gene, so DIP2C's independent contribution remains uncertain; a few de novo or rare variants in DIP2C have been noted in autism sequencing cohorts without convincing replication or statistical support. Biologically, DIP2C is highly expressed in brain and belongs to the DIP2 family (DIP2A has itself been implicated in autism/dyslexia-related phenotypes), giving a plausible mechanistic rationale. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing" (limited, non-definitive human association, largely via CNVs) with substantial probability for "Hypothesized" if the gene-level human variant evidence is judged insufficient, and little support for "Established."

SPPL3 encodes a Golgi-resident intramembrane aspartyl protease that regulates glycosyltransferase shedding and thus cellular glycosylation; it is not a recognized autism risk gene and does not appear among high-confidence SFARI/exome-derived ASD genes, so an "Established" causal role is very unlikely. Weak, indirect human evidence could exist through 12q24.31 deletions (a region containing SETD1B, a bona fide neurodevelopmental/ASD gene) that also encompass SPPL3, or through incidental de novo/rare variant reports in large ASD sequencing cohorts, which would only support a limited "Existing" claim. Biologically, glycosylation defects and Golgi protease activity are plausible neurodevelopmental mechanisms (congenital disorders of glycosylation frequently feature autistic traits), and SPPL3 is expressed in brain, providing a reasonable "Hypothesized" pathway link, though largely from in vitro and mouse work rather than human genetics. Given the absence of any well-known, replicated human genetic association specific to SPPL3, most probability mass belongs to "Novel" with substantial weight to "Hypothesized."

De novo missense variants in TRAF7 are established as causing a multisystem developmental disorder (CAFDADD: cardiac, facial, digital anomalies with developmental delay; Tokita et al. 2018 and subsequent cohorts), in which developmental delay and intellectual disability are core features and autistic features/ASD diagnoses have been reported in a subset of patients. This provides human genetic evidence linking TRAF7 variants to a neurodevelopmental phenotype strongly related to ASD, supporting "Existing," and TRAF7 has appeared in some large NDD/autism sequencing datasets. However, ASD is not a consistent or defining feature of TRAF7-related disorder, and there is no replicated, ASD-specific association across independent autism cohorts, so "Established" is unlikely. Some weight remains for "Hypothesized," since much of the mechanistic support (MEKK3/MAP kinase and NF-κB signaling roles in neural development) is functional or non-human, and a small residual probability for "Novel" reflects the possibility that ASD co-mentions are incidental to the broader syndromic delay.

FBXW7 encodes the substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase with well-documented roles in neural progenitor proliferation, neuronal differentiation, and degradation of substrates such as NOTCH and cyclin E, giving strong biological plausibility for neurodevelopmental involvement. In humans, de novo loss-of-function and missense FBXW7 variants have been reported in a cohort-defined neurodevelopmental disorder (developmental delay, hypotonia, intellectual disability), with autistic features/ASD diagnoses in a subset of probands, and FBXW7 has appeared among de novo variants in large autism/NDD sequencing studies. This constitutes credible human genetic evidence linking the gene to an ASD-related neurodevelopmental phenotype, but ASD is not the core or consistently replicated presentation, so the evidence falls short of "Established" for autism specifically. Some weight remains on "Hypothesized" because much mechanistic support comes from mouse and cellular models rather than ASD-specific human association studies, and a small residual on "Novel."

ACTG1 (cytoplasmic gamma-actin) is a well-established human disease gene for Baraitser–Winter syndrome 2 and autosomal dominant deafness (DFNA20/26); Baraitser–Winter cases frequently include intellectual disability and, in some reports, autistic features, which supports a link to a broader neurodevelopmental phenotype rather than ASD specifically. Rare de novo missense variants in ACTG1 have been reported sporadically in large autism/NDD exome sequencing cohorts, and the gene appears in curated autism gene resources (e.g., SFARI) at a lower evidence tier, but it has not reached exome-wide significance in ASD-specific analyses such as Satterstrom or Fu et al. Biologically, actin cytoskeleton dynamics are central to neuronal migration, dendritic spine formation, and synaptic plasticity, providing a strong mechanistic rationale, and mouse/in vitro models show cortical and synaptic phenotypes. Overall, the human genetic evidence is suggestive and limited rather than replicated for ASD as a primary phenotype, so "Existing" is most probable, with substantial weight on "Hypothesized" given that much supporting evidence is mechanistic or from syndromic/animal contexts.

GABRA4 lies within the 4p12 GABA-A receptor gene cluster and has been directly tested in human autism association studies, most notably Ma et al. (2005, AJHG), which reported significant SNP association with autism and epistatic interaction with GABRB1, with partial replication by Collins et al. (2006) in AGRE families and additional candidate-gene reports (including studies noting interaction with autism-related epilepsy phenotypes and some Asian cohorts). These are human genetic data, so the evidence exceeds purely biological/animal plausibility, supporting "Existing." However, the findings are common-variant candidate-gene associations with inconsistent replication, no genome-wide significance, and no clear set of causal rare variants in independent probands, so "Established" is unlikely. A modest share remains for "Hypothesized," reflecting the strong but non-genetic supporting rationale of GABAergic excitatory/inhibitory imbalance in ASD and animal/expression data, in case the human association literature is judged too weak.

NACC1 is best known for a recurrent de novo missense variant (p.Arg298Trp) causing a severe neurodevelopmental syndrome with epilepsy, cataracts, microcephaly, feeding difficulties and delayed myelination (Schoch et al., AJHG 2017), in which stereotypies and autistic features are frequently described among affected human probands. Additional de novo loss-of-function/missense variants in NACC1 have been reported in large neurodevelopmental and autism sequencing cohorts, and the gene appears on curated autism candidate gene lists (e.g., SFARI), supporting a credible but not definitive human genetic link to ASD. Because the core phenotype is syndromic intellectual disability/epilepsy with autism as an accompanying feature rather than replicated ASD-specific causation, "Existing" receives the most weight. Some probability remains for "Established" given multiple independent human probands with autistic phenotypes, and for "Hypothesized" since NACC1's role as a BTB/POZ transcriptional repressor in neuronal chromatin regulation provides strong biological plausibility that could be the main basis of the link.

SRSF1 encodes a core SR-family splicing factor, and a 2023 human genetics report (AJHG, Bogaert et al.) described a cohort of individuals with de novo loss-of-function/missense SRSF1 variants causing a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder in which autism spectrum disorder or autistic features were present in a substantial subset of probands. This provides credible human evidence linking SRSF1 variation to ASD as part of a broader NDD phenotype, supporting at least the "Existing" category and arguably "Established" for NDD. However, replication across multiple independent clinical studies specifically for ASD as the primary phenotype is still limited, and ASD is a variable feature rather than the defining outcome. Additional support comes from strong biological plausibility—splicing dysregulation and SR protein function are recurrent themes in ASD pathophysiology, and SRSF1 interacts with other ASD-related RNA-binding proteins—which underpins the residual "Hypothesized" weight. Very little probability is assigned to "Novel" given the direct human variant data.

BCR (breakpoint cluster region, 22q11.23) is best known for the BCR-ABL fusion in leukemia, but it also encodes a RhoGAP/Rac1 regulator expressed in brain, and Bcr/Abr double-knockout mice show altered Rac1 signaling, dendritic spine abnormalities, and hippocampal/cognitive and behavioral deficits — biology directly relevant to autism-related synaptic pathways, which supports a "Hypothesized" classification. Its location near the distal 22q11.2 low-copy-repeat region means it can be included in rare distal 22q11 CNVs associated with neurodevelopmental phenotypes, and it occasionally appears in large-scale autism exome/CNV gene lists, giving some weak, non-specific human genetic support. However, BCR is not a SFARI high-confidence autism gene, and I am not aware of replicated human studies demonstrating that BCR variants cause or are robustly associated with ASD, so "Established" is very unlikely. Some probability remains for "Novel" since much of the supporting evidence is murine or pathway-level rather than variant-based in humans.

RANBP2 (Nup358) is best established as the gene for autosomal dominant acute necrotizing encephalopathy type 1 (ANE1), a febrile infection–triggered encephalopathy that can leave neurological sequelae, but it is not a recognized autism gene and is not among the high-confidence ASD risk genes emerging from large exome studies (ASC, SSC, SPARK). Because RANBP2 is an extremely large gene, rare de novo or inherited variants are occasionally reported incidentally in ASD/neurodevelopmental cohorts, so a limited "Existing"-type report cannot be excluded, but no replicated, statistically supported human association exists. Biologically, RANBP2 is plausibly relevant: nucleocytoplasmic transport, SUMOylation, kinesin-mediated mitochondrial and mRNA trafficking in neurons, and roles in neuronal development and axon growth, with mouse/in vitro data supporting neurodevelopmental function — this supports a "Hypothesized" relationship. Given the weak and mostly indirect literature, points are concentrated in Hypothesized and Novel, with modest weight to Existing and essentially none to Established.

ZBTB18 (ZNF238/RP58) is a well-characterized neurodevelopmental gene: de novo loss-of-function and missense variants cause autosomal dominant intellectual disability (MRD22), and haploinsufficiency contributes to the 1q43-q44 deletion phenotype with microcephaly and corpus callosum anomalies. Several affected individuals in these human case series are reported with autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis, and the gene appears in ASD/neurodevelopmental de novo variant datasets and curated autism gene lists (e.g., SFARI), supporting at least "Existing" evidence in humans. However, ASD is typically a secondary feature of a broader ID/DD syndrome rather than a replicated, gene-specific autism phenotype, so "Established" is less likely. Strong supporting biology (RP58 role in cortical neurogenesis, neuronal migration, and mouse models with brain phenotypes) provides an additional hypothesized-level basis, and outright novelty is improbable given repeated human co-reporting.

De novo truncating variants in the terminal exons (5–6) of PPM1D cause Jansen–de Vries syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability/developmental delay in which autism spectrum disorder or prominent autistic features are reported in a large proportion of the described probands. These variants were originally identified through large-scale human exome studies of developmental disorders and autism cohorts (e.g., DDD and ASD trio sequencing), with subsequent multi-patient case series (Jansen et al. and later cohorts) replicating the phenotype in independent individuals. PPM1D is accordingly listed as a high-confidence gene in autism gene curation resources such as SFARI. The main uncertainty is whether ASD is a core causal outcome versus a frequent comorbid feature of a broader syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype, which keeps meaningful probability on "Existing." Purely biological/animal-model evidence (Wip1 phosphatase, p53/DNA damage signaling) is secondary to the human genetic data, so little weight goes to Hypothesized or Novel.

HSF2 (heat shock transcription factor 2, 6q22.31) has well-documented roles in corticogenesis, neuronal migration, and neural progenitor behavior, and Hsf2-null mice show brain malformations and behavioral abnormalities, plus HSF2 mediates responses to prenatal stressors such as hyperthermia and alcohol — biology that is directly relevant to neurodevelopmental disorder risk. This supports a strong "Hypothesized" weighting. However, I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies implicating HSF2 variants in autism; it is not a recognized high-confidence ASD gene (e.g., not prominent in SFARI/large de novo sequencing gene lists), so "Established" is very unlikely. There is some possibility that HSF2 appears as a candidate in a rare-variant, CNV (6q22 deletion), or expression-based ASD study, which leaves modest weight on "Existing." Given the plausible but largely animal/mechanistic basis, remaining probability is split between "Hypothesized" and "Novel."

ZCCHC14 (16q24.2) is a highly constrained, broadly brain-expressed zinc-finger protein best characterized as a partner of the TENT4A/B non-canonical poly(A) polymerases in RNA tailing/stability (notably in hepatitis B virus biology), not as a recognized neurodevelopmental disease gene. It is not among the high-confidence ASD genes from large exome studies (e.g., Satterstrom/ASC, SPARK) and is not, to my knowledge, a well-scored SFARI gene, so an "Established" classification is very unlikely. It is plausible that isolated de novo or rare variants in ZCCHC14 have been reported in ASD/NDD proband sequencing tables or in 16q24 CNV cases, which would support a limited "Existing" claim, but I cannot recall a specific credible human genetic association study. Its high mutational constraint, neuronal expression, and role in post-transcriptional mRNA regulation—a pathway class enriched in ASD risk genes—provide a reasonable biological rationale, favoring "Hypothesized." Given the uncertainty about whether any human variant-level report exists, I split the weight mainly between Hypothesized and Novel, with meaningful probability for Existing.

INTS6 (formerly DDX26/DICE1) is primarily characterized as a 13q14 candidate tumor suppressor and a subunit of the Integrator complex involved in snRNA 3' processing and RNA polymerase II pause-release; it is not a recognized autism gene and, to my knowledge, is not a scored SFARI gene. Other Integrator subunits (INTS1, INTS8, INTS11) have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability and sometimes autistic features, which provides a plausible pathway/biological rationale for INTS6 involvement, supporting some weight on "Hypothesized." Direct human genetic evidence—replicated de novo or rare variants in ASD probands—is not something I can recall from large exome/CNV studies, though incidental single de novo variants in large ASD cohorts cannot be excluded, leaving modest weight on "Existing." Given the absence of any replicated clinical or family-based causal data, "Established" is very unlikely, and the largest share belongs to "Novel," with substantial probability retained for a purely mechanistic/pathway-based link.

KIF1A is a firmly established human disease gene for KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (NESCAV/MRD9, SPG30, HSAN2C), with de novo missense variants causing intellectual disability, spasticity, neuropathy and often neurodevelopmental/behavioral features. Autistic features and formal ASD diagnoses have been reported in subsets of KIF1A variant carriers, and de novo KIF1A variants have been detected in large autism/neurodevelopmental exome sequencing cohorts (e.g., Simons Simplex/ASC datasets), leading to its inclusion among candidate ASD risk genes in curated databases such as SFARI Gene. However, ASD is not the primary or consistently replicated phenotype, and evidence is largely from case series and broad NDD cohorts rather than dedicated, replicated autism-specific studies, so the association falls short of "Established." Supporting biology (axonal transport of synaptic vesicle precursors, dendritic/synaptic development, mouse models with behavioral deficits) provides mechanistic plausibility, justifying residual weight on "Hypothesized." Very little support exists for "Novel," given the human genetic co-occurrence data.

GNAO1 encodes Gαo, and de novo pathogenic variants are firmly established as causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (EIEE17) and neurodevelopmental disorder with involuntary movements — severe neurodevelopmental phenotypes in which autistic features/ASD diagnoses have been described in a subset of patients. GNAO1 is included in autism gene resources (e.g., SFARI Gene) at a suggestive-evidence level, based largely on rare de novo variants identified in NDD/ASD sequencing cohorts and case reports, which supports "Existing" rather than "Established" for ASD specifically. The causal, replicated human evidence points primarily to epilepsy/movement disorder rather than to ASD as a core, reproducibly demonstrated outcome, so the strict "Established" criterion is likely not met. Strong biological plausibility (Gαo is highly abundant in neurons, mediates G-protein-coupled signaling, synaptic transmission, and neurite outgrowth; mouse models show behavioral abnormalities) also supports at least a "Hypothesized" relationship, leaving little weight for "Novel."

ZNF644 is best established as a Mendelian gene for autosomal dominant high myopia (MYP21), not for neurodevelopmental disease. Its biology is nonetheless highly relevant to ASD: it is a zinc-finger component of the G9a/GLP (EHMT1/EHMT2) histone methyltransferase complex, a chromatin-regulatory pathway strongly tied to autism and intellectual disability (EHMT1/Kleefstra syndrome; the paralogous complex partner WIZ has recently been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders), which supports a "Hypothesized" mechanistic link. There may be sporadic de novo or rare loss-of-function ZNF644 variants reported in large ASD/developmental-disorder exome cohorts or candidate lists, which would justify limited "Existing" evidence, but I am not confident such reports are replicated or curated at high confidence. There is no replicated multi-proband clinical evidence establishing ZNF644 as a cause of ASD, so "Established" receives minimal weight, and some probability remains that co-mentions are incidental.

CERT1 (formerly COL4A3BP) encodes the ceramide transfer protein, and recurrent de novo missense variants (notably around p.Ser132) were first identified in human intellectual disability cohorts (Deciphering Developmental Disorders) and later characterized in a multi-patient series showing a neurodevelopmental disorder with disrupted sphingolipid homeostasis, in which several probands displayed autistic features or a formal ASD diagnosis. The gene has also appeared in autism/NDD de novo variant datasets and curated autism gene resources, supporting a human genetic link, though ASD is typically part of a broader syndromic ID phenotype rather than an isolated, replicated ASD association. This makes "Existing" the most probable category, with some chance that curators consider the multiple independent probands sufficient for "Established." Supporting mechanistic and mouse/cellular sphingolipid work would only justify "Hypothesized" if the human variant evidence were discounted, and outright "Novel" is unlikely given the documented human de novo variants.

MKX (Mohawk homeobox) is best characterized as a transcription factor governing tendon and ligament development, intervertebral disc homeostasis, and mesenchymal lineage specification, with no established role in neurodevelopment. It is not a recognized autism risk gene (e.g., not among high-confidence SFARI/ASC/SPARK genes), and I am not aware of replicated human genetic studies linking MKX variants to ASD. At most, it could appear incidentally in large exome/CNV datasets (e.g., 10p12 rearrangements) or in broad transcriptomic/network analyses, which would be weak, non-definitive support at best. Because it is a homeobox transcription factor expressed during embryogenesis, a purely biological/pathway-based hypothesis is conceivable, so some weight goes to Hypothesized, but the bulk of probability rests on Novel.

PLXNA1 encodes a plexin-A semaphorin co-receptor central to axon guidance, neuronal migration and synaptic development, making it biologically plausible for neurodevelopmental phenotypes; related family members (PLXNA4, PLXNB1) have been implicated in autism and schizophrenia, and Plxna1 mouse models show neurodevelopmental/behavioral abnormalities, which supports at least a "Hypothesized" level. In humans, mono- and biallelic PLXNA1 variants have been reported in a neurodevelopmental disorder with variable cerebral and ocular anomalies, developmental delay, and autistic features, and rare de novo/likely gene-disrupting variants have appeared sporadically in large ASD and NDD sequencing cohorts. However, PLXNA1 does not reach exome-wide significance in the major ASD gene discovery studies (e.g., Satterstrom et al.), and no replicated ASD-specific case series exists, so "Established" is unlikely.
